- **The secure build: `npm run build-secure`** (`c80c9315`; new `webpack.secure.js`, `scripts/secureStubs.js`, `scripts/secureClientEnv.js`, `scripts/auditBundleEgress.js`, `scripts/secure-egress-allowlist.json`, `scripts/secure-server-allowlist.json`, `src/secureFlags.js` and 23 stubs under `src/secureStubs/`; `isSecureBuild` in `src/configUtils.js`; `src/envUtils.js`, `src/index.js`, `src/CustomManagerMenus.js`, `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`, `src/CClientNLU.js`, `src/nodes/WindSources.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayWindField.js`, `webpackCopyPatterns.js`, `scripts/auditBundleSecrets.js`, `Dockerfile.release`, `test-all-builds.js`, `package.json`; new `docs/dev/Secure-Build.md`; `tests/secureStubs.test.js`, `secureClientEnv.test.js`, `envUtilsSecureRatchet.test.js`, `auditBundleEgress.test.js`, `auditBundleSecrets.test.js`). A production server build written to `dist-secure/` with every outbound feature removed at compile time, for a hardened deployment on an isolated network: a site that runs its own server, saves through it, and must contact nothing else. It reuses the full server build (`sitrecServer/` and all), so the result is a normal install behind a web server with PHP. **Stubs.** `secureStubs.js` maps 23 originals to inert stand-ins that keep the originals' export sets: the startup geolocation lookup, menu-click and tile-usage telemetry, the local compute bridge, the direct model client and the provider key store, dialog, catalogue and provider list, the voice session, the sky-mask client, the three live-feed modules, the forum-thread, source-video and records importers, the aircraft trace and live fetchers, the sounding fetcher, the photorealistic-tiles authentication, the street-level panorama node, and the OCR loader (the library fetches its worker and language files from a public CDN by default). `webpack.secure.js` applies the map with `NormalModuleReplacementPlugin` in its afterResolve phase rather than `resolve.alias` — an alias key is matched against the request as written, so an absolute key would never match a relative import — and rebases the stub's `context` so its own relative imports resolve beside the stub. The build warns if the map is absent (nothing stubbed, said loudly), fails if a named stub file does not exist, and reports any map entry it never resolved. Each stub leaves a `__SITREC_SECURE_STUB__:<Module>` marker in the bundle and appends it to `globalThis.__SITREC_SECURE_STUBS__`. **Forced settings.** `secureClientEnv.js` merges `shared.env.example` under the live `shared.env`, blanks every sensitive key by the serverless build's `isSensitiveEnvKey` rule, forces `IS_SECURE_BUILD=true` and the seven security flags to `false` — `CHATBOT_ENABLED`, `SITREC_TRACK_STATS`, `LOG_UI_INTERACTIONS`, `SITREC_ENABLE_DEFAULT_MAP_SOURCES`, `SITREC_ENABLE_DEFAULT_ELEVATION_SOURCES`, `SITREC_ENABLE_DEFAULT_TLE_SOURCES`, `USE_S3_PRESIGNED_URLS` — and embeds only the settings the container entrypoint's `CLIENT_VARS` block forwards to the page (plus any `SITREC_CUSTOM_MAP_*` / `SITREC_CUSTOM_ELEVATION_*`), read from `docker/entrypoint.sh` at build time, so a server-only value never lands in the bundle as a literal. Deliberately not forced: `SAVE_TO_SERVER`, `SAVE_TO_S3`, `SETTINGS_SERVER_ENABLED` — the server decides where a file may go. **The ratchet.** `getEnv()` in `src/envUtils.js` — in this build only; `process.env.IS_SECURE_BUILD` is a DefinePlugin constant, so elsewhere the branch is dead code — ignores a runtime `window.__SITREC_ENV__` value that is a sensitive key, or that would set a security flag the build forced to `"false"` to anything else, so an override can tighten but never loosen. `src/secureFlags.js` mirrors the flag list for the bundle (scripts are not bundled), and `tests/secureClientEnv.test.js` fails if the two copies drift. **Gates.** Modules with other work to do are gated on `isSecureBuild` instead of stubbed: the help menu's *External Links* folder and the configured `extraHelpFunctions`, *Google Maps Here* in the ground context menu (entry and handler both), the wind field's weather lookup (`fetchOpenMeteoUV` throws and `WIND_SOURCES` drops the `openmeteo` option at its one definition), the place-name geocoder in the command box (`_geocodeAndGoto` returns an error result), the startup approximate-location call, and the visit counter. **Audits**, run by `postbuild-secure` and `npm run audit-secure-bundle`: `auditBundleSecrets.js --mode=secure` (a `SERVER_SHAPED_MODES` member: `sitrecServer/` and the guarded `shared.env.php` are expected, and no credential may appear anywhere else, the two client-public keys included), then `auditBundleEgress.js`, which extracts every `http(s)://host` literal from the emitted `.js`, `.mjs`, `.html`, `.css` and `.json` (skipping rendered docs, `tools/`, `data/`, `sitrecServer/vendor/` and `tests/`) and fails unless each host is classified in `secure-egress-allowlist.json` as `inert` (never a request; `mayReceive` must be `["none"]`), `link` (a click the user starts; must state what it carries) or `gated` (must name a compile-time gate: `isSecureBuild` or one of the forced flags) — a host the application would actually contact is never an entry of any class. It also fails on any `.map` file or `sourceMappingURL=`, a stub marker missing from the output, an original host surviving, a gated literal without a gated entry, a server file outside `secure-server-allowlist.json`, a required server file missing, or a packaged `config.php` without the `AUTH_MODE` seam. `webpackCopyPatterns.js` turns every `sitrecServer/` file not on the server allow-list into an ignore pattern for this build only (left out: every endpoint that fetches from a public provider, the assistant relays and their logs, the diagnostics pages, the telemetry writers), always packages the tracked `config/config.php.example` — warning when it skips a checkout's own `config.php` — and does not copy the `tests/` tree. `Dockerfile.release` takes `--build-arg DIST_DIR=dist-secure` so the secure output packages with the standard image; `test-all-builds.js --config=secure` serves `dist-secure` with `php -S`; `npm run build-secure-debug` is the unminified variant with eval source maps, audited with `--allow-source-maps` and never the deployed artifact. `docs/dev/Secure-Build.md` describes all of this, how to check the artifact in a real browser (one request origin, the stub list, thumbnails via `s3-proxy.php`), and what is still to come: mirror data sources, gates on the menu entries of stubbed features, and an automated browser-level proof. The response-header policy it listed as missing is supplied by the deployment module below.

- **A Terraform module for a hardened AWS deployment** (`be40bfeb`, with the fixes from the first live rehearsal in `94d3d70f`; new `deploy/aws/` — `network.tf`, `storage.tf`, `registry.tf`, `edge.tf`, `compute.tf`, `iam.tf`, `observability.tf`, `variables.tf`, `outputs.tf`, `providers.tf`, `versions.tf`, `README.md`, `rehearsal.tfvars.example`, `target.tfvars.example`, `rehearsal-scp.json`, `.terraform.lock.hcl`; `.gitignore`). The shape `docs/dev/Installing-Hardened-Sitrec-on-AWS.md` describes, as code. Network: a VPC with two private task subnets and two public balancer-only subnets, an internet gateway routed from the public subnets only, **no NAT gateway**, a gateway endpoint for S3 and interface endpoints for `ecr.api`, `ecr.dkr`, `logs`, `secretsmanager` and `ssmmessages` (`bedrock-runtime` behind `enable_bedrock_endpoint`); the task's security group admits 8080 from the balancer only and lets out only HTTPS to the endpoints and S3. Storage: four buckets (`data`, `mirror`, `truststore`, `logs`) with public access blocked, versioning on and bucket-owner enforced; customer-managed KMS keys on the first three and S3-managed keys on `logs`, which the log delivery services require; the delivery policies for balancer logs, flow logs and the trail; and an object-level deny on the data bucket for any request not through the VPC endpoint or from `admin_role_arn` (listing and configuration stay under IAM, so the deploying identity can still manage the bucket). A registry with immutable tags, scan on push and its own key. Edge: an ACM certificate validated by DNS when `route53_zone_id` is set (plus the alias record), otherwise an imported `certificate_arn`; a trust store built from the operator's CA bundle with an optional revocation list, both uploaded by Terraform; a listener with `mutual_authentication { mode = "verify" }`, CA-name advertisement on, a TLS 1.3 policy (the FIPS variant when `fips` is true), inserted `Strict-Transport-Security`, `X-Frame-Options`, `X-Content-Type-Options` and `Content-Security-Policy` headers, `xff_header_processing_mode = "remove"`, invalid header fields dropped, and both access and connection logs on. Compute: an ECS cluster, a task definition (user 1000, port 8080, init process, awslogs) carrying the hardened environment — `AUTH_MODE=cert`, the header source, a trusted-proxy list derived from the balancer subnets, the trust file paths, `S3_CREDENTIAL_SOURCE=role`, `S3_READS_VIA_SERVER`, chat and telemetry off, the default data sources off, `LOCAL_DOCS=true` — with `task_environment` merged over it for the operator's own values, the image pinned by digest (a tag is refused by validation), and a service in the private subnets with no public address and ECS Exec behind `enable_exec`. The execution and task roles, a log group with `log_retention_days`, VPC flow logs and a trail with S3 data events for the data bucket. Every ARN, service principal and endpoint name is built from the `aws_partition`, `aws_caller_identity` and `aws_region` data sources, so no `.tf` file names a region or a partition and the module applies unchanged in any partition; the two example variable files name a commercial rehearsal region and placeholders respectively, and a filled-in `.tfvars`, plan, state and lint snapshots are gitignored. It deliberately does not build or push the image, hold deployment-specific values, stage mirror data, or open the task's egress beyond the endpoints. The first live rehearsal (`94d3d70f`) — the module applied in a commercial region, as `rehearsal.tfvars.example` and section 12 of the guide lay out, with the guide's verification table run and the observed results written back into it — fixed four things: the task now pulls by the registry's standard hostname (`local.registry_host`), because with FIPS endpoints on the provider's `repository_url` names the FIPS hostname, which the registry interface endpoint does not resolve inside the network — the failure looked like a pull timeout followed by the deployment circuit breaker rolling back; one revocation entry per CRL, since the balancer refuses a file holding more than one, so `local.crls` splits a concatenated `crl_path` bundle with `regexall` into `crl-<n>.pem` objects and one `aws_lb_trust_store_revocation` each; the default `csp` now allows `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` for the decoders and `style-src 'unsafe-inline'` for the control-panel library's injected stylesheet — without them the page rendered unstyled and the decoders failed — while scripts stay same-origin only with no inline allowance, which is what the entrypoint change below makes possible; and an `allow_destroy` variable (default `false`) sets `force_destroy` on the buckets and `force_delete` on the repository so a rehearsal can be torn down, while a real deployment refuses. `rehearsal-scp.json` records the guard-rail deny policy used for the rehearsal (the resource families an isolated deployment never uses, NAT gateway creation, and account or billing changes) as the reference boundary for the deploying role. The image must be built for the `X86_64` the task declares — `--platform linux/amd64` on an ARM machine, or the task stops with "exec format error".

- **Partition lint for the deployment module** (`be40bfeb`, corrected in `547e35e9`; new `deploy/aws/lint/partition-lint.mjs`, `refresh-services.mjs`, `README.md`; `npm run lint-partition`; a `partition_lint` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`; `tests/partitionLint.test.js`, 16 tests). The proof that the module stays partition-neutral. Static checks, run by CI on every push over `deploy/aws`, `sitrecServer`, `src` and `docker` with comments stripped: an `arn:aws:` literal anywhere fails; an `amazonaws.com` literal fails in `.tf` and `.tfvars` and is informational elsewhere (the PHP and JavaScript parse and build commercial S3 URLs on purpose, with tests); a region name in `.tf` or `.tfvars` fails (the `.tfvars.example` files are exempt, since they show what to fill in); and a `resource` of a forbidden family (`aws_cloudfront_*`, `aws_apprunner_*`, `aws_amplify_*`, `aws_lightsail_*`, `aws_nat_gateway`) fails. Plan checks, for an operator before an apply: every `resource_changes[].type` is mapped through `RESOURCE_SERVICE_MAP` to a service code and checked against a snapshot of the target region's services, which `refresh-services.mjs` fetches through the AWS CLI from the public global-infrastructure parameters (queryable only from a commercial region); a snapshot names the target, so `deploy/aws/lint/snapshots/` is gitignored and never committed; an unmapped `aws_*` type is a named warning so the map can grow. `547e35e9` fixed the plan checks' premise: they compared every ARN against the commercial prefix and every hostname against `--region`, so a plan made in a rehearsal account could never pass. `planContext()` now reads the plan's own `aws_partition` and `aws_region` data sources, and `plan-arn-partition` and `plan-endpoint-region` flag only a value that differs from them — which is exactly a hard-coded partition or region — with a warning when a plan carries no `aws_partition` source at all. `isGeneratedOrLocal()` keeps `plan.json`, `*.tfplan`, `*.tfstate*` and a real `*.tfvars` out of the static scan, since those legitimately hold one account's ARNs and region; the load-balancer service code is `elb`, as the infrastructure parameters name it (the earlier `elasticloadbalancing` would never have matched a snapshot); and the report line says which partition and region a plan was made in.

### Improvements

- **Error hints: the likely cause when a tile or a shared situation fails to load** (`9a02a6ae`; new `src/errorHints.js` — `tileLoadHint()`, `customSitchLoadHint()`, `resetTileLoadHints()`; `src/QuadTreeMapTexture.js`, `src/QuadTreeTileMaterial.js`, `src/index.js`; `tests/errorHints.test.js`, 12 tests; noted in `docs/dev/Secure-Build.md` and the hardened guide). An error that says only "HTTP 404" sends a first-time tester of a self-hosted deployment into the code. The helpers turn the facts the code already has — which source, which address, what the server answered — into a sentence about the likely cause and what to do, in the words of the settings involved. For a tile: a 404 on a `/sitrec-terrain/` address names the directory, the container mount point `/var/www/html/sitrec-terrain`, `SITREC_TERRAIN_URL` and `scripts/download_local_tiles.js`; a same-origin 404 says the tile path does not exist; a remote 404 points at the URL template (`{z}/{x}/{y}` order and extension) and the maximum zoom (`SITREC_CUSTOM_MAP_<NAME>_URL` and `_MAX_ZOOM`); 401 and 403 at a key that is missing, blank or expired, or an origin the provider does not allow; the follow-on "ServiceUnavailable" errors, raised after a source is marked unavailable for the session, point back at the first failure above them in the console; and a network error (`Failed to fetch` and its relatives) at no route from an isolated network and the mirror settings. The secure build adds one sentence about its disabled providers. For a shared situation (`?custom=`): a 404 inside `/sitrec-upload/` is explained as scratch storage emptied when a container was replaced or restarted, with `SAVE_TO_S3` or a volume at `/var/www/html/sitrec-upload` as the fix; any other 404 as a stale, mistyped or deleted link; 401/403 as a refusal, adding for a same-origin link that under client certificate authentication the request must carry the certificate; a network error as no route. Wired into the texture error dialog (`showErrorOnce` in `QuadTreeMapTexture`, which fires only on development hosts via `isLocal`), the `console.warn` in `QuadTreeTileMaterial` (every build — the console is the only place a production build reports it), and both `showError` paths for the custom situation in `index.js`. One hint per source and kind of failure per page (`hintsGiven`), so a tile flood does not repeat it; the helpers never throw and every call site wraps them anyway. The module has no imports and reads `IS_SECURE_BUILD` at compile time, so it is testable without the application. The author verified it in a container started without its tile directory: the console carried the new text (the `/sitrec-terrain/` case above, which names that container's mount point).

- **The container entrypoint writes its runtime settings as an external script, not an inline one** (`926dc744`; `docker/entrypoint.sh`; `tests/dockerEnvCRLF.test.js`). The entrypoint used to inject `<script>window.__SITREC_ENV__=…</script>` into `index.html`, which a page policy of `script-src 'self'` refuses — an inline script needs `'unsafe-inline'`. It now writes `sitrec-runtime-env.js` beside `index.html` (delete-and-recreate, as for the HTML) and references it as `<script src="sitrec-runtime-env.js?v=<start time>">`; the query string changes every start so a cached copy of a previous container's settings is never used. The test now asserts the tag shape, that the HTML carries no `window.__SITREC_ENV__`, and that the file's JSON is valid.

- **SitrecBridge 1.0.62 attaches on sitrec.work hosts** (`836e37d8`; `tools/SitrecBridge/extension/manifest.json`). The manifest matched only the local and metabunk hosts; `https://*.sitrec.work/*` is added to `host_permissions` and to both content-script `matches` lists, covering the bare host and its subdomains.

### Bug Fixes

- Fixed every elevation tile failing under a Content-Security-Policy that lacks `'unsafe-eval'` (`8da59d65`; `src/js/get-pixels-mick.js`). `ndarray` compiles a constructor per shape with `new Function`, which such a policy refuses, so on a hardened deployment — whose balancer sets exactly that policy — no elevation tile could decode. The tile decoders (`computeElevationFromRGBA*` in `QuadTreeTile.js`) read only `shape` and `data`, so a new `pixelBuffer(data, shape, stride)` returns a plain `{data, shape, stride, offset: 0}` in the same layout (`shape` `[height, width, 4]`, `stride` `[4 * width, 4, 1]`). Nothing else in `src/` imported the library; the `package.json` dependency is left in place. Maintainer note: the rationale comment above the CSP meta tag in `webpack.common.js` still says `ndarray` is what forces `'unsafe-eval'` — that reason is gone, and only OpenCV's `'wasm-unsafe-eval'` remains; the meta tag itself sets no `script-src`, so no build's behaviour changes.

- Fixed the *AI Model*, *Voice Model* and *Enable old AI models* controls (Settings) reading "Loading..." forever on a site with the assistant off, and every page load asking the server for a model list it does not have (`ce1a3fc0`; `src/CustomSupport.js`; `docs/dev/Secure-Build.md`). With `CHATBOT_ENABLED` false the chat view is never built and there are no models to list, so the three controls are now created only when `getEnvBool("CHATBOT_ENABLED")` is true; `chatModelController` and `voiceModelController` stay `null`, which `updateChatModelSelector()` and `updateVoiceModelSelector()` already return on. `fetchAvailableChatModels()` returns an empty list without the request, which used to be a 404 from `chatbot.php?fetchModels=1` (a hardened deployment omits the file altogether) followed by a JSON parse error in the console.

### Documentation

- **Installing Hardened Sitrec on AWS** (`docs/dev/Installing-Hardened-Sitrec-on-AWS.md`; `8043459a`, updated in `9a02a6ae`, `be40bfeb` and `94d3d70f`; linked from the README beside the other deployment guides and from the install guide's production section; listed with `Secure-Build.md` in the `tests/docsRegistry.test.js` exemptions, so neither appears in the in-app Help menu). The secure build behind an application load balancer in mutual-TLS verify mode, a private bucket reached with the task role over FIPS endpoints, no route to the internet, and every setting named. It opens with a status table of what exists and what is planned, gives the build, registry, storage, load balancer, task-definition and verification steps with commands, describes the commercial-region rehearsal including the certificate path on a development machine with nginx, and ends with a maintenance table saying which sections to update when a named file changes — written for a person doing the deployment and for an agent maintaining it. The rehearsal added the image-architecture snag, the pull hostname, the rationale for each allowance in the response policy (8.1), one CRL per revocation file (8.2), the trail fields that prove FIPS endpoints are in use, and the connection-log failure reasons in the verification table; `be40bfeb` pointed its status table, section 8 and section 12 at the module and the lint.

- `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md` gains "Object storage in another partition or with role credentials" (the five `S3_*` settings, and a note in the Kubernetes secret section that a role-bound service account needs no secret at all), "Client certificate authentication" (the settings table, the two certificate sources, the mapping file, the refusal reasons, and what the proxy still owns), the `npm run build-secure` row, and a pointer to the hardened guide (`8043459a`). `docs/dev/FileRehosting.md` describes `getS3Client()` and `s3ObjectUrl()` (`3b1bbc13`). `docs/dev/Secure-Build.md` is new (`c80c9315`; error-hint and assistant-off notes in `9a02a6ae` and `ce1a3fc0`). `deploy/aws/README.md` and `deploy/aws/lint/README.md` document the module and the lint (`be40bfeb`, `547e35e9`, `94d3d70f`).

## Version 2.147.3 (2026-09-02)

### New Features

- **Shift + mouse wheel changes the field of view in every view** (`b023bcb6`, `1dc37054`; `src/js/CameraControls.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeCamera.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeControllerPTZUI.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeControllerVarious.js`; documented in the Main View list of `docs/UserInterface.md`). The look view's wheel already zoomed the field of view, because a PTZ controller drives that camera. The main view's wheel moves the camera instead, and so does the look view's once *Free Look Camera* has suspended the PTZ controller, so in those two views there was no way to reach the field of view from the mouse at all. The wheel handler now takes the FOV branch when `event.shiftKey` is set **or** `getInteractivePTZController()` returns one, and calls a new `zoomFovBy(delta)`; the old `zoomBy()` delegates to it in the PTZ case and dollies otherwise. Under a PTZ controller Shift therefore changes nothing, since the plain wheel is already that. `zoomFovBy` writes through the PTZ controller whenever the camera has one — found with `getPTZController`, not `getInteractivePTZController`, so this includes a controller Free Look has suspended: that controller owns `fovUI`, and the camera's `fovController` re-reads `fovUI` every frame, so a write straight to `camera.fov` would be undone on the next update. The main camera has no PTZ controller and nothing writes its fov per frame, so that one is set directly (`camera.fov` + `updateProjectionMatrix()`; `CNodeCamera.modSerialize` saves it from there). The gesture also had to be read correctly: a Shift+wheel arrives as a **horizontal** scroll — the browser moves the value into `deltaX` and leaves `deltaY` at 0 — so `Math.sign(event.deltaY)` was 0, `zoomScale` returned the fov unchanged, and the gesture reached the right code and silently did nothing. A `wheelDelta` now falls back to `deltaX` only while Shift is held, because an unmodified `deltaX` is a genuine horizontal swipe and must not be taken for a zoom; the fisheye branch was dead for the same reason and is fixed with it, and the dolly paths keep reading `deltaY`, which Shift never reaches. The follow-up `1dc37054` guards the direct write on a new `CNodeCamera.hasFOVController()` — true when any enabled controller input carries `isFOVController` — because a look camera can hold an FOV controller instead of a PTZ one: the code comments name Porterville and MISB (fov from the camera track) and Jellyfish (focal-length keyframes). On those the direct write was undone by the very next controller pass, so the gesture did nothing while appearing to be supported. Now it is dropped rather than fought: such a field of view is a measurement of what the real camera did, and overriding it would silently de-sync the look view from the video beside it, the same rule `applyHandoffLookFraming` states in `index.js`. A camera under a PTZ controller never reaches the guard. Verified in the browser: on the main view `hasFOVController` is false and Shift+wheel moves the field of view 30 → 27.78 → 30; on the MISB look view it is true and the value does not change at all — no write, rather than a flicker that settles.

- **A public serverless copy of Sitrec on GitHub Pages**, https://mickwest.github.io/Sitrec2/ (`9a65d352`, `a3300d99`; new `.github/workflows/pages.yml`; `src/nodes/CNodeTerrainUI.js`, `src/configUtils.js`, `webpack.common.js`, `webpackCopyPatterns.js`, `site.webmanifest`, `config/shared.env.example`, `SERVERLESS.md`). The serverless build was already a browser-only Sitrec — no PHP, no accounts, no server-side file hosting, every provider key blanked by `buildServerlessClientEnv()`. What it could not do was run from a static host that publishes one directory and nothing above it. Three things blocked it. **Terrain:** `filterSourcesForServerless()` drops every source not marked `allowInServerless`, leaving "Local", whose tiles come from `../sitrec-terrain/` — a sibling of the app directory that such a host cannot serve — and serverless builds forced `"Local"` as the default map and elevation type regardless of configuration. `CNodeTerrainUI` now reads `DOCKER_MAP_TYPE` / `DEFAULT_MAP_TYPE` (and the elevation pair) in serverless too, with "Local" only as the final fallback, so a deploy can name a `SITREC_CUSTOM_*` source, which does carry the flag; `pickAvailableSourceType()` still falls back to "Local" when the configured default was stripped, so no existing install changes. A new `SITREC_TERRAIN_URL` overrides the Local tile path in `setupConfigPaths()` for a deploy that ships its own mirror. **Icons:** see the Bug Fixes entry below. **The secret audit:** see the `EXAMPLEKEY` entry under Bug Fixes. The workflow copies the example configs, blanks every `=EXAMPLEKEY` placeholder, defines keyless, CORS-open ESRI World Imagery and AWS Terrarium sources through `SITREC_CUSTOM_MAP_ESRI_*` / `SITREC_CUSTOM_ELEVATION_AWS_*` and makes them the defaults, runs `npm run build-serverless` (whose `postbuild-serverless` audits the output), and publishes with `upload-pages-artifact` / `deploy-pages` — an artifact, never a commit or a `gh-pages` branch, so deploying never grows the repository. It requires Settings → Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions". `a3300d99` changes the trigger from every push to `main` to pushes of release tags matching `[0-9]+.[0-9]+.[0-9]+` plus `workflow_dispatch`, so a tag-triggered deploy always shows a release, with the tag as its `git describe` version string; the `github-pages` environment needs a tag rule in its deployment-branch settings for that, and the workflow trigger is what restricts deploys to release tags. The staged release-commit change corrects the comment and the guide: a manual run builds whatever ref is chosen for it, so only a tag-triggered deploy is guaranteed to be a release. Verified by serving the build from a subdirectory: the app loads, ESRI and Terrarium tiles stream, icons resolve, the audit passes on both a real config and a fresh clone, and a planted Mapbox token still fails it.

### Improvements

- The *Live Feeds* folder (Contents) starts closed (`0fc677dd`; `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`, `.close()` appended after `.moveToFirst()` on `feedsFolder`). The folder sits first in Contents so it can be found, but it opened unfolded, so its switches, radius slider and status readouts were the first thing every visit to Contents showed — and each switch opens a network connection. It is now a heading the user opens deliberately. Fresh-load default only: `CUIBar._serializeFolderStates` records each subfolder's open state by title, so a saved sitch that had *Live Feeds* expanded still restores it expanded.

- *Free Look Camera* no longer freezes the field-of-view controls (`b023bcb6`; `CNodeCamera.applyControllers()` / new `applyFOVControllers()` in `src/nodes/CNodeCamera.js`; new `applyFOVOnly()` in `src/nodes/CNodeControllerPTZUI.js`; `isFOVController = true` on `CNodeControllerGUIFOV`, `CNodeControllerFocalLength`, `CNodeControllerFOV` and `CNodeControllerATFLIRCamera` in `src/nodes/CNodeControllerVarious.js`). Free Look previously returned from `applyControllers()` before applying anything, suspending the FOV sources along with the pose sources, which froze the Zoom / HFOV / 35mm sliders at whatever a track-driven value happened to be when it was switched on. The field of view is not part of the pose — flying the camera by hand and choosing what lens it has are separate decisions — so those controllers now keep running: under `freeLook`, `applyFOVControllers(f)` walks the enabled controller inputs, applies the ones flagged `isFOVController` as usual, and calls `applyFOVOnly?.()` on the rest. The PTZ controller's `applyFOVOnly` re-reads `fovSwitch` into `this.fov` — the field the sliders display, via `listen()` — without touching the camera, so a track-driven FOV keeps showing its live value while the camera is flown by hand.

- One checkout can build for more than one deployment (`2408e441`; new `scripts/buildTarget.js` with `sharedEnvPath()`, `sharedEnvLabel()` and `prodPath()`). Two environment variables override the defaults for a single build: `SITREC_SHARED_ENV` names the settings file (relative to the repo root) and `SITREC_PROD_PATH` the directory the production bundle is written to. Every step that reads the env file or writes the output resolves it there — the `dotenv` load and the `Dotenv` plugin in `webpack.common.js`, the output path in `webpack.prod.js` (which now throws if neither the override nor `config/config-install.js` provides one), the freshness gate in `webpack.common.js` and `webpack.copy-files.js`, the `shared.env.php` copy in `webpackCopyPatterns.js`, `scripts/serverlessClientEnv.js`, `--copy-to-prod` in `scripts/generateThirdPartyNotices.js` and `resolveConfiguredProdPath()` in `scripts/auditBundleSecrets.js` — so the JS bundle, the PHP settings file and the audit always agree on which file a build used. An override that names a missing file throws instead of falling back, so a deployment can never be built with another site's keys by accident. `scripts/sharedEnvVersion.js` names the file it actually checked, so a stale target env no longer sends the operator to edit the main one. `config/shared.env.*` is gitignored, the example excepted. Documented under "Building for another deployment" in `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md`.

- The server-side tile cache is retired (`974c49fd`; `sitrecServer/cachemaps.php` deleted; `config/config.js.example`, `config/config.php.example`, `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md`). `cachemaps.php` fetched a map tile on the browser's behalf, kept a copy, and redirected to it. Measured on the production server it was all but unused — 584 tiles ever cached, 13 in the last month — and only two sources still routed through it: EOX, and the hidden (`excludeFromMenu`) road-highlight variant of OpenStreetMap. The `osmHighlight` source is removed from the example config, EOX is fetched directly (its tile server allows cross-origin requests), and the `$acceptable_domains` / `$acceptable_extensions` lists that existed only for the proxy leave `config.php.example`. `sitrec-cache` stays: the satellite element sets, ADS-B, sounding and live-feed proxies and the usage counters keep their short-lived files there. The water-colour code still recognises `osmHighlight` as a key, which costs nothing and keeps an older config working. The install guide's URL test for the proxy is replaced by `proxy.php?request=CURRENT_STARLINK`.

### Bug Fixes

- Fixed the ground clamp lifting the look camera — and anything else it keeps above the ground — onto the whole-planet elevation tile while a sitch loaded (`857cc4e3`; new `MIN_CLAMP_ELEVATION_ZOOM = 1` and `elevationGroundIsLocal(point)` in `src/threeExt.js`, consulted by `clampAboveGround()` and `groundClearance()`). The elevation map streams coarse to fine, and z0 is a **single** tile for the entire Earth. While only that had arrived, the ground under Malibu read 174 m against a true -24 m, and `clampAboveGround` dutifully lifted the look camera from its authored 48 m up to it — measured as `ELEVCLAMP point=48 -> ground=174 elev=174 tileZ=0`. That was the real source of the intermittent LOS bug: the camera is not AGL and its track never moves; the lift came entirely from the clamp, which `CNodeControllerTrackPosition` applies every frame because `forceAboveSurface` is undefined and the test is `!== false`. `CNodeLOSFromCamera` evaluates the camera with its controllers applied, so it reported 174 too, and any `CNodeDisplayLOS` bake inside that ~330 ms window captured a line running off screen; real elevation then arrived, the clamp released, and nothing re-baked. So the data was never *missing* — an "is elevation loaded?" test would have said yes — it was present at planet resolution, and the tile zoom is the only thing that distinguishes that from a real answer. `elevationGroundIsLocal()` asks `TerrainModel.getPointBelowWithTileInfo(point).tileZ >= 1` (it returns `true` when there is no terrain model or the method is absent, so nothing else changes), and `clampAboveGround()` now returns the point untouched — and `groundClearance()` reports `Infinity` — when the sample is the planet tile, so the vertical clamp and the along-line march cannot disagree about where the ground is. The guard is placed after the existing early-outs, so the common case pays nothing for it, and it sits only on the elevation-map path: a hit on the visible tile surface returns before it, and needed no guard because `groundBelow()` already rejects coarse-LOD hits (instrumenting that branch logged zero events). Not clamping is the failure-safe direction — an object left where its author put it may briefly sit below a surface and self-corrects when real elevation lands, whereas a clamped one writes a position other nodes bake and never revisit. The threshold is z0-only, and that is measured rather than judged: an initial z8 attempt moved the 2017 Eclipse test's lines by 2450 px, because that global-scale view legitimately clamps against z0–z6 (24310 hits at z6) and never loads finer elevation, while the pathological case uses z0 and nothing else. Verified: the camera now only ever holds 48 or 9961 — its two real track values — across 5 runs, with the bake correct in all of them; full regression 38 pass with **no** baseline regenerated, which is the point: this removes a wrong transient rather than changing any correct render. Jest 4648 pass.

- Reverted the 2.147.2 settle-time re-bake of camera-derived nodes (`bdfe2664`, reverting `c4eb5cfc`; `rebakeCameraDerivedNodes()` and its call from `renderMain()` removed from `src/indexRender.js`). The 2.147.2 entry describing it stands — it did ship in that version — but it treated the symptom: the LOS lines were being baked from a camera that the clamp above had lifted 126 m, and this re-baked them afterwards to paper over that. With `857cc4e3` there is no longer a bad transient to re-bake from. It was also unreliable in its own right. It hung off the "No pending actions" settle log, and that whole block only runs when `Globals.pendingActions` has gone positive and then drained while the render loop is running — measured firing in only 4 of 6 loads of the sitch it was meant to fix. The live incognito repro that prompted it had `pendingActions` 0, `wasPending` 0 and a stale bake, and a manual `lookCamera.recalculateCascade()` in that page corrected it immediately: the cascade worked, it had simply never run. So it cost a cascade over every camera-bearing node on each settle and guarded nothing demonstrable. The graph is left to do its normal job.

- Fixed the favicon, touch icon and web-app manifest pointing at the wrong place on any install not served from the host root, and two manifest icons that no build ever shipped (`9a65d352`; `webpack.common.js` `HtmlWebpackPlugin` meta, `webpackCopyPatterns.js`, `site.webmanifest`). The four `<link href>` values were root-absolute (`/favicon-32x32.png`, `/apple-touch-icon.png`, `/site.webmanifest`, …), so they resolved against the *host* root rather than the app directory — wrong for every install under a path such as `/sitrec/`, and a guaranteed 404 on a static host that publishes only a subdirectory. They are now relative. That exposed a second bug: `site.webmanifest` named `android-chrome-192x192.png` and `android-chrome-512x512.png`, and nothing ever copied them into a build, so every build published a manifest pointing at icons it had not shipped; it went unnoticed because on an install under a path the manifest itself 404'd first. Both are now copied, and the manifest's own `src` values are relative too.

- Fixed a self-hosted Sitrec behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS building `http://` URLs for an `https://` page (`6a007526`; new `sitrecServer/requestScheme.php`; `sitrecServer/config_paths.php`, `getsitches.php`, `metadata.php`, `object.php`; "Behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS" in `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md`). The backend built absolute URLs from `$_SERVER['REQUEST_SCHEME']` — the app, cache, upload and terrain paths handed to the page, and the origin used for CORS checks. Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer that speaks plain HTTP to Apache, that scheme is `http` while the page is `https://`, and a browser refuses to fetch `http://` resources from an `https://` page. `requestScheme.php` defaults the scheme to `http` when unset (the PHP built-in server never sets it — this replaces the fallback `config_paths.php` carried for that), then takes `https` or `http`, and nothing else, from the standard `X-Forwarded-Proto` header when present. `config_paths.php` requires it first; `getsitches.php`, `metadata.php` and `object.php` require it directly because they build their CORS origin before loading `config_paths.php`. `REMOTE_ADDR` is deliberately **not** taken from the proxy: the localhost rule in `config.php` grants administrator rights, so a client-supplied address must never reach it — which is also why the guide says to run the proxy and Sitrec as separate containers on a shared network rather than one pod proxying to `127.0.0.1`. Verified against PHP's built-in server: a forwarded `https` is honoured, a bogus value is ignored, and `getsitches` echoes an `https` origin.

- Fixed MapBox imagery on the public site failing with a 401, and gave the Mapbox token one home (`95a6ab56`; `config/config.js.example`). Per the commit, the first run of the new server-mode secret audit (see Security) found that the live `config.js` carried a literal Mapbox token of its own — a second home that a key rotation had missed — so production was serving a revoked token and MapBox tiles returned 401, quietly rather than loudly. The example's MapBox `mapURL` now reads `${process.env.MAPBOX_TOKEN}`, as the MapTiler source a few lines below it already did, so the token lives only in `shared.env`; and the audit now fails a production build that carries a `pk.eyJ` token of any value other than the currently configured one, which is exactly what a rotation that misses a second copy leaves behind.

- Fixed the container entrypoint silently dropping eight settings from `shared.env.example` (`29c3e455`; `docker/entrypoint.sh`). The entrypoint copies only the variables on its `CLIENT_VARS` and `SERVER_VARS` lists into the container's settings and ignores the rest, and these were on neither list, so setting them for the image did nothing. `SITREC_USE_CUSTOM_WIND`, `SITREC_CUSTOM_WIND_MENU_NAME`, `SITREC_CUSTOM_WIND_TOOLTIP` and `LOG_UI_INTERACTIONS` join `CLIENT_VARS` (menu flags the page needs); `CUSTOM_WIND_URL`, `CACHE_CUSTOM_WIND`, `ADSBX_RAPIDAPI_KEY` and `GEMINI_API` join `SERVER_VARS`, so the URL and the keys never reach the page. A run of the entrypoint with each set confirmed where each one lands.

- Fixed a fresh clone failing its own secret audit, so `npm run dev-serverless` could not finish on a clean checkout (`9a65d352`; `UNSET_CREDENTIAL_SENTINEL = "EXAMPLEKEY"` in `scripts/auditBundleSecrets.js`). `shared.env.example` sets every credential to the literal `EXAMPLEKEY`, and `src/` compares against that same literal to decide a key is not configured (`hasRequiredToken` in `CNodeTerrainUI.js` and `WaterMaskTiles.js`) — so the audit searched the build for a "secret" and found the app's own check for it. Both value collectors now skip that exact string. Exact, and deliberately not the `isPlaceholderValue()` heuristic: that is justified by Mapbox and MapTiler tokens always being mixed case, which is not true of an AWS access key id, so reusing it here would have waved through a real `S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID` that happened to contain "FAKE".

- Fixed the elevation-tile decoders reading their pixel array's axis order backwards — latent, not live (`3b05ba81`; `computeElevationFromRGBA()` and `computeElevationFromRGBA_MB()` in `src/QuadTreeTile.js`). `get-pixels-mick` builds its ndarrays as shape `[height, width, 4]` with stride `[4*width, 4, 1]`: axis 0 advances by a whole row, so `shape[0]` is the height. Both decoders read `shape[0]` as the width and `shape[1]` as the height. On the square tiles this actually receives (256/512) the old and new loops are the same computation under a rename, so nothing rendered changes; a non-square tile would have produced garbled terrain. What could have bitten is that the two elevation sources disagreed about their own axis order: `computeElevationFromGeoTIFF` stores `this.shape` as `[width, height]`, while the PNG paths passed `pixels.shape` straight through as `[height, width, 4]`, and `QuadTreeTileMaterial` destructures it as `[ancestorWidth, ancestorHeight]` — correct for GeoTIFF tiles, transposed for PNG. `this.shape` is now normalised to `[width, height]` in both PNG paths (nothing depended on the three-element form), and the loops iterate `y` over height and `x` over width with `ij = x + width * y`, so the row-major layout is stated rather than implied. Verified with the full visual-regression suite: 38 pass.

### Security

- Scripted-video scripts now run inside the worker sandbox or not at all (`f63d14aa`; `src/scriptedVideo/ScriptRunnerClient.js`; `tests/scriptRunnerWorker.test.js`). Script text from a sitch is compiled with `new AsyncFunction`, and a sitch is parsed automatically when it loads — `deserializeScriptedVideo` ends in `doParse()` — so opening a shared link runs its author's script with no user action. That is safe only while the run happens inside `ScriptRunnerWorker`, which has no DOM and whose network and storage globals are removed. The client had four routes around it: no `Worker` constructor, a worker that failed to spawn, a `postMessage` that threw, and `worker.onerror` — which drained **every** pending script into the page at once (`drainPendingToFallback`), so an induced crash did not even have to be the attacker's own script. Each turned a shared link into same-origin code execution with full DOM, storage and network access. All four now resolve an error-shaped model (`errorModel("script sandbox unavailable — the script was NOT run")`, `drainPendingToError`), and the `runScriptJS` import is gone, so no path remains from this module into the page. The refusal is deliberately not prefixed "syntax error", because `CScriptedVideo.parse()` reads that prefix as "keep showing the last good timeline", which would hide the fact that nothing ran. Two induction routes were already closed by construction and are recorded so they are not re-investigated: `postMessage` cannot be made to throw from sitch data (`viewPresets` is a hardcoded literal and tabs are strings, so both always clone), and the worker's `onmessage` wraps everything in try/catch and posts an error model rather than throwing, so a script error never reaches `onerror`. The cost is that scripted video now requires a working `Worker`: support is universal, the desktop app loads over http from its own local server rather than `file://` (where Chromium refuses to spawn workers), and the current CSP sets no `default-src`, so nothing governs `worker-src` today — whoever lands a stricter policy must add `worker-src 'self'` explicitly. jsdom has no `Worker`, which is where the test now asserts the refusal. The follow-up `e109a25c` (comments only) corrects the security notes on `setScriptedVideoScript` / `previewScriptedVideo` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js` — the `llmCallable:false` gate stays, but because setting a script is an action that drives the real scene, not because of page code execution — and the CSP rationale in `webpack.common.js`, which now records that `'unsafe-eval'` is forced by `ndarray` (reached only from `src/js/get-pixels-mick.js`), not by scripted video, and that the emitted `index.html` carries no inline script or style.

- Shared sitch links are now the capability they were meant to be (`42787cbb`; `getDateTimeFilename()` and new `screenshotFilename()` in `src/utils.js`; `src/CFileManager.js`, `src/CFileManagerSave.js`, `src/CustomSupport.js`; `sitrecServer/getsitches.php`, `metadata.php`, `object.php`, `object_helpers.php`). A share URL is `<userid>/<name>/<version>.js`, and knowing that complete key is the permission to read it. The name half is not secret — it is human-readable and appears in full in every shared link — so the version token has to carry the secrecy on its own, and it was a plain timestamp: not a secret but a clock reading, with only 86,400 possibilities for a known day. Version tokens now append 48 bits from `crypto.getRandomValues` (12 hex characters). The timestamp still leads, so filenames stay readable and sortable, the "latest version is the lexicographically greatest" rule `resolveLatestObjectKey` relies on is unchanged, and nothing parses the string back into a date. Three endpoints undercut that by mapping a name to its version. `object.php` resolved a folder reference (`<userid>/<name>/`) to the newest version for any caller; that now requires the prefix owner or an admin (403 otherwise), with identity resolved only on that branch — through `user.php`'s cached `getUserInfo()` — so the common case, a complete key, still costs no session lookup. The cross-user `versions` listing in `getsitches.php` is now limited to your own id, an admin, or a sitch on the published featured list (new `isFeaturedSitch()`, which reads `metadata/featured.json` locally or from S3 and fails closed); an anonymous caller gets the same empty array as before unless the sitch is featured, so nothing throws. The `latestversion` endpoint, which answered before authentication, had no callers anywhere in the tree and is deleted rather than gated. Preview screenshots used one fixed name per sitch, so the name alone reached the most recent one — a later state than the version actually shared. Each screenshot now carries its own token (`screenshot_<token>.jpg`); `isScreenshotFile()` / `newestScreenshotName()` in `object_helpers.php` recognise both forms at the five listing sites, so a screenshot is never mistaken for a saved version, and `refreshFeaturedDates` stores `screenshotName` in the featured list so the featured GET path stays free of storage calls. Objects saved earlier keep their names and resolve through the legacy fallbacks. Verified: 78 Jest tests across CFileManager, configUtils and CSitrecAPI; all four PHP files pass `php -l`.

- The Google and Cesium credentials no longer reach the page (`cfbd879c`; `BUILD_TIME_TOKENS` in `src/nodes/CNodeTerrainUI.js`, `docker/entrypoint.sh`, `sitrecServer/streetview.php`, `config/shared.env.example`). Both were reaching the browser two ways, neither intended. They were baked into the bundle, because they were named in `BUILD_TIME_TOKENS` — a map that had no reader for them, but `dotenv-webpack` substitutes every literal `process.env.X` reference; and the container entrypoint listed them in `CLIENT_VARS`, injecting them into `window.__SITREC_ENV__` in the page source for every visitor. They are meant to reach the browser only through `rehost.php?getuser`, which gates them on group membership and remaining daily quota, and both paths silently defeated that gate. Only Mapbox and MapTiler are declared by a source as a `requiredToken`, and those two are unavoidably public since the browser fetches those tiles directly; the other two are removed from the build-time map and moved from the entrypoint's client list to `SERVER_VARS` — moved rather than deleted, because the PHP env file is written from both lists and the server still needs them (the explanatory comment sits outside the list, because the writer loop word-splits it). `streetview.php` gains an optional `GOOGLE_MAPS_SERVER_API_KEY`: the browser key is referrer-restricted, so using it server-side means sending a matching `Referer`, which is no restriction at all when the header is client-controlled. With a server key configured the file sends no `Referer` and the key can be restricted by IP address instead; it falls back to the previous behaviour when unset. `SHARED_ENV_VERSION` moves to `2026-09-01`. Verified by rebuilding and rescanning the served output: neither credential appears anywhere in it, while Mapbox and MapTiler still do, as required.

- The production build is now gated on a secret audit, and the audit catches stale credentials, not only current ones (`95a6ab56`, `43471d13`; `scripts/auditBundleSecrets.js`; `postdeploy` in `package.json`; new `npm run audit-prod-bundle`). Keys that reached a public bundle were only ever found by hand — nothing checked the tree that gets rsynced to production. `auditBundleSecrets.js` gains `--mode=server`, and `postdeploy` runs it after the third-party notices, so a finding fails `npm run deploy`. The two audits want opposite things, which is why it is a mode: a serverless or desktop build has every key stripped, so a bundled `sitrecServer/` or `shared.env` is itself a finding, whereas a full-server build **is** the server and must carry both — what it must never carry is a credential the browser can fetch. Server mode: `sitrecServer/` and `shared.env.php` are expected; `shared.env.php` holds every key by design and is not content-scanned, so `checkServerEnvGuard()` checks the one thing protecting it instead, the `<?php` prefix that makes a direct request execute the file and return nothing; only `MAPBOX_TOKEN` and `MAPTILER_KEY` (`CLIENT_PUBLIC_ENV_KEYS`) may be published, and only at their **current** value — a `pk.eyJ` of any other value is a stale credential baked into the build; and because production serves the `tests/` tree, its key-shaped fixtures are tolerated by exact value (`SERVER_FIXTURE_ALLOWLIST`) rather than by directory, so a new key-shaped fixture fails until a human lists it. `43471d13` adds a JWT pattern (three segments, the first two starting `eyJ`) so an **old** Cesium Ion token matches somewhere, since Cesium is server-only and any JWT in served output is wrong however stale; and `PROVIDER_URL_CREDENTIALS`, anchored to `api.maptiler.com…key=` and `api.mapbox.com…access_token=`, because a MapTiler key — twenty plain alphanumerics — has no safe shape to match on but is unambiguous in its provider URL: in server mode it must equal the configured value, in bundle mode any literal is a leak, and a URL built from a runtime variable cannot match. Documentation shows those URLs with `YOUR_MAPTILER_KEY`, so `isPlaceholderValue()` excuses a value that is entirely upper case, digits, underscore and hyphen **and** contains one of YOUR / EXAMPLE / PLACEHOLDER / DUMMY / FAKE / SAMPLE / CHANGEME / INSERT / TODO — real credentials carry mixed case and cannot qualify. Boundary-tested each way: a stale MapTiler key, a stale Mapbox token and a stale Cesium JWT are caught; the current values and the placeholder are not; the current Cesium token is still caught as the server-only key it is. `dist-serverless` still passes bundle mode.

- Every push to `main` is checked for new ways user data could leave the app, and where Sitrec sends data is now written down (`1d1beae8`, `7fd9447a`, `fcea7eed`, `a3300d99`, plus the staged release-commit corrections; new `.github/workflows/user-data-egress-check.yml`, `scripts/security-scan-egress.mjs`, `scripts/egress-allowlist.json`, `scripts/egress-review-prompt.md`, `scripts/egress-check-record.mjs`, `tests/securityScanEgress.test.js`, `docs/UserDataEgressCheck.md`). Two layers answer one question in public — did this change create a new way for data a user loads into Sitrec to leave it, or send more than Sitrec is designed to send? The **scan** is deterministic: on the added lines only, it lists every network call and other data sink, every destination host, every server endpoint and every URL that carries a position, and compares destinations against the allow-list, where every destination Sitrec is designed to call has a contract — `purpose`, `trigger`, and `mayReceive`, the most revealing classes of data it may be sent from a fixed vocabulary. It fails outright on a destination or `sitrecServer/` endpoint with no contract, a new server-side file without one, or a position sent to a destination whose contract has no position class. The **review** is an LLM (GitHub Copilot CLI inside the workflow) that reads the scan, the allow-list and the diff against the same contracts, with a spending cap, no write access and no network; a push that changes no code in scope skips it. The verdict and both reports are posted as a comment on the commit, which does not expire, and the workflow is red on ATTENTION or when the review could not complete. `--inventory` lists every destination the tree references, and the test suite checks that the whole tracked tree matches the allow-list. Two fix-ups followed: the diff the reviewer reads was piped through `head` under `pipefail`, so on a diff larger than the pipe buffer git got SIGPIPE and the step aborted (updating the vendored 10 MB `src/js/opencv.js` reproduces it) — it is now written to a file and truncated from there; and the record accepted any output beginning with a verdict line, even from a run that had died — a verdict now counts only when the review's exit file exists and reads 0 (a cancelled step after a job timeout never writes one), and anything else is INCOMPLETE with the partial output shown as such. `a3300d99` adds the Cesium Ion hosts reached through the bundled 3D-tiles library (`api.cesium.com`, `*.cesium.com`) and names the operator settings that gate the usage-statistics endpoints (`SITREC_TRACK_STATS`, `LOG_UI_INTERACTIONS`). The staged corrections, after a review of the contract against the code: a new `session-data` class (whatever the assistant reads through its tool calls — positions, times, identifiers, notes, file names, the serialized situation); the six AI-provider hosts and `chatbot.php` now declare it, together with `precise-position`, `time` and `identifier`, because tool results go back to the provider; `settings.php` declares its automatic load at startup and that a save sends the whole settings set, which includes a startup position if the user has set one; `rehost.php` declares the login check at every startup; and the four proxied live feeds (`api.v2.sondehub.org`, `earthquake.usgs.gov`, `ll.thespacedevs.com`, `proxyLiveFeed.php`) are corrected to fixed, world-wide feed addresses that receive the feed name and nothing about the view, down from `coarse-area` / `precise-position`.

### Documentation

- **The User Data Egress Check** (`docs/UserDataEgressCheck.md`; `1d1beae8`, expanded in `a3300d99`, corrected in the staged release commit; linked from the README, deliberately exempt from the Help-menu registry like `Wind-Internals`). Beyond explaining the check, `a3300d99` adds "Where Sitrec sends data today": what every build requests with no user action (the sitch list, the login check, saved settings, map and elevation tiles), what the public site turns on beyond the defaults, what each self-hosted build does in its default configuration (local, container, VPS, serverless, Pages — with a summary table), and what each feature sends when used, including what the AI assistant can reach through its tool calls; plus how the review is run — its committed brief, the model, the per-run cap, what it reads, and how deep it goes. The staged wording fixes match the contract corrections above.

- **Deploying Sitrec on GitHub Pages** (`docs/dev/Deploying-on-GitHub-Pages.md`; `936c641d`, reworked in `a3300d99`, corrected in the staged release commit): what the serverless build is, what the published site can and cannot do, why terrain needs the two keyless sources, how `pages.yml` publishes without writing to the repository, how to run the build locally, what the site sends where, and how a fork gets its own site and keeps it current — sync by hand, a scheduled sync workflow (which must dispatch the deploy itself, because a push made with the workflow token triggers nothing), or building from upstream on a schedule; the fork instructions are written for tag-triggered deploys, since syncing a branch does not copy tags.

- **Deploying Sitrec on a VPS with Podman and Caddy** (`docs/dev/Deploying-on-a-VPS.md`; `fe428acc`; linked from the install guide's production section): a guide to putting a public Sitrec site on its own domain as the released container image on a small VPS — host baseline, rootless Quadlet units for Sitrec and Caddy, automatic certificates, self-applying updates, persistent data, verification, and day-to-day operation. Half of it is what went wrong: the template with SELinux off, a rootless bridge network that hides every visitor's address, a pod layout that would make every visitor an administrator (the localhost rule in `config.php`), a proxy that reports the wrong scheme (the fix above), and a cache directory that turned out to hold nothing worth keeping (retired above).

- `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md` gains "Building for another deployment" (`2408e441`), "Behind a reverse proxy that terminates TLS" (`6a007526`) and a serverless subdirectory note (`9a65d352`); `SERVERLESS.md` gains "Serving from a subdirectory" and "GitHub Pages" (`9a65d352`); the README links the Pages copy, both deployment guides and the egress page (`936c641d`, `a3300d99`, staged); `docs/UserInterface.md` documents Shift + wheel (`b023bcb6`, `1dc37054`).

## Version 2.147.2 (2026-09-01)

### Bug Fixes

- Fixed the *Traverse Alt (MSL)* and *Traverse Alt (AGL)* readouts (Show → *Sim Info Display*) reading the geoid undulation from the wrong place on Earth (`b2891477`; `getTraverseAltMSLText()` and `getTraverseAltAGLText()` in `src/nodes/CNodeSimInfoUI.js`). `ECEFToLLA_radii` returns **radians** — its name is about which radii it uses, not its output units — while `meanSeaLevelOffset` (`src/EGM96Geoid.js`) takes **degrees**, and both readouts passed the former straight to the latter. It fails silently, which is why it survived: `meanSeaLevelOffset` clamps only latitude, to ±90, and a latitude in radians never exceeds 1.5708, so the value sails through the clamp untouched and simply returns the undulation for somewhere else entirely. Measured off Malibu, 34.0195, -118.5042 became 0.594, -2.068 — a point in the Gulf of Guinea, N of +18 m instead of -35 m — so the displayed MSL altitude was about 53 m (174 ft) too low. The AGL readout's no-terrain fallback assumes the ground sits at mean sea level and so was off by exactly the same amount; the terrain path (`TerrainModel.getPointBelow()` / `getTilesPointBelow()`) was never affected, because it works in HAE at both ends. EGM96's range puts the worst case near 190 m. Both call sites now use `ECEFToLLAVD_radii`, the sibling wrapper that takes a `Vector3` and returns degrees and which the already-correct call sites use — removing the trap rather than papering over it with a conversion. An audit of every other `ECEFToLLA_radii` caller found no further live mismatches: the rest either convert explicitly, keep radians for the `_radii` ENU/ECEF helpers, or use only the altitude component. Every `geoidCorrectionForTile` and `interpolateGeoidOffset` caller was checked too.

- Fixed a line of sight clipped at "sea level" terminating at the WGS84 ellipsoid instead of at mean sea level (`9a8693ae`; new `intersectMeanSeaLevel()` in `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayLOS.js`, plus an optional `altitude` parameter on `intersectSurface()` and `intersectEllipsoid()` in `src/threeExt.js`). `clipSeaLevel` — on by default for every LOS display, only FLIR1 turns it off — terminated the ray at HAE 0. Sea level means the **geoid**, which differs from the ellipsoid by the undulation N: about -35 m off Malibu and roughly -105..+85 m worldwide. So every downward LOS stopped that far from the water; in the sitch measured it ended 24 m above the visible ground, hanging in mid-air short of the surface it was drawn to reach. `intersectMeanSeaLevel()` intersects the bare ellipsoid for a first guess, looks up N at that point, then re-intersects a surface raised by N. N varies by only metres per hundred kilometres, so one refinement is already sub-metre; a second runs as cheap insurance for a long shallow ray whose first guess lands far from its final point. A ray that grazes the ellipsoid can miss the slightly raised or lowered surface, so a failed refinement keeps the last good hit rather than dropping the clip entirely. In `threeExt.js` the new `altitude` argument defaults to 0, and no existing caller passes one — including the indirect use where `TrackManager` hands `intersectSurface` to `collectLOSGroundPoints` (`src/CameraFraming.js:123`), which calls it with two arguments — so the ten other direct `intersectSurface` sites and the `intersectEllipsoid` sites are unchanged. In the ellipsoid path the offset is added to both semi-axes, the standard approximation for an offset ellipsoid: exact along the axes, and for the geoid's range the error away from them is millimetres. Verified off Malibu: the endpoint moves from HAE 0 to HAE -36, which is the EGM96 geoid there, and from 24 m above the local surface to 6 m below it, so the line now reaches the ground and is correctly occluded beyond it. Scope is deliberately narrow — this is the LOS **display** clip only. `CNodeGimbalTriangulate` (`:89`) and the *Track from Camera LOS* synthetic track (`CustomSupport.js:1550`) still intersect at HAE 0. Note also that the conversion from `ECEFToLLA_radii`'s radians to `meanSeaLevelOffset`'s degrees is explicit here, with the reason in the comment, because that same trap is what `b2891477` fixes.

- Fixed LOS lines being baked from a camera position that loading had already superseded (`c4eb5cfc`; new `rebakeCameraDerivedNodes()` in `src/indexRender.js`, called from `renderMain()` at the existing settle point where "No pending actions" is logged). A camera's position and orientation are written by its controllers during the per-frame update. That is an imperative mutation of a Three.js object, not a node change, so the node graph never learns about it — and anything that BAKES geometry from a camera captures whatever the camera held when its cascade last ran, with nothing to re-bake it when a controller moves the camera afterwards. `CNodeDisplayLOS` builds its LOS lines in `recalculate()`; `update()` deliberately does not rebuild them, for cost. Measured during load: the camera track resolves to 48 m HAE and cascades, but `trackPositionController` has not yet copied that onto the camera, which still holds 174 m, so `CNodeLOSFromCamera` returned 174 and the LOS baked it. Roughly 32 ms later the controller moved the camera to 48 and nothing rebuilt the line, which by then ran entirely off screen. Whether the line appeared at all came down to whether some later `recalculate` happened to fire after the controller caught up — intermittent, and reliably absent on a warm cache. The fix walks `NodeMan.list` at the settle point and calls `recalculateCascade()` on every node that either is a camera (`isCamera`) or holds one (`node.camera !== undefined` — the view nodes, the frustum display, the night-sky and sky-overlay displays, the flow orbs), so only what actually derives from a camera is rebuilt. By then execution is inside the render loop, so every controller has applied at least once, and loading has finished so the camera is where it will stay; `recalculateCascade` also arms `setRenderOne(true)`, so the rebuilt geometry is drawn rather than waiting for the next redraw. The cost is one cascade per settle, not per frame, and it fires again on any later settle because `Globals.wasPending` resets whenever new work starts. Verified against a sitch that reproduced 4 times out of 4: the drawn origin now matches the computed one in every run, and the line renders. **This is a phase fix, not the underlying one.** The general problem remains that camera-derived nodes read a Three.js object living outside the graph; deriving them from the controller's source track instead would remove the race rather than time around it.

## Version 2.147.1 (2026-08-31)

### Bug Fixes

- Fixed a camera that has never been displayed drawing a wrong-shaped frustum, and the rendered scene depending on how long startup took (`11b947e1`; `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`, in the constructor immediately after `setupRenderPipeline()`). Every writer of `camera.aspect` is on the render path — `preRenderCameraUpdate()` (`src/nodes/CNodeView.js:740`), the `matchVideoAspect` blocks, and the `prepareCameraForLOD()` / `restoreCameraAfterLOD()` bracket (`CNodeView3D.js:1147`, `:1203`, `:1244`) — and the render loop skips any view that is not `_effectivelyVisible` (`src/indexRender.js:500`). So nothing ever *initialised* aspect. A view suppressed before it first drew — a sitch saved with `mainView` `doubled` fullscreens on load, which suppresses `lookView` — kept `PerspectiveCamera`'s constructor default of `1` instead of its true 960/1022 = 0.9393. That is not cosmetic: `CNodeDisplayCameraFrustum` builds its geometry straight from `camera.aspect` (`w = h * aspect`, `CNodeDisplayCameraFrustum.js:331`), so the sensor cone drawn into the main view was about 6.5% too wide — a wrong-shaped frustum in a tool used to reason about what a sensor could see. It also made the render timing-dependent: a single frame slipping through before suppression would initialise the aspect, so the scene settled into one of two states depending on startup speed (this is what made an unrelated IndexedDB delay during startup change the rendered image). The constructor now sets `camera.aspect = widthDiv / heightDiv` — the same value `preRenderCameraUpdate()` would compute — and calls `updateProjectionMatrix()`. Two residual gaps are noted in the code: the initialisation is a one-shot, so a view whose rect changes while it is still suppressed can hold a stale (but deterministic) aspect, and `renderedFOV` has the same freeze pattern on a render-then-suppress path.

- Fixed `widthPx` / `heightPx` meaning two different things during view construction (`11b947e1`; `setupRenderPipeline()` in `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`). `updateWH()` writes **layout** pixels, but `setupRenderPipeline()` was writing the canvas **backing-store** size into the same fields, so the meaning depended on which had run last. For a view with a fixed `canvasWidth` the two diverge widely (1600×925 against 960×1022 for `lookView`). Views positioned `relativeTo` another read that view's `widthPx` / `heightPx` (`CNodeView.js:670-677`), which is how the hidden `WescamMXUI` overlay, sized relative to `lookView`, snapshotted a rect of [1600,925] in some runs and [960,1022] in others. The backing size now stays in locals (`canvasWidthPx` / `canvasHeightPx`) and reaches only `this.canvas.width` / `.height`; `preRenderCameraUpdate()` already treats `widthPx` as layout pixels, so layout pixels is the meaning the rest of the code expects. This does **not** make the meaning uniform everywhere — for a view that actually renders, `adjustSize()` writes `canvasWidth` back into `widthPx` on every frame (`CNodeViewCanvas.js:255`), a pre-existing dual meaning left untouched. What changes is the construction window, and the suppressed case, which never reaches `adjustSize()` at all.

## Version 2.147.0 (2026-08-31)

### New Features

- **Control Sitrec with ChatGPT — WebMCP site tools** — Help → Documentation → *Control Sitrec with ChatGPT* (`545dbc53`, `94cfcef9`, `89b5cc82`; new `src/WebMCP.js`, `docs/WebMCP.md`, `scripts/security-scan-ai-surface.mjs`; `registerSitrecWebMCP()` called from `src/index.js`; i18n `menus.help.documentation.webmcp` — *Control Sitrec with ChatGPT*; README link and `docsRegistry` entry). `registerSitrecWebMCP()` publishes **13 curated site tools** on `document.modelContext`, so a model running in the ChatGPT desktop app's built-in browser can inspect and drive the open Sitrec page with no OpenAI API key configured in Sitrec, no SitrecBridge installation, no Chrome extension, no local WebSocket and no separately configured MCP server. The tools are `sitrec_get_state`, `sitrec_list_sitches`, `sitrec_load_sitch`, `sitrec_seek_frame`, `sitrec_set_playback`, `sitrec_get_camera`, `sitrec_goto_lla`, `sitrec_list_tracks`, `sitrec_get_track_position`, `sitrec_list_views`, `sitrec_set_datetime`, `sitrec_list_menu_controls` and `sitrec_set_menu_value`, over a pinned allowlist of 20 `CSitrecAPI` operations. Registration is progressive enhancement and non-blocking: an ordinary browser has no `document.modelContext` and behaves exactly as before. **This does not replace SitrecBridge**, which remains the route for Codex CLI/IDE and Claude and keeps its trusted installed-extension model.

  Every operation routes through `CSitrecAPI.handleAPICall(..., "webmcp")`. A new `UNTRUSTED_MODEL_SOURCES` set (`{"chat", "webmcp"}`) gives WebMCP the same prompt-injection controls the in-app chat already had — `llmCallable:false` gating, external-URL parameter refusal, confirmation before a write into an externally-sourced sitch, and result fencing — while `AGENT_SOURCES` (`{"chat", "mcp", "webmcp"}`) stays separate because it only decides where a failure is presented, and SitrecBridge needs that routing without inheriting the untrusted treatment. The adapter validates its own inputs rather than relying on `CSitrecAPI` coercion, checks sitch and track identifiers against the live catalogs, reads visible state back after every mutation, and cancels per invocation without cancelling application work.

  The time and menu tools (`94cfcef9`) exist because a request with no matching tool does not merely fail — the ChatGPT browser agent falls back to driving the DOM, so "set the time to 10pm" took 26 seconds of screenshotting and clicking the Time menu where the in-app assistant does it in one call. `sitrec_get_state` also reports `wallClock` (with the IANA zone name as well as the offset), because simulation time is UTC and a local time the user asks for is otherwise unresolvable; `setDateTime` requires an explicit zone, since on a daylight-saving changeover day tonight's offset is not today's and the error would render as plausible-looking sun and star positions for the wrong instant.

  The generic menu setter needed guards the specific ones could not provide. `CHAT_DENIED_URL_PARAMS` keys off `{function, parameter}` pairs and is structurally blind to a generic setter, so the tool refuses URL values itself, normalizing the way WHATWG `URL` does first. `89b5cc82` corrected that normalization after review: `looksLikeURL` tested the string as typed, but the parser also strips **leading and trailing C0 controls and spaces** before parsing, so a value beginning with NUL resolved to an external origin while matching neither pattern. All three parser normalizations (leading/trailing C0 and space, tab/CR/LF anywhere, backslash folded to slash) are now applied before testing, confirmed against `new URL()` rather than reasoned from the spec, with a test asserting the filter agrees with the parser instead of restating the regex. lil-gui inherits `setValue` from `Controller`, so writing a string over a button would replace its function and over an array-backed color would replace the array — the setter reads the control first and refuses anything not already a primitive, discriminating on the value rather than `constructor.name`, which Terser mangles in a production build; those controls are listed as `settable: false`. `89b5cc82` added a second read-back guard: `CSitrecAPI` reconciles dropdown options but assigns everything else as given, so a string `"false"` on a boolean control stayed truthy — the checkbox did not move and the tool still reported success. The setter now requires the value's type to match what the control holds and returns that value with the refusal (`VALUE_TYPE_MISMATCH`) so the model can correct itself. Control names are sanitized rather than passed through, since a folder title can be sitch-authored and a name carrying a line break would otherwise smuggle text into the model's context. Buttons stay out of the surface entirely — `executeMenuButton` is not allowlisted. `scripts/security-scan-ai-surface.mjs` pins both the public tool set and the underlying API allowlist, and fails if `WebMCP.js` dispatches non-literally or routes through the trusted `ui`/`mcp` sources.

- **Run the assistant against your own AI server — Custom endpoint** — Sitrec → Settings → *API Keys…* → *Custom endpoint* (`964cc540`; new `custom` provider in `src/BYOKProviders.js` with `optionalKey: true`, `endpoint: true` and `endpointFormats`; `testEndpoint()` in `src/BYOKKeyDialog.js`; endpoint storage in `src/BYOKKeyStore.js`). A new AI provider pointing at a server the user names — a model on their own machine, or an endpoint inside their network. They supply an address, the wire format it speaks, and a key **only if it needs one**: the credential is optional here alone, because a local runner usually wants none and requiring one would make the commonest case impossible to express. Both formats are transports Sitrec already had, so the choice just picks between them — *OpenAI-compatible (/v1/chat/completions)* covers Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp's server, vLLM, LocalAI, Jan, text-generation-webui and LiteLLM, and *Anthropic-compatible (/v1/messages)* covers gateways serving that shape. The address resolves forgivingly: a base with or without a trailing slash, or a full path taken as given, since a gateway mounting the API somewhere unusual is exactly the case this serves. Usage is banked under `custom/&lt;model&gt;` so a locally-named model cannot be mistaken for a hosted one with the same id. Verified end to end against a real local model: browser to own server, 105 tools, a real tool call, nothing touching Sitrec's server or any hosted provider.

  A page served over HTTPS **can** reach `http://127.0.0.1` — loopback is potentially trustworthy, so mixed content does not block it and no private-network preflight was demanded. CORS is the only real obstacle and it is the user's to fix, so the dialog gained a **Test** button that names which of three things went wrong: nothing listening, origin not permitted, or key refused. A browser reports a CORS rejection as a bare "Failed to fetch", so guessing once, out loud, is worth more than a generic error; the dialog also names the page's own origin and points at `OLLAMA_ORIGINS`.

- **Every model your own key reaches, newest generation by default** — Sitrec → Settings → *AI Model*, with *Enable old AI models* beneath it (`830dd54b`, `5b0b1cb9`; new `src/BYOKModelCatalog.js`; `getBYOKModels()` in `src/CDirectLLMClient.js`; i18n `custom.settings.enableOldAIModels`). The *AI Model* dropdown offered a hardcoded shortlist of five, which was wrong twice over: it hid models the user is already paying for, and it went stale the moment a provider shipped anything new. The list now comes from the provider's own `/v1/models`, which all three serve to a browser — `api.anthropic.com` with the direct-browser header, `api.openai.com` and `openrouter.ai/api/v1/models` with `ACAO *`. `BYOK_MODELS` survives only as the pre-fetch fallback. `BYOKModelCatalog` caches per provider in IndexedDB, refreshed on any key change and at most daily otherwise, speaks only key-provider ids, and never imports `CDirectLLMClient` (which would close a cycle through `BYOKUsage`); a version stamp on the stored entry forces a refetch when its shape changes.

  Filtering is a **denylist** on purpose — an allowlist is what produced the problem being fixed, since anything unrecognised would stay invisible until someone edited a constant. Only families that cannot run a typed tool-using assistant are dropped (`OPENAI_NON_CHAT`: embeddings, speech, image, moderation, video, `realtime`, legacy completion) plus the search-preview and deep-research variants, which carry their own fixed tool set and reject a caller-supplied one. Because a long list needs trimming, only each vendor's newest generation is offered by default, with *Enable old AI models* to see the rest; the generation is **derived from the ids** rather than listed anywhere, so a family released tomorrow is current the day it appears. Two guards matter: the filter never returns an empty list, and always keeps the currently-selected model, because hiding it would let `updateChatModelSelector` treat the saved setting as invalid and silently change which model answers. The setting is registered in **both** sanitizers — `sitrecServer/settings.php` is a whitelist, so without the PHP half the checkbox would work until the first reload and then revert.

  `5b0b1cb9` also made OpenAI a direct transport. `api.openai.com` now answers a browser preflight on `/v1/chat/completions` with `access-control-allow-origin` echoing the caller and `authorization` among the allowed headers, so the reason for routing GPT through OpenRouter is gone: `chatOpenRouter` generalises into `chatOpenAIFormat` over one URL/header switch, with a new `byok-openai` provider and bare `gpt-5-mini` / `gpt-5-nano` models. `session_id` and `X-Title` stay OpenRouter-only, because OpenAI rejects unknown body fields rather than ignoring them. OpenRouter remains, since it reaches models OpenAI does not serve and reports exact charged cost.
