The measurement is read at the keyframe's exact frame, because keyframes can be fractional and rounding one to the nearest frame miscalibrated a half-frame keyframe by 9.3%. `AngularSizeMath.js` is a leaf module importing nothing so it stays Jest-testable (in the manner of `FOVUtils`); it uses the endpoint form `(S/2)/sin(theta/2)` rather than the midpoint `(S/2)/tan(theta/2)`, since Sitrec's tracked point is an endpoint and start distance is measured along its line of sight, and the chord form of the angle rather than `acos(dot)`, which throws away half the mantissa at the milliradian angles involved. The measured segment is assumed side-on to the camera: a foreshortened segment subtends a smaller angle, so it reads as a longer range and a higher speed, making these upper estimates under that assumption rather than hard bounds. Cross-checked on a 3-keyframe Perspective sitch by deriving the size points from the existing traverse and feeding them back in — ranges reproduced to within 0.4% and speed to 4.6 kt against the traverse's 4.62 kt. Alt-deleting a keyframe now removes its size point with it, since a size point is a measurement handle on its keyframe rather than an item in its own right.

- **Ordinariness and implied object size on every traverse candidate** — **Traverse → *Analyze Traverse Methods...*** (`7b3f9597`; new `src/TraverseMundaneness.js` with `MUNDANE_CLASSES`, `mundanenessCost`, `mundanenessSummary` and `impliedDiameter`, consumed by `hypothesisStats(h, dataset)` in `src/AnalyzeTraverse.js` for the gallery tile, the Details pane and both HTML report builders). Every candidate now carries an **Ordinariness** row — a number plus a plain-English line such as *"consistent with an ordinary balloon"* or *"nearest ordinary object is a jet, and this misses that envelope by 40x on size and speed"*. The score is **disclosure only and does not move the ranking**; the gallery order is still decided by `TraverseRanking`'s comparator exactly as before, so the number can be judged against real files before it is ever allowed to move anything. It is deliberately **not** a search for mundane explanations at the expense of anomalous ones: an anomalous explanation that fits the sightlines perfectly always exists (the exact-ray track is one), so finding one proves nothing — the falsifiable question is whether a *mundane* explanation exists anywhere in the solution space, and a high cost here is a positive finding about the object rather than a failure to explain it away. Each of seven envelope classes (balloon, bird, multirotor, small fixed-wing, light aircraft, jet, airliner) is scored jointly on size, sustained speed and sustained g, and the candidate keeps the best class it can find — Occam's razor made mechanical. Joint rather than marginal, because a size test alone cannot refute a collapsed solution: a candidate at 500 m implies a 0.28 m object, which is a perfectly ordinary size; what refutes it is 0.28 m sustaining 300 knots. Bands are deliberately generous, since the score exists to identify the impossible rather than enforce a preference, and units are decades outside an envelope, so 0 means every quantity sits inside some real object's envelope and 1 means the best class is off by a factor of ten somewhere. A measured dead end is recorded in the module header so it is not rebuilt: a one-sided range floor at `D_min / theta_max` reduces to `[f/(f + 1/N)] * (D_min/D_true) * R_true` with the field of view cancelling, capping it at about 1% of true range, and over 23 benchmark scenarios it cut 39 of 345 candidates and moved the median result not at all. Alongside it, an **Implied object size** row appears whenever the file carries an angular measurement, and it no longer prints a lower bound it does not have: when the target is under a pixel the published angular bound sits at its floor of exactly `2 * IFOV`, the interval collapses to `[0, hi]`, and *"0.00–2.11 m"* reads as a measurement when only its upper half is one. `impliedDiameter` now returns `oneSided` and the display reads *"under 2.11 m at this range — target is sub-pixel, so there is no lower bound"*. Measured on the straight-balloon set, where a 0.35 m party balloon is 0.05–0.67 px across, the bound was at that floor in all 20 scenarios. The cost arithmetic is deliberately unchanged: a sub-pixel bound is still real evidence — it refutes any candidate collapsed inside `D_min/theta_max`, 611 m for the smallest class — so the size term keeps using the interval exactly as before and only the wording changed. Feeding this, `src/analysis/BotBenchIngest.js` gains BOT interchange **v1.2** `AngularDiameterMaxDeg` ingestion, published onto the dataset as `angularDiameterMaxDeg` along with `fovFullDeg` and `pixelsAcross`. The value is a **median** over the frames the analysis kept, not over every parsed row — `parsed` still holds rows dropped as invalid, rows belonging to another TrackID and rows outside the longest uniform run, and a median over those would describe data the analysis never saw while reaching the reader as an implied object size — and a median rather than a mean because the bound's floor is one IFOV, giving a receding target a long flat tail a mean would let dominate. It is null (not zero) on a v1.1 file or one whose column is entirely blank, and a CSV imported without its sidecar has no sensor block and therefore no IFOV, so its interval stays one-sided rather than collapsing to a false exact size.

- **Historic dates: the Time menu now reaches back to 1700** — **Time menu, and Help → Documentation → *Historic Skies*** (`ade1da58`; `adjustYearRange` and `adjustDaysInMonth` in `src/nodes/CNodeDateTime.js`, new `allowInputExpandMin()` in `src/js/lil-gui.esm.js` mirrored in `src/MenuMirror.js`, new `docs/HistoricSkies.md` registered in `src/docsRegistry.js`, i18n `time.rangeNote.*`; `tests/DateTimeParser.test.js`, `tests/celestialFrame.test.js`). The *Year* slider's minimum was hardcoded to 1947 — the Kenneth Arnold year — and lil-gui clamps typed input to the minimum as well as dragged input, so 1897 was simply unreachable. Everything downstream already worked: the EQJ→ECEF transform matches an independent topocentric solve to 0.004″ across 1700–2200, precession from J2000 to 1896 (1.45°, over three lunar diameters) is applied correctly, and astronomy-engine's Espenak–Meeus ΔT covers the period — so this makes the sighting waves of 1896–1918 reachable. The floor now *moves*: 1947 normally, dropping to 1700 while the date needs it and returning afterwards, so everyday dragging stays fine-grained; lil-gui captures `_originalMin` on the first `min()` call, so the slider-settings *Reset* still restores 1947. `allowInputExpandMin()` is the mirror of `allowInputExpandMax`, letting a year typed into the box lower the floor instead of being clamped up to it, with a hard limit so a slip like "18" cannot reach the range where `Date.UTC()` remaps two-digit years into the 1900s; `MenuMirror` carries both flags to twins so a mirrored menu answers the same keystrokes the same way. A one-line *Note* row appears in the Time menu when the date falls outside 1700–2200 (*"Outside 1700-2200 - Sun, Moon and planet positions degrade"*) or before 1957 (*"Before 1957 - no artificial satellites existed"*, where an empty satellite layer would otherwise read as a bug). `docs/HistoricSkies.md` states what is accurate at these dates and what is not — stellar proper motion is still frozen at catalogue epoch J1991.25, a few arcminutes by 1897 — plus clocks before standard time and what stays anachronistic (modern imagery and buildings, no satellites before 1957).

### Improvements

- **The big slider can resize an elastic range from the bar's end zones** (`b4fb73f7`, merge `f26f9a8e`; `ZONE_PX` / `ZONE_FIRST_STEP_MS` / `ZONE_STEP_MS`, `makeZone` / `zoneAt` / `setZone` / `stepElasticZone` in `src/BigSlider.js`, new `_elasticStepRange()` and an `allowElasticRange` flag on `_setValueFromX` / `_dragStart` / `_dragMove` in `src/js/lil-gui.esm.js`, styles in `src/extra.css.js`; `tests/BigSliderElastic.test.js`). The big slider shipped in 2.133.0, but elastic sliders were the one thing it could not simply inherit. An elastic range grows when the pointer goes *past* the end of the track, so the real budget for growth is the screen between the slider and the edge of the window: a menu slider is about 80 px wide with sixteen track widths of room to its right and doubles its way to `_elasticMax` happily, while the big slider's bar is as wide as the window with a ~48 px gutter, so the mapped value could only reach about 1.03× the starting maximum — one doubling, then stuck. Shrinking failed the other way, halving `_max` once per `pointermove` event, so its speed depended on the pointer's report rate. The bar now stands the distance rule down (`allowElasticRange = false`) and grows the range from **time** instead: a 60 px zone at each end, marked « and », where holding a drag steps the range every 300 ms after a 450 ms initial wait — so crossing a zone on the way to the end of the bar resizes nothing. `_elasticStepRange()` doubles or halves `_max` with no pointer position involved and re-seeds `_maxClick` so the new headroom is reachable; each step re-applies the value from the held pointer X, because a pointer that is not moving sends no `pointermove`. The zones reach outward past the end of the bar, so the gutter behaves the same as the strip, and they are inert to pointer events so the press still lands on the track. Menu sliders keep the distance rule and are unchanged.

- **One color for camera, target and truth tracks everywhere** (`f3ee2749`; the role block in `VIZ` in `src/TraverseHypotheses.js`, `roleHintForColor` in `src/TrackManager.js`, `TRACK_COLORS` in `src/CTrackBrowser.js`, `commonTargetTrack` / `commonTrackedCamera` in `src/sitch/CommonSitch.js`; `tests/trackRoleColors.test.js`). A camera track was a different color in each of four places: the 3D scene gave it whatever palette slot its name sorted into, the traverse charts drew it warm grey, the Track Browser light blue, and `CommonSitch` yellow — the same yellow as the "other" track, so in a legacy sitch the camera and the other track could not be told apart. `VIZ` now holds the three role colors and every surface reads them. The 3D scene gains role coloring at all: `trackRoleHint()` was already consulted to *choose* the camera and target tracks and was simply never used to color them. The three roles do not all share a surface, which is what makes one palette possible — target is never drawn on a traverse chart, because there the target *is* the hypothesis — so target only has to clear truth. Values were measured rather than picked (weighted-RGB separation; under about 0.4 reads as a collision at a glance): camera `#7fd4e8`, 0.63 from its nearest hypothesis color, against 0.50 for the Track Browser's old `#4fc3f7` versus `constAir`, the most common line on a chart, and chromatic rather than grey so it reads as a role in 3D instead of sinking into terrain; target `#ff0000`, the legacy value and also the best separated at 1.14 from truth and 1.10 from `slowObj`, against 0.47 and 0.61 for a softened `#e8564d`; truth `#e0569f`, unchanged, and now dashed in the Track Browser as well, since it shares a surface with target only on a BOT file where they are the same object, so the dash rather than the hue says which one is the answer key. Reserving three hues costs the open palette their neighbours: `TRACK_PALETTE` drops salmon (0.46 from target red) and rose (0.43 from truth), from 16 entries to 14. Role tracks are deliberately **not** marked `paletteColored`, so `reassignTrackColors()`'s deterministic rank-by-`shortName` pass skips them — a role is stable, so its color must not depend on how many other tracks loaded or what they were called. `VIZ.sensor` remains as an alias of `VIZ.camera` so chart code can keep reading "sensor" where that is the domain word. The tests pin the values *and* the two measurements that decided them, because an assertion on the hexes alone reads as arbitrary preference and invites exactly the "improvement" that reintroduces a collision.

- **BOT Bench reports how ordinary each result is, in bulk** — **File → File Analysis → *BOTBench...*** (`7b3f9597`; `mundaneness` in `summarizeRun` in `src/analysis/BotBenchRunner.js`, the `Ord` / `OrdMin` / `OrdErr` columns and ten new `CSV_COLUMNS` entries in `src/analysis/BotBenchUI.js`; `tests/botbench/csvColumnsCoverRecord.test.js`, `tests/botbench/mundanenessSize.test.js`). The runner never imported `TraverseMundaneness`, so a bulk run could not measure what the gallery displayed, which made the score unfalsifiable at scale. Rows now carry the same score from the same function on the same dataset, as **two separate claims**: `Ord`, how ordinary the candidate we picked is, and `OrdMin`, how ordinary the data *allows* any candidate to be. On a bearings-only problem the second is routinely far lower, because choosing a different range makes almost any motion ordinary, and a single column would hide exactly that. `OrdMin` is deliberately ungated by residual — no threshold here is calibrated yet — so `OrdErr`, that candidate's own mean angular error, sits beside it and the reader applies their own bar; a bare `0.00` would otherwise read as "an ordinary explanation fits" when it does not. A low `OrdMin` at a low `OrdErr` beside a high `Ord` is the real finding: an ordinary explanation exists *at a different range* and the sightlines alone cannot choose between them. Both numbers use the same admission rule and an at-infinity winner is excluded from both, because an astronomical hypothesis carries an artificial finite helper track and scoring it would report a star as "consistent with an ordinary balloon". Ten fields join the CSV (`ordTop`, `ordTopClass`, the per-term `ordTopSize` / `ordTopSpeed` / `ordTopG` breakdown that makes a cost falsifiable, `ordTopSizeOneSided`, and `ordMin` / `ordMinClass` / `ordMinName` / `ordMinErrDeg`). The export builds each line from `CSV_COLUMNS` rather than from the record, so a populated key the list omits is dropped in silence — that has happened, and `csvColumnsCoverRecord.test.js` now asserts the record is a subset of the columns so the next added field cannot vanish the same way. Sidecar pairing moves into `botBenchPairingKeys` (`src/analysis/BotBenchIngest.js`), which supports both layouts: sibling (`Input/x.input.csv` + `Input/x.scenario.json`, sealed releases) and meta (`Input/x.input.csv` + `meta/x.scenario.json`, the botset trees). A sidecar inside a `meta/` directory indexes one level up and a CSV tries its own directory then its parent; both keys still carry the full batch path, so pairing a scenario with another batch's frame origin — a wrong answer that looks like a right one — stays impossible.

- **The Help menu no longer lists the bespoke case studies** — **Help → Documentation** (`c58a9c9c`; the `examples` section removed from `DOC_SECTIONS` in `src/docsRegistry.js` and from `menus.help.documentation.sections` in `src/i18n/en.js`; `tests/docsRegistry.test.js`). *Recreating Gimbal*, *Nimitz / Tic Tac* and *Football and Cable Cam* are one-off case studies rather than things a typical user needs, and the *Worked Examples* folder they occupied only made the menu longer. Omitting `section` from a registry entry now means "keep this doc out of the Help menu entirely": it stays listed in `README.md` (under *Bespoke examples (not typical)*) and, with a `chatDesc`, stays available to the AI assistant. The registry test was relaxed accordingly, but only in a way that keeps the failure it exists to catch — a doc with no section must have a `chatDesc`, or nothing can ever reach it.

- **Full-width admin dashboard layout** — **the admin dashboard** (`48152ea0`; `sitrecServer/admin_dashboard.php`). Reorganized into a dense full-window presentation with a seven-metric summary row, compact history charts and a balanced multi-column flow for the operational cards, removing the large unused regions around *Visitors Today* and the other partially filled grid rows while keeping every existing metric and drill-down. Table and card spacing tightened, inactive history series labelled instead of rendering blank charts, and per-model AI cost details moved into their own card. Responsive breakpoints retain useful packing on narrower screens; verified at 1548 px, 1200 px and 700 px.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed the traverse analysis penalising its own most precise fits** — **Traverse → *Analyze Traverse Methods...*** (`b711b542`; the collapsed-simplex early return in `localFitCompletionWarnings` in `src/TraverseRanking.js`). The function flagged *every* `iteration_limit` stop as an incomplete search. Nelder-Mead here stops only on **both** a flat objective and a collapsed simplex, so a fit can exhaust its budget with the simplex already at `xTol` while `costSpread` still sits above `tol` — and at that point no further iteration can help, because there is no x-movement left to shrink the cost spread with. Calling that "budget exhausted before convergence" is a false negative, not a cautious one, and it penalised **precision**, which is the wrong way round: measured on a benchmark balloon (`botset_balloons_orbit`, r3.219 km, steady wind), the fit that recovered truth to relSep 0.00015 drove its simplex to a full collapse, was stamped incomplete, lost the balloon class its viability, and the file reported *"Unresolved"* — while a deliberately sloppier fit of the same file (residual 100× worse, range 200 m out, relSep 0.032) landed in a broad flat basin, met the cost tolerance, was stamped complete, and resolved. The better the answer, the likelier it was refused. A fully collapsed simplex now returns no warning. This is the complement of `settledButUnidentifiable` below it — that one handles "cost settled, some parameters still wide", this handles "all parameters collapsed, cost not settled" — and between them the only remaining `iteration_limit` stop is a search that really was still moving. The per-parameter `parameterSpreads` array is preferred over the scalar `parameterSpread`, because one wide dimension is what "still moving" means, and absent metadata keeps the warning: silence is never inferred from a missing measurement. Measured over 43 scenarios (balloons_orbit + mundane + anomalies, 20 s, clean): unresolved 18→17, consistent-one 17→15, consistent-several 8→11, with anomalous files reporting a conventional verdict unchanged at 2/15 — six scenarios changed, all mundane balloons, four gaining the balloon class they should always have had, and no new conventional explanation appearing on a declared-anomalous file, which was the risk worth watching. The flag also feeds `plausibilityRating`'s `eligible`, so the incompleteness stamp was demoting the most accurate fits out of the top slot: `topRelSep` improved from 0.044, 0.066, 0.016 and 0.011 to under 0.00002 on five files, with one moving the other way (`anom-figureeight-implausible`, 0.051→0.187, verdict unchanged and still correct).

- **Fixed a sky-lantern fit being called an incomplete search because of the wind's compass direction** — **Traverse → *Analyze Traverse Methods...*** (`d901ba04`; the `windE` / `windN` bounds and the matching seed clamp in `getParameterDefs` / the seed block of `src/SkyLanternModel.js`; `tests/SkyLanternModel.test.js`). The wind was bounded per component at ±20 m/s, and a per-component box cuts the corner off a circle: a bound *b* makes wind of magnitude *b* reachable from every bearing but *b*·√2 only along the diagonal, so ±20 gave 39 kt omnidirectional against 55 kt diagonal. Measured on a benchmark scenario, a true wind of 21.5 m/s on bearing 68° needed `windE = 20.0` — exactly the ceiling — so an ordinary 42 kt wind aloft pinned for no reason but its direction, and an active pin makes `judgeRepresentative()` report "search incomplete", which cost the balloon class its viability on a file whose balloon fit was exact. Bounds are now ±40 m/s and the seed clamp moves with them, since a seed clamped tighter than the search starts the optimizer on the wall it exists to let the fit leave. **The bound's role changes with this, deliberately.** At ±20 the box was doing double duty — bracketing the search *and* quietly excluding non-lantern motion — and the two jobs wanted different numbers. Exclusion now rests where it can be reasoned about: the `extraCost` speed prior, which still prefers light winds, and the kinematic ordinariness screen. The box declines to *prefer* a fast wind rather than refusing one. The cost is recorded rather than glossed: the diagonal now admits 110 kt, which is not lantern-like, so the test no longer asserts that the wind box forbids non-lantern motion (it does not) and instead asserts what remains true — symmetric, finite, and generous enough to reach ordinary winds aloft from any bearing — while pinning the 110 kt diagonal as a known consequence. The vertical-rate bounds, which do still exclude, are unchanged; a magnitude constraint (speed and bearing, with speed bounded) would give the circle the physics describes and restore the exclusion honestly, and stays queued. Measured over the same 43 scenarios against the collapsed-simplex fix alone, two verdicts moved (both mundane balloons, one gaining the balloon class and one losing it), anomalous files reporting a conventional verdict stayed at 2/15, and `topRelSep` moved on seven files — close to a wash in aggregate, with the file that prompted it now viable at relSep 0.00001.

- **Fixed a sitch that names its own time zone having that setting ignored** (`c75fec6c`; the `Sit.timeZone` block in `src/nodes/CNodeDateTime.js`, documented in `docs/HistoricSkies.md`). `Sit.timeZone` was looked up into `timeZoneName` and then immediately thrown away again, because `setTimeZoneNameFromOffset()` was called unconditionally a few lines later and overwrites the name *and* the offset with the browser's — so the setting had no effect at all for a sitch defined in code. `SitAriel` asks for EET (UTC+2) and rendered its clock nine hours out from a California browser; `SitFlir1`'s PST only looked right because the machine happened to agree. Saved sitches were never affected, because `modDeserialize` restores their serialized `timeZoneName` afterwards — which is why this survived unnoticed and why no regression baseline moves. The browser zone is still the fallback when nothing names one, and is still read off the simulation date so it carries the right daylight-saving rule for that date; a `Sit.timeZone` matching no known entry now warns rather than being silently ignored. The fallback is derived once from the sitch's own start time, so typing a historic date into a modern sitch does not re-derive it.

- **Fixed the celestial direction arrows swinging off the body they name after a recalculate** — **Show → Celestial → *Sun Vector*, *Moon Vector*, *Venus Vector* and the rest** (`9a803ac4`; `directionOverride`, `directionFromCode` and the `pointed` getter on `CNodeLabeledArrow` in `src/nodes/CNodeLabels3D.js`, and the arrow construction in `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayNightSky.js`). `updateDirection()` wrote straight onto `this.direction`, which `calculateVectors()` then overwrote from the `direction` **input** on the next recalculate. That input is only the placeholder the node was constructed with — ECEF (0,0,1), the north celestial pole — so every cascade swung the arrows about 80° off the body they name until the next night-sky `update()` re-pointed them; `lookCamera` is their `start` input, so every camera-driven cascade did it (startup, terrain and tile loads, navigation). A direction pushed in from outside is now kept in `directionOverride` and preferred over the input from then on, and the override is set *before* recomputing so start, end and label position are built from the new direction rather than from the placeholder. Separately, `directionFromCode: true` marks an arrow whose direction is pushed in by code, and such an arrow is not drawn at all until it has been pointed once — enabling the toggle or deserializing a sitch makes the arrow visible several rendered frames before the next night-sky update points it, and the placeholder it showed meanwhile was the north celestial pole.

- **Fixed manual tracking mapping video pixels to sightlines with an equirectangular projection instead of a lens one** — **Traverse → Manual Tracking** (`6d1c332d`; new `rayForVideoXY` replacing the yaw-then-pitch construction in `getValueFrame` in `src/nodes/CNodeTrackingOverlay.js`; `tests/AngularSizeMath.test.js` pins the old error). The line of sight was built by yawing `atan(dx/f)` about up and then pitching `atan(dy/f)` about the already-yawed axis. That is an equirectangular mapping: a vertical pixel step subtended the same angle wherever it sat in the frame. A real lens compresses that step away from the vertical centre line, because the ray to an off-axis pixel is longer and the effective focal length in that plane is `hypot(f, dx)`, not `f`. At 1920×1080 and a 22.76° vertical FOV the old mapping overstated a vertical step by 2.15% a third of the way out and 6.21% at the frame edge — invisible for a single tracked point near the centre, but it scales the whole line of sight near the edges, and it directly corrupts angular-size ranging, which reads the local scale of the mapping rather than just a position. The ray is now a true rectilinear pinhole projection built directly in original-video pixel space. **This changes existing manual-tracking sitches**, most where points were tracked away from the centre of the frame. Also relabels the *Limit AB* checkbox to *Limit In/Out to Tracked Range* and corrects its tooltip: it does not prevent extrapolation, it sets the In/Out range to the keyframe span plus a 10% margin at each end.

- **Fixed 29 February being offered in 1900** — **Time menu** (`ade1da58`; `adjustDaysInMonth()` in `src/nodes/CNodeDateTime.js`; `tests/DateTimeParser.test.js`). A bare `year % 4` test offered 29 February 1900, which `Date.UTC()` then rolled silently to 1 March. The full Gregorian rule now applies.

- **Fixed the downloaded SitrecBridge package failing to start its MCP server on macOS and Linux** — **Help → Documentation → *Download MCP Bridge*** (`f2a43ea1`; `tools/SitrecBridge/run.sh`, `run.bat`, `tools/SitrecBridge/tests/launcher.test.js`). The launchers hardcoded `mcp-server.js`, which exists in a source checkout but not in a distribution build, where the bundled server is `mcp-server.mjs`. Both launchers now prefer `mcp-server.mjs` and fall back to `mcp-server.js`, with a clear error when neither is beside the script, so downloaded packages work while the repository development workflow is retained; regression coverage added for both layouts. The bundled guide (`tools/SitrecBridge/README.md`) gains platform-specific Codex and Claude Code configuration, connection checks, scope guidance, usage examples, update steps and startup troubleshooting, with links to the official client documentation and Claude Desktop kept as an optional path.

- **Fixed a transport stream's audio track deciding the frame rate and length of the sitch** (`f07fbc78`; new `definesSitchTimeline()` guarding the two `Sit.videoFrames` / `Sit.fps` / `updateSitFrames()` write sites in `decodeMP3Audio` and `startAudioExtraction` in `src/CVideoAudioOnly.js`, with `ownsTimeline` now also passed at the two `CVideoAudioOnly` construction sites in `src/nodes/CNodeVideoView.js` and `src/nodes/CNodeVideoWebCodecView.js`). A `.ts` demuxes to elementary streams, and each is registered as an entry in the **same** video view — so an H.264 video and its AAC audio track become `video[0]` and `video[1]` of one view. `CVideoAudioOnly` then wrote `Sit.videoFrames` and `Sit.fps` unconditionally on load, while every other video class guards that write with `ownsTimeline`: *"only the timeline-owning (primary) video defines the sitch timeline; a secondary 'video2' must not"* (`src/CVideoH264Data.js:542`, C1 of the 2.70.0 review). This class never did, which is a real defect once a single view holds more than one entry. `ownsTimeline` cannot separate these two, because both entries sit in the same timeline-owning view and it is true for both. The distinction that actually matters is not which **view** owns the timeline but which **entry** the view is showing, which `videoData` already answers: `definesSitchTimeline()` short-circuits on `ownsTimeline` as before, then iterates `NodeMan` for any node whose `videos` array contains this entry and returns true only when that node's `videoData === this` — an audio track nobody selected does not get to say how long the sitch is. An entry not yet registered in any view (a standalone audio file still mid-load, or a unit test) keeps the historical behaviour, because there a lone audio file genuinely *is* the timeline. **The frame rate was the worse half of this, and it was fabricated rather than mismeasured.** `this.originalFps` is a constructor constant — `this.originalFps = 30` — not a value read from the file: sound has no frame rate, and the same class describes the figure elsewhere as "a synthetic 30fps invented to give the timeline something to step through", with `getMediaInfo()` deliberately declining to report it as media metadata because doing so "would be simply untrue". Publishing it through `Sit.fps` handed the whole sitch an invented rate. Measured on the Truck regression sitch, `Sit.frames` was 4445 against the video's 4439 PES timestamps, and `Sit.fps` was that flat 30 rather than the video's 29.97; both now read the video's values. The two symptoms decompose from that one bad write rather than being independent bugs, and the split matters because the intuitive reading has it backwards: of the six extra frames roughly four and a half come from the invented 30 fps applied across the same wall-clock duration (4439 frames at 29.97 fps is 148.11 s, and `Math.ceil(148.11 × 30)` is 4444), and only about one more from the audio genuinely outlasting the video through AAC encoder padding, plus the `ceil()`. Six frames past the end of the footage is enough to extrapolate every track beyond its data — on Cheyenne, where the evidence was visual rather than numeric, a target's AGL read 3 ft where it should read 2, a track ran off the edge of the view, and the sightline fan shifted with the sub-frame time offset. Separately, the guard needed the construction sites fixed to have any teeth: `CVideoData` defaults `ownsTimeline` to `v.ownsTimeline ?? true`, and the two `CVideoAudioOnly` branches never passed it although the H264/Mp4 branches beside them always had — so `definesSitchTimeline()`'s `ownsTimeline` test could never fail, and an audio file dropped into a secondary "video2" view redefined the timeline regardless. This affects any transport stream carrying an audio track alongside video, which is the normal case for MISB/FMV `.ts` files, not just the two sitches it was found on. Both had been failing visual regression against baselines captured sixteen days earlier at 41157 px and 28551 px, and now pass at 857 px and 399 px — the latter matching its historical figure exactly, so the baselines were right and regenerating them would have made the defect permanent.

### Documentation

- **BOTBench documentation brought back in line with the window, and its provenance half split out** (`94fa1333` plus the release-commit changes to `docs/BOTBench.md`, new `docs/BOTBenchScenarios.md`, `src/docsRegistry.js` and `src/i18n/en.js`; **Help → Documentation → *BOTBench — Bearings-Only Traversal Bulk Analysis*** and the new ***BOTBench Scenario Files — where they come from***). The page had drifted fifteen commits to `src/analysis` behind the window it describes. The generated scenarios are now documented as two families — the curated interchange set, and beside it the five botsets (456 scenarios over five swept grids) with their folder layout, npm commands and the four design decisions a reader needs before quoting any number off them. The table documentation adds *Target*, *Platform*, *Spd*, *Alt* and *Best* and removes *Rate* and *Decl*, which no longer exist (*Decl* folded into *Noise*, now a ratio; the *Probe* column retired into the *Src* tooltip); `|err|` is documented with its noise floor, since the residual is nearly invariant to where along the sightline a track sits and a column showing it alone invited the opposite conclusion. New sections cover the column scatter plots, opening a row in Sitrec, the result cache, the ordinariness score and implied object size, plus *"Why a good fit can still read Unresolved"*, which explains the simplex, why these fits require both a flat objective and a collapsed one, and the two ways of reaching the iteration budget that are really convergence. The accepted-format list extends to track CSVs, DJI `.srt` and STANAG 4676; the flat-terrain caveat is corrected now that an FMV ground plane comes from the file's own frame-centre elevations; and eleven glossary entries were added. The screenshot was removed rather than re-captioned — it showed *Choose Folder*, *Rate* and *Decl*, three controls that no longer exist, and a caption cannot fix an image that misrepresents the interface. The page then stood at 61,229 bytes, past the 60,000-byte truncation limit `getHelpDoc` applies, which cut it off mid-document with the assistant unable to see what was removed and failed `tests/docsRegistry.test.js`. Provenance is the self-contained half, so it moved to `docs/BOTBenchScenarios.md` (9,471 bytes) with its own registry entry and `chatDesc`, leaving the main page at 52,972 bytes with room to grow.

- **Plans, roadmaps and review reports removed from `docs/`, and dot-files no longer published** (`88be7b1d`; the registry header rules in `src/docsRegistry.js`, the skip in `MarkdownToHtmlPlugin` in `webpack.common.js` and the copy `ignore` list in `webpack.standalone.js`; `tests/docsRegistry.test.js`). Everything under `docs/` is published to the live site both as rendered `.html` and as raw `.md`, and the raw `.md` is what `getHelpDoc` feeds the assistant, so a plan left in `docs/` ships and gets quoted. Roughly two dozen plan and review documents were deleted from `docs/` and `docs/plans/`; the rule is now written into the registry header — plans belong in `docs/temp/`, which is gitignored and skipped by the build. The build was also publishing dot-entries: `docs/.DS_Store` encodes the **names** of everything in the directory, including the local-only ones. `MarkdownToHtmlPlugin` now skips any entry starting with `.`, and the standalone copy adds `**/.*` and `**/.*/**` to its ignore list, because `copy-webpack-plugin` globs with `dot: true`.

- **BOT interchange format taken to v1.2, and the benchmark scenarios republished as five botsets** (`6d4c9b1a`, merge `d490db84`; `benchmarks/botbench/BOT-Interchange-Format.html`, new `lib/angularSize.js`, `lib/botsetManeuvers.js`, `lib/botsetBalloons.js`, `lib/botsetManeuverBatch.js`, `lib/botsetBalloonBatch.js`, `lib/botsetErrors.js`, `botset-maneuvers.bench.test.js`, `botset-balloons.bench.test.js`, `run-botset-maneuvers.mjs`; `bench-bot-m1` / `bench-bot-m1-par` / `bench-bot-m2` become `bench-bot-maneuvers` / `bench-bot-maneuvers-par` / `bench-bot-balloons` in `package.json`). Benchmark infrastructure, with one consequence that reaches the app: the format spec now publishes an **angular-diameter bound**, `max(theta, IFOV) + IFOV`, which is what the ingest change above reads. It is a bound and never an exact size — the extra pixel is deliberate, because overstating theta only weakens the range floor `D_min/theta` the bound implies, which is the safe direction. The `m1` and `m2-balloons` trees are replaced by five published sets over the same 456 scenarios, cut differently: `botset_anomalies` (180), `botset_mundane` (96), and `botset_balloons_straight` / `_curve` / `_orbit` (60 each). The maneuver taxonomy is partitioned by anomaly so "did we find the mundane answer" and "did we correctly report an anomaly" stop being one mixed number over one mixed folder, while both halves share a spec builder, a seed and both ladders so they stay comparable. The error ladder is a percentage of the field of view (0/5/20) rather than an absolute angle, because a fixed 0.15° error was 33% of the frame in one scenario and 3.9% in another, sweeping difficulty and geometry together with no way to separate them downstream; the resolved angle is still published in `scenario.json` and every manifest row. Both sidecars live in a `meta/` folder so the CSV folders hold only CSVs, which costs the folder-level blinding a sealed release needs — so `writeInterchange` keeps the sibling layout as its default and refuses to combine `sidecarDir` with `descriptiveName`.

## Version 2.139.0 (2026-08-18)

### New Features

- **OpenRouter BYOK for OpenAI models** — **Settings → *API Keys…*, then Settings → *AI Model*** (`85e6209a`; the `openrouter` registry entry in `src/BYOKProviders.js`, `BYOK_OPENROUTER_PROVIDER` / `callOpenRouter` / `chatOpenRouter` in `src/CDirectLLMClient.js`, and provider dispatch in `src/nodes/CNodeVIewChat.js`). Saving an OpenRouter key adds *OpenAI GPT-5 Mini (your OpenRouter key)* and *OpenAI GPT-5 Nano (your OpenRouter key)* to the model list. The browser calls `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions` directly, so neither the credential nor the conversation passes through Sitrec’s server; the key goes only to OpenRouter, while the system instructions, chat history, tool definitions and tool results necessarily reach both OpenRouter and its selected upstream provider. The OpenAI-format tool loop preserves assistant calls and results across iterations, refuses a length-truncated action instead of executing it with missing arguments, and sends a stable per-chat `session_id`. OpenRouter’s reported `usage.cost` is banked as the authoritative charge when present, with model-price fallbacks otherwise; the API Keys dialog filters Anthropic and OpenRouter totals separately instead of showing their combined spend on both rows. `docs/APIKeys.md` documents the storage, routing and disclosure boundary explicitly.

- **Auto (economy) model selection** — **Settings → *AI Model*** (`85e6209a`; the synthetic `auto:economy` option in `sitrecServer/chatbot.php` and `economyModelFor` in `sitrecServer/ai_models.php`). The selector now offers *Auto (economy)* when the account has at least one server-funded model. Each request resolves that choice to the lowest estimated-cost model among the models the user’s groups and the server’s configured keys actually permit, using the assistant’s input-heavy workload to weight input and output prices. `sitrecServer/aimask.php` resolves the same saved choice against the vision-capable subset for AI ground masking, so a globally selected economy mode does not turn into an invalid provider at the image endpoint.

- **Server AI spend accounting** — **the admin dashboard and AI usage page** (`85e6209a`; pricing and cache multipliers in `sitrecServer/ai_models.php`, normalization and `recordAISpend` in `sitrecServer/ai_log.php`, and the new displays in `sitrecServer/admin_dashboard.php` / `sitrecServer/ai_usage.php`). Provider-reported usage from chat and AI masking is normalized into full-price input, cached reads, cache writes and output, then accumulated across every provider call and browser continuation belonging to one user request. Cost is banked at the price in effect when the call occurs, stored in integer micro-dollars, attached to the rolling 500-request log, and rolled into persistent 28-day totals by model. The admin dashboard now shows total and daily spend, provider-call and request counts, token totals, cache-read share, per-model cost and warnings for reachable models without a price; individual request rows and the per-user usage page expose recent-window calls, tokens and cost.

### Improvements

- **Assistant turns use fewer tokens and unnecessary provider calls** (`85e6209a`; `buildSystemPromptParts` / `buildToolSet` in `src/CDirectLLMClient.js`, the matching prompt and tool construction in `sitrecServer/chatbot.php`, `CHAT_MODEL_RESULT_CALLS` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, and continuation handling in `src/nodes/CNodeVIewChat.js`). The simulation clock previously appeared near the start of an approximately 100 KB cached prefix, changing almost every turn and forcing Anthropic to write a new cache entry rather than read the old one. The prompt is now ordered into static instructions and help-document index, per-sitch menu IDs, and an uncached volatile clock, with cache breakpoints only after stable tiers. The menu appendix names menus rather than shipping roughly 409 controls on every request; `listMenuControls` supplies paths on demand. Tool descriptions no longer repeat their parsed `Parameters:` tails, and the large schemas for `createWalker`, `createSynthBuilding`, `createSynthOverlay` and `createSynthClouds` load only after `discoverSpecialistTools` requests them. Finally, a successful batch containing actions only is acknowledged locally with “Done.” instead of buying another model turn merely for confirmation, while failures and calls whose returned information the model must interpret still continue normally. The same behavior is maintained across the server, Anthropic BYOK and OpenRouter BYOK paths.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed mixed query-and-action requests losing the query result** (`85e6209a`; `runToolLoop` in `sitrecServer/chatbot.php` and `allSucceeded` / `actionOnly` / `requiresContinuation` handling in `src/nodes/CNodeVIewChat.js`). When a model requested a server-handled query and a browser-executed action together, the old loop stopped at the action before adding the query result to history; the browser then saw only successful actions and could skip the continuation the query needed. Handled results are now recorded first, mixed batches explicitly require continuation, and only genuinely action-only success is completed locally.

- **Fixed incomplete model output being able to run an action with its arguments missing** (`85e6209a`; `refuseIfTruncatedToolCall` in `sitrecServer/chatbot.php` and the equivalent OpenRouter guard in `src/CDirectLLMClient.js`). OpenAI-compatible providers return `finish_reason: "length"` when an output cap cuts off a tool call; decoding that partial argument string previously produced null and the parser converted it into an empty argument object, allowing the action to run in the wrong form. OpenAI, Groq, Grok and OpenRouter now refuse such a call and tell the user to retry with a shorter request.

### Security

- **AI spending and request bounds now fail closed** (`85e6209a`; validation and `consumeProviderRateLimit` in `sitrecServer/chatbot.php`, locking in `checkRateLimit`, and permission checks shared through `sitrecServer/ai_models.php`). Rate limits now consume one unit for every actual provider call—including tool-loop iterations and continuations—and remain active when analytics logging is disabled; exclusive file locking prevents concurrent requests from losing increments. The chat endpoint rejects oversized or wrongly typed structured fields before prompt construction, and an explicitly requested provider/model pair must match the account’s server-generated allowlist instead of silently falling back to another model. AI masking applies the same authorization after resolving *Auto (economy)*.

## Version 2.138.0 (2026-08-18)

### New Features

- **Label List — draw only the sky labels you name** — **Show → Celestial → *Label List*** (`00746533`; `labelList` / `labelListPrefixes` / `labelPasses` / `labelPassesAny` in `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayNightSky.js`, `satelliteLabelText` / `satelliteLabelNames` and the filter tests in `renderStarNames` / `renderSatelliteNames` in `src/nodes/CNodeDisplaySkyOverlay.js`, i18n `nightSky.labelList`). A text box, empty by default and then a no-op — everything is labelled as before. When it holds a comma-separated list, only labels whose name matches an entry are drawn: star common names, planets, the Sun and the Moon (both are entries in `CPlanets.planetSprites`, so the planet loop covers them), and satellites alike. Matching is case-insensitive and by PREFIX, the same rule the satellite *List* filter already uses, so `sl-30` catches every SL-30xx and `polaris` catches Polaris. IT FILTERS LABELS, NOT OBJECTS — the stars, planets and satellites themselves are still drawn; this decides what text gets written beside them, underneath the per-view *Star Names* / *Only Label Planets* toggles it further narrows. The GUI row is added in `addNightSky()` rather than in the constructor so it lands BELOW those per-view rows in the folder, with the toggles it qualifies. A SATELLITE MATCHES ON EITHER NAME IT ANSWERS TO: the abbreviated text its label is drawn with (`SL-1234`) and the catalog name behind it (`STARLINK-1234`, with any TLE line-0 marker stripped). Keeping that equivalence on the satellite, in `satelliteLabelNames`, rather than widening the typed prefix is deliberate — rewriting a typed "STARLINK-1" into a bare "SL-1" would also catch the unrelated SL-16 R/B Zenit rocket bodies that appear in mixed catalogues. The parsed prefix list is cached against the source string rather than invalidated from the GUI `onChange`, because deserializing a saved sitch assigns `labelList` directly and never passes through the GUI; `addSimpleSerial("labelList")` means a filter saves and restores with the sitch. Cost is the other way round from the obvious: in the satellite pass the test sits AHEAD of the screen projection and the Earth-occlusion raycast, so a filtered-out name costs less rather than more, and with the box empty it is one null check per label. `satData` runs to ~11,000 entries, so the label text — previously rebuilt with two `String.replace` calls for every visible satellite every frame — is now cached on the record by `satelliteLabelText`, which is safe because loading a new TLE/OMM file builds fresh `satData` objects.

### Improvements

- **A failed API call now carries enough detail for an AI agent to repair it** (`ba4ac81d`; `_suggestControls`, `_withControlSuggestions`, `_suggestFunctions`, `tokenizeControlAddress` / `nearWord`, and the qualified-path parse in `_resolveControl`, all in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). Every agent-facing exit was a dead end: "Control 'X' not found" with nothing to try next, which is how one wrong menu id turned into a run of identical retries. A failed control lookup now comes back with near-miss addresses in fully qualified `menu:Folder/Control` form, both appended to `.error` (for a caller that reads only the string) and as a structured `suggestions` array. They are scored on SHARED WORDS, not substrings, so a typo still lands — "Annotate/Edt Mode" shares *annotate* and *mode* with `video:Annotate/Edit Mode` — with `nearWord` accepting a prefix of three characters or more; a plain substring test recommended "Export Debug Log" for `xyzzyphlogiston`, which contains *log*. Only the joint-best score is returned, shortest address first, capped at six, because a query matching a dozen unrelated controls on the word "Mode" alone buries the answer. CRUCIALLY `_resolveControl` now PARSES the `menu:Folder/Control` form it hands out, so a suggestion is valid input; without that, retrying a suggestion failed with the same suggestion attached — a loop that looks like progress and never ends. It splits only on a prefix that really is a menu id, so a control name keeps its own colons. An unknown API function name comes back with `_suggestFunctions` (substring either way, else a shared four-character opening); a handler that throws comes back with `expected`, the parameter list it actually takes; an unknown menu id comes back with the real menu ids. Separately, `handleAPICall` no longer wraps an inner `{success:false}` in an outer `success:true` — the MCP bridge hands that whole object to an agent, where it reads as "it worked". This applies to every caller, not just agent ones. Scoring walks every menu once and runs only on the failure path.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed a lone number typed into the chat being answered by Sitrec instead of reaching the assistant** — **the *Assistant* chat window** (`8f67bd4c`; the `math_expression` and `set_time_simple` patterns in `src/CClientNLU.js`). Every message goes through the local NLU before the assistant sees it, and a matched intent SHORT-CIRCUITS — `CNodeViewChat` renders the local response and returns, so the model never sees the text. Two patterns claimed a bare number. `math_expression` evaluated it and replied "2 = 2" (`${expression} = ${answer}`); `set_time_simple`, whose every keyword was optional, read it as a clock time and `setHours(2, 0, 0)` silently moved the sitch clock to 02:00. Either way, answering "2" to a numbered list of options the assistant had just offered left it waiting on a choice the user had already made. Both patterns now decline, on the principle that a message which is nothing but a number is an ANSWER, not a command. `math_expression` splits the "did the user ask me to evaluate" test from the punctuation strip, and the bare-number guard runs after the strip — which now also removes a trailing `.` — so "2.", "2?" and "2!" route to the assistant too, while "what is 2" is still answered locally because the user explicitly asked. `set_time_simple` CAPTURES the "time" keyword as `match[1]` and, without it, requires a time-shaped value (minutes or am/pm), so "2:30", "2pm" and "time 2" still work; note this is broader than a bare number — "set 2" no longer sets the clock either, which is the point, since the "set" is doing no work that "2" alone did not.

- **Fixed a failed assistant call raising modal error dialogs at the user instead of going back to the assistant** — **the *Assistant* chat window, and external agents over the SitrecBridge extension** (`ba4ac81d`, mechanism corrected before release in `dfdc3741` and `da37e5bf`; `AGENT_SOURCES` and `handleAPICall` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, `Globals.errorDialogSinks` / `Globals.errorDialogTarget` in `src/Globals.js`, the capture branch in `src/showError.js`, `toolPayloadForModel` / `errorTextOf` in `src/nodes/CNodeVIewChat.js`, `"mcp"` source in `tools/SitrecBridge/extension/page-bridge.js`). A chat session asked for `setMenuValue {menu:'view', path:'Annotate/Edit Mode'}` and the user got a stack of `setMenuValue failed:` modals about a call they did not make and could not fix, while the model — which got only the inner result — retried the same wrong call until its continuation depth ran out. A MODAL IS THE WRONG DESTINATION TWICE OVER: the agent cannot read it, and the person cannot act on it. `handleAPICall` now classifies its caller — `"chat"` (in-app chatbot) and `"mcp"` (an external agent through SitrecBridge, new here, extension 1.0.61) are agents, everything else is a person — and for an agent it registers a sink that `showError` writes into instead of putting a dialog on screen; the text returns as `errorDialogs`. The hook catches dialogs raised deep inside a handler, not just the one in the API. A person still sees the dialog, and `showChoice` is untouched — the external-sitch write confirmation runs before the sink is armed and still prompts. Both chat paths now forward the WHOLE failure envelope to the model rather than the inner result (`toolPayloadForModel`), since that is where the suggestions and `expected` live, and the chat pane's "Error:" line keys off the OUTER success flag so a throw or an unknown function name surfaces too — with no modal, that line is the user's only signal. THE MECHANISM TOOK TWO CORRECTIONS BEFORE RELEASE, both found by review, and they are why the state lives in `Globals` in the shape it does. `dfdc3741`: a single saved-and-restored slot is correct only for synchronous LIFO nesting, but these calls await and genuinely overlap (the MCP bridge answers each request independently, and a chat turn can be in flight beside one), so whichever call finished first put ITS value back — disarming the hook while another call was still running, then leaving it non-null pointing at an array nobody reads, silently swallowing every later dialog including the user's own. One slot became `errorDialogSinks`, a Set of live arrays; each call adds its own on entry and deletes that same one on exit, so the bookkeeping is membership and carries no ordering assumption. `da37e5bf`: that first correction then gave every in-flight call a copy of each dialog, so an independent caller received — and could act on — another call's failure text. `_runAttributed` now sets `errorDialogTarget` around the handler's SYNCHRONOUS body only, which nothing can interleave with, so attribution there is exact and covers almost every handler; it is deliberately not awaited, since holding the window across a handler's own awaits would rebuild the ordering bug. `showError` routes to that target, or to the single in-flight call when there is no target, and otherwise to NO ONE — a wrong attribution is worse than none, because an agent acts on it, and each call's own `error` is correct regardless. NESTING IS NOT OVERLAP and the two had been collapsed together: a nested call's dialogs do belong to its caller, since the agent only ever sees the outermost result, so they are copied up the real stack (the parent sink captured at entry), never sideways. THE STANDING TRADE-OFF: while any agent call is in flight no `showError` dialog reaches the screen, including one raised by unrelated activity, and with several overlapping calls and no target that text reaches only the console. `showErrorOnce` therefore only records its ID when a dialog was actually shown, so a later occurrence still gets its dialog; `showError` returns a boolean to say which happened, and `validationMode` reports true so a validation run still fires each ID once.

- **Fixed a control being unreachable because the caller named the wrong menu** (`ba4ac81d`; `_resolveControl` and `_executeMenuButton` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). `menu` is documented as optional — "omit/null to scan ALL menus" — but supplying it made it a HARD CONSTRAINT, so a wrong guess hid a control that the no-menu scan finds at once. Annotate lives in the `video` menu, not `view`; the chatbot guessed `view` and the control became unreachable. The menu id is now a HINT: a miss inside the named menu falls back to the all-menu scan, and only when that misses too is the named menu's own error returned, which is the one that usefully lists what that menu does contain. `_executeMenuButton` resolved separately and did not even fall back to scene objects; it now goes through `_resolveControl` like the others, so buttons, `setMenuValue` and `getMenuValue` all resolve by one rule and all get near-miss suggestions on a real failure.

- **Fixed an error dialog showing its headline with the reason missing** (`ba4ac81d`; the `showError` JSDoc in `src/showError.js`, the `setMenuValue` handler in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, the fatal-decoder branch in `src/CVideoH264Data.js`). `showError(message, error)` takes an Error OBJECT second and appends only its `.stack`, so a plain string passed there is dropped without trace and the dialog renders the headline over an empty body. Two call sites made that mistake: `showError("setMenuValue failed:", result.error)` and, user-facing in ordinary use, `showError("Fatal H.264 decoder error:", e.message)` — a video that failed to decode reported that it had failed and not why. Both now concatenate into the message and pass the real Error, and the JSDoc warns about the trap for the next caller.

- **Fixed a camera-move call with no coordinates breaking the render loop** (`ba4ac81d`; the `gotoLLA` entry in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). A missing `lat`/`lon` reached `camera.gotoLLA` as `undefined`, and the resulting NaN propagated through the camera track and out into the render loop — the caller got a broken scene and no clue why, and nothing in the failure path said what was absent. `lat` and `lon` are now checked with `Number.isFinite` and the call returns `{success:false, error:"lat and lon are required, in degrees"}` before touching the node graph. `alt` remains optional.

## Version 2.137.0 (2026-08-18)

### New Features

- **Reset on Track Import** — **File → File Tweaks → *Reset on Track Import*** (`7571d1cc`, extension list narrowed in `a5cf08a4`; `fileTweaksFolder` / `resetOnTrackImport` in `src/CFileManager.js`, `uploadDroppedFiles` / `shouldResetBeforeImport` / `drainPendingDrops` in `src/DragDropHandler.js`, `TRACK_EXTENSIONS` / `isTrackFilename` / `filesAreTrackImport` in `src/DroppableTypes.js`, i18n `file.tweaks.*`). Off by default. With it set, importing a track into an established sitch throws the current scene away first and starts a fresh one, so the result is the same as dropping that track onto an empty sitch. It re-uses the route the sitch browser already takes for files dropped onto it (`CSitchBrowser._loadCustomSitchForQueuedDrops`) — park the files on `pendingDropFiles`, `setNewSitchObject` the custom sitch, let the new scene drain the queue — so the result IS that path rather than an imitation of it. THE DECISION IS MADE ONCE FOR THE WHOLE SELECTION, through a new `uploadDroppedFiles(files)` that both the drop handler and File → Import now call; asked per file it would reset for the first, import it, then reset again for the second and throw the first away. Three conditions must all hold (`shouldResetBeforeImport`): the tweak is on, `Globals.sitchEstablished` (during startup the files being imported are what is *building* the scene), and the batch can carry a track. WHICH IMPORTS COUNT is judged from the FILENAME before anything is parsed, so it cannot be exact — `TRACK_EXTENSIONS` is therefore drawn to fail safe, since a false positive throws a scene away while a false negative is just the old behaviour. The shipped list is `kml kmz ksv csv geojson srt tle 2le 3le klv pcap pcapng ts m2ts mts`: transport streams are IN, because a `.ts` is the common case of "import a track" with the video riding along, while plain video is out, because dropping a video onto an existing track is how a scene gets built. `json`, `xml`, `txt`, `dat` and `raw` were on the first draft of the list and were removed before release (`a5cf08a4`) — `.json` is also exported FOV keyframes, saved sitches and the BOT `.scenario.json` / `.truth.json` sidecars, so dropping any of those on an established sitch would have discarded unsaved work; each exclusion has its reason recorded beside the list, and a track in one of those formats still imports, it just does not reset. The folder and the flag are both `perm` so they survive a sitch change, which matters here because the tweak CAUSES one — a flag that cleared itself on the reset it triggered would work exactly once. Menu order is creation order and Sub Sitches is built later during custom-sitch setup, so `FileManager.fileTweaksFolder.moveAfter("Sub Sitches")` in `src/CustomManagerSubSitch.js` places the folder after it at the one moment there is anything to move it after; in any other sitch it keeps the place it was created in. A LATENT BUG THIS EXPOSED: the deferred-drop queue was drained at the BOTTOM of `addDropArea`, past `if (this.dropZone !== undefined) return`, so it ran exactly once in the life of the page — the first sitch. That was invisible while the only thing queueing files was the sitch browser, which queues BEFORE that first load; queueing later left the files in the array forever, so the scene was thrown away and nothing arrived to replace it. The drain is now `drainPendingDrops()`, called at the TOP of `addDropArea` ahead of every early return including the mobile one, since a queued file has to arrive on a phone too whether or not a drop zone is built for it.

- **Imported tracks are framed as a PAIR, once, after every track exists** (`f32ee091`; new `src/CameraFraming.js`, `CTrackManager.frameLoadedTracks` and `pendingFramingTracks` in `src/TrackManager.js`). Importing a two-track file left the main camera somewhere useless, and the cause is structural rather than arithmetic: `centerOnTrack()` positions the camera once per track, so with a Sensor and a Truth the second one's framing simply replaced the first's and whichever track lost was left off screen. `frameLoadedTracks()` now runs once, after `NodeMan.recalculateAllRootFirst()` (it reads track positions, and before the recalc a lazily-built track has none), and fits both together: platform on the left, target on the right, looking down at 15–30°, every point inside the frustum with margins of 10% left, 20% right and 12% vertical. THE FIT IS EXACT RATHER THAN ESTIMATED. With the orientation fixed, "every point is inside the frustum" is a set of linear inequalities in the camera's lateral offset, vertical offset and distance — and the distance term carries no per-point data, because all the points share one camera — so the whole track collapses into four running bounds and the tightest distance drops out in closed form, in one pass. That is also why the fit uses EVERY imported point rather than a decimated sample: there is no search to make affordable, and a point left out of the fit is a point that can end up off screen. Left/right comes out of the camera basis (screen-right IS the platform-to-target direction), so nothing downstream has to correct for it and the recentring step cannot undo it; it means centroid ordering, not a promise that no point of one track ever appears on the other's side — a sensor orbiting its target has points both sides of it from every viewpoint. The look-down angle is picked from the scene's shape measured against its extent along the VIEW direction, not its total width, because depth only appears on screen in proportion to sin(tilt) and a shallow look flattens an orbit into a line; a second pass re-fits with up taken where the camera ended up, so the angle stays in band for tracks long enough for the Earth to curve between scene and camera (a 90 km airliner track already puts the camera a degree out). DELIBERATELY NARROW ABOUT WHAT IT REFRAMES: one track, or a file that DECLARES which track is the camera and which is the target via `trackRoleHint` (`CTrackFileBOT`, `CTrackFileSTANAGBase`). Three or more aircraft tracks with no declared roles keep the existing per-track centering, because fitting all of them would pull the view off the closest approach the re-timing just found. Registration happens inside the existing `Sit.centerOnLoadedTracks && (!Globals.dontAutoZoom || forceCenter) && (!Globals.sitchEstablished || forceCenter)` gate, so nothing is reframed that was not already allowed to move the view. The result is stored with `mainCameraNode.snapshotCamera()`, so `resetCamera()` returns to it. Verified against all ten BOTBench real-scenario files through the real import path: every track point on screen, platform centroid left of target centroid, look-down 20.6–29.2°.

- **The framing also contains where the sightlines meet the ground** (`400873a9`; `collectLOSGroundPoints` in `src/CameraFraming.js`, wired in `frameLoadedTracks` with `intersectSurface` from `src/threeExt.js`). Framing an imported sensor file on the platform and the target frames the two ENDS of one ray and cuts off everything between them. The subject of such a file is the FAN of sightlines — where the sensor was looking and how the geometry changed — and on a real 7 km go-fast clip the fan ran off the right edge with its far half never on screen. `collectLOSGroundPoints` intersects each frame's sightline with the ground and returns those points for the fit to contain, ADDED to the right-hand set rather than substituted for it: the target normally sits ON the ray between the two so the ground contains it anyway, but a target ABOVE the sightline's ground hit would fall out of frame if the target's own points stopped counting. TWO GUARDS, because a sightline near the horizon reaches the ground somewhere else entirely. PER POINT: any hit further from the sensor than `DEFAULT_MAX_GROUND_RANGE_RATIO` (3) × the target's centroid distance is dropped — a centroid barely notices one horizon-grazing ray (99 hits at 7 km and one at 200 km average to 8.9 km, inside a 15 km limit) while the framing is an exact fit over every point and that one would back the camera off until the encounter was a few pixels. THEN THE SET: what survives still has to be near the scene, so a clip whose sightlines ALL land far away has no outlier to drop and is simply pointed somewhere else. Nothing is returned when there is no target track to set the scale, when the sightlines never reach the ground (null is the ordinary case for a ray at or above the horizon, not an error), or when the file has no pointing at all. The intersector is INJECTED rather than imported: `CameraFraming.js` is deliberately free of every Sitrec dependency but three, which is what lets it be unit tested without a scene, so `TrackManager` passes `intersectSurface` in and the tests pass a flat-earth stand-in. Measured on the go-fast scenario: ground 17.84 km, truth 8.22 km, ratio 2.17 — the ground is framed and the whole fan fits with its far end inside the frame. Seven new tests in `tests/CameraFraming.test.js`, including one showing the old framing left ground points outside the frustum where the new one contains them.

- **Raise Toward Camera** — **Objects → *(the object's folder)*** (`3c4898a1`; `forceAboveSurfaceAlongLOS` and `syncForceAboveSurfaceGUI` in `src/nodes/CNode3DObject.js`, `clampAboveGroundAlongLine` in `src/threeExt.js`, `lookCameraPositionAt` and the `CNodeControllerTrackPosition` branch in `src/nodes/CNodeControllerVarious.js`, i18n `nodes3dObject.forceAboveSurfaceAlongLOS`). A traverse candidate is a point ON a recorded sightline; lifting it up the ellipsoid normal to clear the ground moves it OFF that line, so the object stops sitting where the camera saw it (measured at 10.77° off the sightline). With this option set, `clampAboveGroundAlongLine` slides the object toward the camera instead and bisects to the sightline's own crossing of the ground — the farthest point along the line that still clears, so it gives up the least range (measured 0.000000° off the sightline afterwards, with 40.1 m of clearance against 40 m asked). It falls back to the vertical clamp when the line cannot help, and is never applied to a camera object, which is the thing the sightline starts at. The checkbox greys out with *Force Above Surface*, since it only means anything while the object is being forced above the surface at all, and the greyout is re-derived in `modDeserialize` because the flags are restored as plain properties. There is a sitch-level default (`Sit.forceAboveSurfaceAlongLOS`) so a scenario made entirely of line-of-sight solutions can ask for it once instead of per object — the BOTBench handoff sets it BEFORE its import, because this is the default every track marker reads in its constructor and the import is what builds them. The sightline's start point is found through the look camera's own `CNodeControllerTrackPosition` rather than by guessing a node id (the custom sitch flies the camera on `cameraTrackSwitchSmooth` while `cameraTrackSwitch` is what the menu shows), and is read at frame `f` rather than off `camera.position`, so controller order cannot silently change where the object lands. A defect found in review before release (`a5cf08a4`): the step length is a FLAT-ground estimate, so ground falling away toward the camera clears far sooner than predicted — a step whose estimate overshot the camera was abandoned rather than clamped and the solution went untested, so the far end is now tested once before the fallback is taken.

### Improvements

- **The File menu closes after *Import*, but only when it is a menu-bar dropdown** — **File → *Import File*** (`7571d1cc`; `#closeFileMenuIfDropdown` in `src/CFileManager.js`). The menu was left hanging open over the scene the files had just landed in. Docked in the bar it is a dropdown — transient, covering the view, expected to go away once used — but torn out to float, or docked into a sidebar, it is a window the user deliberately placed, and closing that would discard an arrangement they set up to save them a click they never asked to be saved. The test is therefore all three of the conditions the tear-out drag already uses in `lil-gui-extras`: `mode === "DOCKED"`, the menu really is a `Globals.menuBar.slots` entry, and it is currently open. Cancelling the picker leaves it alone, since `selectAndLoadLocalFile`'s new `onAllSelected` completion callback only fires when files were chosen. "Successful" here can only mean the files reached the importer: `uploadDroppedFile` queues the parse for the main loop and resolves before it runs, so the parse outcome is not knowable at that point, and a file that fails raises its own dialog — better seen against the scene than through a menu.

- **A BOTBench cache hit is now indistinguishable from a fresh run: Gallery, Report and *Open in Sitrec* all work** — **File → File Analysis → *BOTBench...*** (`3c4898a1`; new `src/analysis/BotBenchCacheCodec.js`, `readBatteryBlob` / `writeBatteryBlob` / `blobName` in `src/analysis/BotBenchUI.js`, `battery` option in `src/analysis/BotBenchRunner.js`). The per-folder cache shipped in 2.135.0 stored only the finished ROW, so a cached row had no Gallery, no Report and a handoff with no candidates — a documented limitation with the reason on the tooltip. WHAT IS CACHED IS NOW THE FIT, NOT THE ANSWER: the expensive part of a run is `runTraverseBattery`, and everything after it (truth scoring, range compliance, the report series, the manifest, the row) is cheap arithmetic over its output. So the cache stores the fitted BATTERY, one per file under a `.botbench-cache/` directory beside the `.botbench-cache.json` index (which stays small), and a hit re-ingests the file and replays `runBotBenchAnalysis` around the stored battery, so every line below the fit runs exactly as on a fresh analysis. Serializing the finished results could not have worked: `buildHtml` is a closure over values that never reach it. A hit now needs the input hashes, the analysis options AND the app version to match — a replay runs today's ingest over yesterday's fit — and the replayed row must reproduce the stored one, so the cache validates itself on every hit and a stale cache normally re-runs itself rather than needing *Flush Cache*. `BotBenchCacheCodec` encodes what JSON silently breaks: typed arrays, `NaN`/`Infinity`, `undefined`, `Map`, and fields hung off an array object (`rangeProfile` attaches `boundaryLimited` and friends to the array it returns; losing those inverted a manifest completeness flag while every track stayed identical). Anything it cannot represent exactly throws and the write is abandoned. Two defects found in review before release (`a5cf08a4`): `packForCache` refused a real `Map`, and `runTraverseBattery` returns the solution families as one — keyed by `"key|windEvidenceRole"` and read back with `.get()` — so with solution families on, every cache write was silently abandoned and the cache simply did not work in that mode; Maps are now encoded as themselves rather than flattened to plain objects, which would have handed a cached run something with no `.get()`, a silent break instead of a refused write. And `blobName` took the first 40 characters of `"<csv>|<sidecar>|<truth>"`, which falls entirely inside the 64-hex csv hash, so two copies of one CSV with different sidecars (a different declared MaxRange) produced the same blob name and the second analysis overwrote the first while both index entries still pointed at it; the name now carries all three. Verified live through the real dialog path: row identical, whole results object identical, 1.97 MB HTML report identical but for its own "Generated" timestamp.

- **A traverse report now says when the balloon-against-measured-wind fit was NOT tested** — **Traverse → *Analyze Traverse Methods...***, under *Unavailable checks* (`f53954f4`; the `else` branch of the `if (windPrior)` guard in `src/TraverseBattery.js`, with the blanket `ABSENT_HYPOTHESES` entry removed from `src/analysis/BotBenchRunner.js`). `runTraverseBattery` guards a second balloon fit — drift softly pinned to an external wind — behind `if (windPrior)`. It is unavailable to a bulk run, and equally unavailable in a fresh sitch where the wind field is "manual / Not loaded" and returns no sample. Previously it simply did not appear, which left a reader unable to tell "the balloon was tested against the winds aloft and did not survive" from "nobody ever asked" — opposite conclusions. It now pushes a `failures` entry, "Sky Lantern / Balloon (measured wind) — not tested — no wind was supplied to pin the drift to (load winds aloft, or set the sitch wind, to include it)", which the report renders under *Unavailable checks*. NO WIND IS SYNTHESISED for it: "no wind given" is not evidence for calm, and a zero prior would pin the balloon to zero drift, which is a different claim. The statement is made in the battery's own `else` branch, the only line that knows whether a prior arrived, and the bulk runner's duplicate entry for the same fit was removed — the same fact in two places is two places to drift apart. Verified: identical text from a live run and a bulk run. Measured with an accurate prior supplied, for the record: the wind-pinned fit recovered truth exactly at zero pointing drift (0 m against 168 m for free wind), 103 m at 0.1°, and 743 m at 0.5° — worse than free wind there, because pinning to a wind the drift-corrupted geometry disagrees with hurts.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed the traverse gallery handoff opening a window whose camera heading was *Manual*, with no recorded-angles option to select** — **Traverse → *Analyze Traverse Methods...*, *Open Consistent* / *Open Consistent+Weak*** (`2c187157`; `contextTrackCSVs` in `src/TraverseHandoff.js`, `showResultGallery` meta in `src/AnalyzeTraverse.js`, `cameraTrackName` branch of `applyHandoffCameraTrack` in `src/index.js`). The sensor travelled as a bare `TIME,LAT,LONG,ALTITUDE` track, and Sitrec builds an `Angles_<name>` heading source from a file's OWN pointing — no pointing in the file, no option to select, so the Camera Heading menu offered only Manual / To Target / Celestial Lock and the reader saw the candidates from a camera aimed wherever the sitch happened to leave it, which is the one view that cannot show what the analysis did. (The camera TRACK being right was luck: it was the first file imported, so arrival-order auto-selection took it.) `contextTrackCSVs` now writes the sensor in MISB columns — position plus `SensorRelativeAzimuth`/`SensorRelativeElevation`, with platform heading/pitch/roll all zero. That is not a simplification but the convention `botLOSToAzEl` already returns and `CNodeLOSTrackMISB` already reads: with a level platform frame, azimuth IS the compass bearing and elevation IS the angle above the horizon, and splitting the same direction across a platform attitude and a gimbal offset would encode one fact twice. It falls back to the plain position track when the dataset has no directions, rather than emitting pointing-shaped columns with nothing in them. AIMING AT THE TRUTH TRACK WOULD HAVE BEEN SIMPLER AND IS NOT THE SAME THING: the sightlines are the sensor's RECORDED directions, and where the operator drifted off the target those are different rays — sending the angles reproduces the analysis, sending a target reproduces it only for a perfect operator. The gallery's meta now sets `cameraOnScenarioTrack` (reusing the receiver the bench handoff already uses) and NAMES the track (`cameraTrackName: "platform"`), because the receiver's fallback picks the first non-candidate primary track and the gallery synthesises two — a sensor and a truth — so without the name it could point the camera from the very thing it is meant to be looking at. Verified on a generated 2-mile balloon scenario: frame 0 comes out at az 360.000, el −59.602, matching that scenario's stated 59.6° depression, and the bearing swings west as the platform flies east; `Angles_platform` appears and both lookups the receiver makes resolve. The reconstructed sightlines match the originals to 0.0002–0.065° — a second az/el round trip on top of the one the source track already did, below the smallest drift level in the balloon set but not zero. `contextTrackCSVs` and `consistentTrackCSVs` are also exposed on the local-only `_traverseDebug` hook, so a handoff's payload can be inspected without a popup (`window.open` needs a real click's transient activation, which a test harness cannot supply).

- **Fixed the camera, heading and zoom in a window opened from a BOTBench row being decided by a load-order race** — **File → File Analysis → *BOTBench...*, the filename link** (`07d97dc8`; `applyHandoffCameraTrack` in `src/index.js`, `candidateTrackNames` / `cameraOnScenarioTrack` in `src/analysis/BotBenchUI.js`). `TrackManager` auto-assigns the camera by ARRIVAL ORDER (`autoSelect = trackNumber === selectNumber`). A bench handoff hands the importer `[scenario, ...candidates]` in that order, but `uploadDroppedFile` returns once a file is ACCEPTED, not once its tracks exist — so the order that decides the camera is the order the PARSES finish in, and demuxing a transport stream takes far longer than reading six small CSVs. On a `.ts` scenario every candidate landed first and the camera ended up on a RECONSTRUCTED object path — one that, when the weak band travelled, the analysis had explicitly declined to endorse. Nor could it recover: that auto-selection is gated on `!Globals.sitchEstablished`, which has flipped by the time a slow scenario's tracks finally arrive. `applyHandoffCameraTrack` now claims the camera track, the heading and the field of view once the sensor track exists, identified from sender-provided `candidateTrackNames` rather than by sniffing the `c_`/`w_` prefixes (which would quietly capture a real track a user happened to name that way). THE HEADING GOES WITH IT — a camera on the right platform pointing the wrong way still shows the wrong thing — and it selects `Angles_<sensor>` only when that option actually exists, so a scenario with no recorded angles keeps whatever heading it had rather than being given a fabricated one. THE RECORDED FOV WAS BLOCKED BY THE SAME GATE: `TrackManager` adds an FOV-carrying track to `fovSwitch` but only SELECTS it while `!Globals.sitchEstablished`, so the sensor's own zoom was offered and ignored and the computed look framing stood in for it — 3.45° computed against 1.72° recorded on Truck.ts, so the look view opened at twice the real angle and nothing in it lined up with the video. That computed framing now stands down when the scenario records its own FOV; it exists for BOT scenarios, which state no FOV and whose 1 m markers are invisible without it, and a recorded sensor zoom is a measurement that outranks it. The claim backs off if the reader has since chosen a camera, and has NO wall-clock deadline: the slow scenario it exists for is exactly the one a timeout would abandon, and the listener is inert — it acts only on a track this handoff created, only once, and never over a camera the reader chose.

- **Fixed a BOTBench row for an "unresolved" scenario opening with nothing to look at, and candidate tracks named after internal keys** — **File → File Analysis → *BOTBench...*** (`07d97dc8`; `handoffCandidateCSVs` and the slug table in `src/TraverseHandoff.js`).
