## Version 2.132.0 (2026-08-16)

### New Features

- **35mm equivalent focal length — the field of view expressed as the lens that would produce it, with the file's real lens beside it** — **Camera → FOV (Zoom) → *35mm Equiv (mm)*** and ***Lens (EXIF)*** (`b45a4863`; `FULL_FRAME_LONG_MM`, the `focal35` accessors, `focal35Controller`, `lensController` and `updateLensReadout()` in `src/nodes/CNodeControllerPTZUI.js`, `ptzUI.focal35.*` and `ptzUI.lens.*` in `src/i18n/en.js`). Like `hfov`, `focal35` **stores nothing** — the getter reads the one stored angle and the setter writes back through it (`hfov` in landscape, `fov` directly in portrait, both clamped to the same 0.0001–170 the vertical slider stops at), so VFOV, HFOV and the 35mm readout can never disagree with each other or with the camera. `.onChange(() => this.refresh())` for the same reason the other two have it: `apply()` re-reads the fov from `fovSwitch` every frame, and for the Manual source that switch reads `fovUI`, so an edit that never reaches `fovUI` is overwritten on the next frame. The slider is `.elastic(50, 100000, false, true)` over a 1–200 base, because focal length spans four decades — about 1 mm for a fisheye up to several thousand for a narrow sensor field — and a fixed linear range is useless at one end or the other.

  It is anchored on the frame's **long axis** against the 36 mm long side of the full-frame (135) gate, not on the width and not on the diagonal. The rule that choice expresses is *the number must not move unless the frame was actually cropped*, and only the long axis satisfies it in both directions. A camera shooting 3:2 stills and 16:9 video cuts the top and bottom off the same sensor through the same lens: the long axis is still the 36 mm one, so a 24 mm lens reads 24 mm both ways. Turning the camera to shoot portrait crops nothing at all: an 85 mm lens reads 85 mm both ways. Width-anchoring gets the first case right and the second wrong — it calls that portrait 85 mm a 127 mm lens (re-derived: the portrait horizontal field is 2·atan(tan(11.955°)·2/3) = 16.08°, and 18/tan(8.04°) = 127.4). The manufacturers' diagonal convention gets the second right and the first wrong — it calls the 16:9 clip a 25.1 mm lens. The one edge is that "longer axis" flips at exactly square, and nothing real is shot that close to 1:1.

  ***Lens (EXIF)*** is a read-only row showing what the imported photo says was actually on the camera — `importMetadata.optics.focalLengthMm` and `importMetadata.camera.lensModel` off the `video` node, formatted as `24 mm  (RF24mm F1.8 MACRO IS STM)`. It is the **true** focal length on that camera's sensor, not a 35 mm equivalent, so on a full-frame body the two rows match and on a smaller sensor the equivalent above is the longer number. That makes the two agreeing a real check rather than a tautology: the slider is a property of the camera *setting*, this is a property of the *file*, and when they disagree the import got something wrong. `updateLensReadout()` runs every frame from `apply()` but diffs the assembled text against `_lensText` first, so `show()`/`hide()` and the string write only happen on an actual change; the row hides itself entirely when no photo with lens metadata is loaded, rather than leaving a permanent "-" in every sitch.

- **Use Relative Altitude — a drone's height above its takeoff point offered as an alternative when its own altitude has buried the camera** — **Camera → Location → *Use Relative Altitude (N m)*** and the **Camera is Underground** dialog (`b45a4863`; `offerRelativeAltitude()`, `applyRelativeAltitude()`, `waitForGroundMSLBelow()`, `groundMSLBelow()` in `src/EXIFUtils.js`, `RelativeAltitude` picked up in `extractJPEGImportMetadata()`). A drone's absolute altitude is barometric, seeded from GPS at takeoff, and drifts. Measured on a DJI Mini 3 Pro shot: the file reported 239.9 m while the terrain under it settles at 256.9 m, so the camera landed **17.0 m underground** and 59 m below where the file's own `RelativeAltitude` (42 m above takeoff) put it. Sitrec still places the camera **exactly where the file says** — silently substituting a guessed altitude is how a reconstruction stops being checkable — and instead says so and offers the swap as one click the user chooses to make. Two ways in, deliberately different in reach: the button in **Camera → Location** appears for any photo carrying the field (named at runtime with the value, so it reads *Use Relative Altitude (42 m)*, and hidden again when a later import has none), while the `showChoice` dialog titled **Camera is Underground** only interrupts when the camera has actually ended up below the terrain, because that is the case the user cannot be expected to notice — the look view just goes brown. Accepting sets the altitude to the measured ground MSL plus the recorded relative height; declining leaves it underground exactly as the file states.

  The check **waits for the terrain to settle** before deciding, which is the part that took the work. Elevation tiles stream in coarse first and fine later, and the coarse pass over that Libyan oasis put the ground at 460 m against a settled 257 m — measuring on the first tile to arrive would have accused a correctly placed camera of being 220 m underground. "No higher-zoom tile loaded" cannot tell *finest* from *not yet arrived*, so it is no help; `waitForGroundMSLBelow()` instead listens for the terrain's own `elevationChanged` event and resolves once nothing has changed for `quietMs = 2000` (hard-stopped at `timeoutMs = 30000`). `groundMSLBelow()` goes through `getPointBelowWithTileInfo` rather than `getPointBelow` and rejects `tileZ < 0`, because with no tile at all the terrain quietly answers **sea level**, and a photo over ground 250 m up would then look like it was 250 m in the air. Both the dialog and the deferred apply re-check `relativeAltitudeOffer === offer` before acting, since a later import can take over while the wait or the dialog is outstanding.

- **Anything droppable is linkable — one shared list of the file types Sitrec can ingest** (`2eae1827`; new leaf module `src/DroppableTypes.js`, read by `src/CFileManager.js`, `src/DragDropHandler.js` and `src/CFileManagerParse.js`; `tests/DroppableTypes.test.js`). Dropping a `.ntf` from the desktop worked; pasting the URL of the same file was refused with *"Unsupported URL host or page type"* — doubly confusing, because the host was fine. The extension was simply missing from a hand-written allowlist regex in `DragDropHandler`'s URL gate that had drifted from what `parseAsset` actually handles. The same set was written out **three** times — the Import dialog's `accept` attribute, the drag-and-drop image routing, and the URL gate — so drift was inevitable. `DroppableTypes.js` now holds `IMAGE_EXTENSIONS`, `VIDEO_EXTENSIONS`, `AUDIO_EXTENSIONS` (re-exported from `AudioFormats`) and `DATA_EXTENSIONS` once, with `isDroppableExtension()`, `urlLooksDroppable()` (path only, so a query string or fragment cannot change the answer) and `droppableAcceptAttribute()`. It is a leaf on purpose — it imports only `AudioFormats`, which imports nothing — so the URL gate, the file picker and any parser can all read it without an import cycle. Newly reachable by URL: `ntf`, `nitf`, `nsf`, `klv`, `zip`, `bmp`, `xml`, `geojson`, `ksv`, `2le`, `3le`, `dat`, `pcap`, `pcapng`, `raw`, `bin`, plus the video and audio containers the old regex missed (`m4v`, `mp4v`, `mpeg`, `mpg`, `wav`, `ogg`, `flac`, `aac`, `aif`, `aiff`, `caf`, `m2v`, `m1v`). The file picker keeps its `video/*,audio/*,image/*` wildcards in front of the generated list, because mobile OS pickers filter by MIME group rather than by extension.

  Two exclusions are deliberate. Bare **`.js`** is not listed: a sitch is a `.sitch.js` file but it is loaded *by reference* through `SitrecObjectResolver` rather than fetched as an asset, and listing it would make every `.js` URL on the internet something Sitrec offers to download. **`.ogv`** is not listed: Ogg/Theora has no signature in `sniffFileType`, no branch in `parseAsset`, and is not among the codecs the video pipeline configures, so fetching it and then registering it as unknown is a worse answer than declining the link. `DragDropHandler` keeps a locally narrowed image list — `tif`/`tiff` are filtered out of its copy only, because a TIFF may be a GeoTIFF that becomes a ground overlay through `parseAsset` rather than one of the "use as video / use as overlay" choices that list drives. `tests/DroppableTypes.test.js` enforces the coupling by reading **both** dispatches out of the source: every offered extension must reach a handler in `parseAsset`, everything that parses as video must have an upload branch, and every container rebuilt from fetched bytes must have a real MIME. It reads both because they key off different things — the filename extension in one, the sniffed type in the other — and that is precisely how they drifted.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed Canon photos importing with no field of view at all** (`b45a4863`; `focalPlaneUnitToMm()` replacing the numeric guard in `deriveSensorSize()`, `src/EXIFUtils.js`). `exifr` translates enum tags to human-readable strings by default and Sitrec does not turn that off, so `FocalPlaneResolutionUnit` arrives as the string `"Inch"`, not the number `2`. The old gate was `toFiniteNumber(raw?.FocalPlaneResolutionUnit)`, which a string fails, so `deriveSensorSize()` returned null and no FOV was derived. That silenced **every Canon body**, which writes the `FocalPlane*` tags and no `FocalLengthIn35mmFormat` — the sensor-size path was the only one such a file had. `focalPlaneUnitToMm()` now accepts both forms, and both are needed: `exifr`'s dictionary only covers units 1–3, so units 4 (millimetre) and 5 (micrometre) still come through as plain numbers. Unit 1, "No absolute unit of measurement", returns null as before, since it cannot size a sensor.

- **Fixed cropped frames — most drone footage — getting a badly wrong field of view from their 35 mm equivalent** (`b45a4863`; `deriveVerticalFov()` and the new `displayedAspect()` in `src/EXIFUtils.js`). `FocalLengthIn35mmFormat` was read as `degrees(2*atan(24 / (2*f35)))` — against the gate's 24 mm **height**, which silently assumes every frame is 3:2. A 35 mm equivalent does not describe the vertical; it describes the frame's **long axis** against the 36 mm long side, the same convention the new slider uses. The assumption is worst exactly where it matters most, on cropped frames: a DJI Air 2S wide crop is 5472×2472 (2.21:1) and still reports 22 mm, because the crop takes height off the same lens and leaves the full width. Read against the height that produced a **100.7°** horizontal field where **78.6°** is right, and the new 35 mm readout would have said 14.9 mm for a lens the file itself calls 22 mm. It now computes the long-axis field, reads the displayed aspect from `ExifImageWidth`/`ExifImageHeight` (swapped for a rotated frame), and converts across to the vertical in landscape or takes it directly in portrait. Named limitation: this is exact when the long axis is the one that was **not** cropped, which covers uncropped frames of either orientation and every letterbox or pillarbox crop. A crop that eats into both axes cannot be recovered from EXIF at all, since nothing in the file says how much was taken. With no pixel dimensions to go on it falls back to the old 3:2 reading — right for the commonest frame shape, and no worse than before.

- **Fixed portrait photos importing with half the vertical field missing** (`b45a4863`; the `dimensionSwapped` parameter threaded through `deriveVerticalFov()` in `src/EXIFUtils.js`, `tests/EXIFUtils.test.js`). `deriveSensorSize()` describes the sensor **as read out**, which is always landscape. A photo shot in portrait carries an Orientation of 90° or 270° and is displayed rotated, so the axis that ends up vertical on screen is the sensor's **width**, not its height. Reading the height regardless made an 85 mm portrait frame report **16.07°** vertical where **23.91°** is correct, and every reconstruction from it wrong by that much. `dimensionSwapped` is derived from three independent signals, because getting it wrong costs half the field and no single one of them is always present: `exifr`'s own `rotation.dimensionSwapped` flag, the rotation angle it reports (90 and 270 being the swapping ones, equivalent to the flag by construction), and the `Orientation` tag as `exifr` translates it (`/rotate\s*(90|270)/i`). It applies to JPEG and HEIC alike — JPEG because Sitrec rotates it downstream, HEIC because libheif already did, so both end up upright on screen and `stripImageRotationMetadata` does not change that. The swap now also reaches the sensor-size branch, whose reported `sensorWidthMm`/`sensorHeightMm` pair is transposed to match the display so anything downstream that pairs them with the image dimensions agrees with what is on screen. `tests/EXIFUtils.test.js` updates its portrait fixture from 26.99° to **39.60°**, which is exactly 2·atan(18/50) for the fixture's 50 mm equivalent.

- **Fixed vertically-shot drone photos coming in rotated a quarter turn** (`b45a4863`; the `roll` field in `extractJPEGImportMetadata()`, `src/EXIFUtils.js`). The camera's own roll and the EXIF orientation can describe the **same physical turn**, and applying both lands it twice. A DJI Mini 3 Pro rotates its gimbal to shoot vertical, so the file states the quarter turn twice over: `GimbalRollDegree` −90 **and** `Orientation` 8 ("rotate 270 CW"). Sitrec already turns the *image* by the orientation, so rolling the 3D camera by −90 as well left the view a quarter turn off the photo. `roll` is now `normalizeSignedDegrees(rollSource.value - (rotation?.deg ?? 0))`, which removes exactly the turn already accounted for: −90 − 270 = −360, i.e. level, which is what a gimbal-stabilised horizon should be. It is a no-op for unrotated photos (`deg` 0) and also resolves the 180° case. Subtraction rather than addition is load-bearing and is pinned by the test fixture — adding would give 180, upside down.

- **Fixed HFOV staying editable while a computed source drives the field of view** — **Camera → FOV (Zoom)** (`b45a4863`; `syncCameraControlGreyout` in `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`). Only `ptz.fovController` (VFOV) was greyed out when `fovSwitch.choice !== "userFOV"`. HFOV stayed live even though it is the same stored angle seen through the aspect ratio and writes back through it, so a computed FOV source overwrote any edit to it on the next `apply()` — a control that accepted a number and silently discarded it. `hfovController` and the new `focal35Controller` now grey out together with `fovController`, which is the honest picture: all three are one angle, so either all three can be edited or none can.

- **Fixed a photo with no GPS fix teleporting the camera to the Gulf of Guinea** (working tree, `src/EXIFUtils.js`; the `hasLocation` test in `extractJPEGImportMetadata()`). Exactly 0/0 latitude and longitude is "Null Island", off the coast of West Africa, and it is what a camera writes when it has **no fix** — a DJI Osmo Action 4 with no GPS fills in zeros for latitude, longitude, altitude and every gimbal angle alike. `hasLocation` now excludes that pair, so such a file is treated as having no location at all. Because `applyImportedImageCameraPositionInternal()` returns early on `!placement.hasLocation` — before it touches `cameraNode.forceAboveSurface` — and the same gate fronts both the orientation apply and the main-view overview, the camera is left **exactly** where it is: measured byte-identical latitude, longitude, altitude and AGL flag across the import. The test is for exact zeros rather than a tolerance, because no genuine fix lands on 0.000000 twice over.

- **Fixed a photo with a position but no usable height dropping the camera to sea level, usually under the terrain** (working tree, `src/EXIFUtils.js`; `DEFAULT_AGL_METRES` and the `noUsableAltitude` branch in `applyImportedImageCameraPositionInternal()`). A photo can carry a real position and no height at all: the altitude tag absent, or a bare 0 of the kind a phone or a barometer-less action cam fills in. Zero MSL is a **real place** — the sea — so honouring it put the camera at sea level and usually below the ground. The camera is now stood at `DEFAULT_AGL_METRES = 2` with the position node switched to **Above Ground Level**, so the number on screen says what it means and the user can raise it from a sane place; measured on a synthetic San Francisco fix with no altitude tag, AGL mode true, altitude 2 m, and 2.0 m above the terrain when queried. Two supporting changes make it stick. The direct `camera.position.copy(importedCameraPosition)` stamp and the `startPosLLA` write are skipped in this case, because that ECEF was built from a sea-level altitude and would undo the AGL placement — the position node resolves the height against the terrain instead, which is the whole point of AGL. And `offerRelativeAltitude()` is skipped too: there is nothing to second-guess when Sitrec placed the camera itself, since it is 2 m above the ground by construction and the file's own heights were the reason it had to.

- **Fixed *Use Relative Altitude* being offered for a height of zero** (working tree, `src/EXIFUtils.js`; the guard in `offerRelativeAltitude()`). The gate was `relativeAltitude === undefined`, so a camera writing a bare `RelativeAltitude` of 0 — again, what a barometer-less camera writes rather than a height it measured — got a button reading *Use Relative Altitude (0 m)* that offered to move the camera nowhere. The gate is now `!(relativeAltitude > 0)`.

- **Fixed the greyed-out Location and FOV boxes describing a camera that does not exist, and switching either back to *Manual* teleporting the camera** — **Camera → Location**, **Camera → FOV (Zoom)** (`ed8ac89e`; two `Switch.choiceChanged` listeners in `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`, new `mirrorECEF()` in `src/nodes/CNodePositionLLA.js`). A dropped file that brings its own camera claims both switches on import — an NTF image nominates its own camera track through `TrackManager`'s `autoSelectAsCamera` and its own FOV. The manual stores behind those switches were left untouched, so Cam Lat/Lon/Alt still read the sitch default 31.98°, −118.43°, 10000 ft and `fovUI` still read 30° while the camera was a satellite over Provence at 8.8°. The greyed-out boxes therefore described a camera that did not exist, and selecting *Manual* again threw the camera half a world away and jumped the FOV. Heading has always had this and kept working — `postApplyControllers` holds `ptzAngles` on the live orientation and a `choiceChanged` listener captures it at the moment of the switch — and this extends the same treatment to the other two. Measured on a Planet RapidEye NTF (500 km, 8.83° vertical field): on import the Location boxes now read 43.7779, 4.9765, 1,640,420 ft and the VFOV slider 8.832, and switching Location, FOV and Heading back to *Manual* moves the camera 5.8×10⁻¹¹ m with the FOV and orientation unchanged. Before, the same three switches moved it from Provence to the Pacific and took the FOV from 8.8 to 30.

  Two directions, two different right answers for what the manual value should be. **Arriving at a computed source**, the right answer is the value that source has at *this* frame, read from the switch — which has already changed by the time `choiceChanged` fires, so it is the incoming source. That is what puts the truth in the greyed-out boxes. **Going back to Manual**, the right answer is what the camera has *right now*: the pose is applied in the render loop, not in the cascade, so at that moment the camera is still as the outgoing source left it, and capturing there is what makes the switch exact at any frame, for a moving track as well as a fixed one. The position read uses `cameraTrackSwitch.p(par.frame)` rather than `getValueFrame()`, because a track's per-frame value may be a row object rather than a bare `Vector3` and `p()` is what unwraps it. `choiceChanged` rather than `onChange` so **programmatic** selections are covered — `TrackManager` claiming the switches on import is the whole case this exists for; it fires twice for one `selectOption()`, and both writes are no-ops after the first because each store skips a value it already holds.

  The write has to be **quiet**, which is why `mirrorECEF()` exists rather than a plain `setLLA()`. `setLLA` dispatches `PositionLLA.onChange`, and `CCustomManager` listens for that on `fixedCameraPosition` to pull the Location source back to *Manual* — right for a hand edit, and exactly wrong for a mirror, which would un-select the track the instant the track claimed the switch. `mirrorECEF()` writes `_LLA` and the GUI values directly, recalculates the cascade, returns whether anything actually changed (sub-millimetre moves are float noise and are skipped, so a parked camera does not cascade every frame), stores the altitude **absolutely as MSL** — AGL is a different kind of answer, "N metres above the ground", which moves as finer terrain streams in, so a measured height stored there would not preserve the position at all — and switches AGL off visibly, its checkbox being `.listen()`ed. `flightSimCamera` and `orbitCamera` are excluded in both directions through `manualFamily()`: they are not alternatives to the manual position but are **built on** it, so writing to `fixedCameraPosition` would drag the origin the jet takes off from, or the point the orbit circles, along behind the camera. `previousChoice` is tracked before the `Globals.deserializing`/`disposing` guards, not after, so a load restoring the choice does not leave the next real change looking as if it came from somewhere else. For FOV the source is `lookCamera.camera.fov`, not `ptzAngles.fov`: the PTZ controller only refreshes its own fov inside `apply()`, which does not run while another heading source owns the camera — exactly the state a dropped angles track leaves it in. The captured value is written to `fovUI` and also straight onto `ptzController.fov`, since the VFOV slider is bound to the latter and would otherwise show a stale number even with `fovUI` correct.

- **Fixed GeoJSON track files named with their own standard extension failing outright** (`2eae1827`; `makeMISBDataTrack()` in `src/TrackManager.js`, plus a `geojson` case in `parseAsset` in `src/CFileManagerParse.js`). The track dispatch tested `ext === "json"` only, so a file named `.geojson` — the format's own standard extension, and one the Import dialog had always offered — bypassed the `CGeoJSON` reader and hit `assert(0, "Unknown file type")`. `parseAsset` likewise had no `geojson` case, so the file registered as unknown before it ever got that far. GeoJSON is JSON, so the case simply falls through to the `json` handler and the track-file detectors below decide what it is.

- **Fixed several file types that could be dropped or offered but then silently did nothing** (`2eae1827`; `parseAsset` in `src/CFileManagerParse.js`). Making the shared list *true* turned up formats already offered somewhere with no handler at the other end, so they fetched and then quietly dead-ended. `.2le` and `.3le` now join `.tle` — `isTLEFile()` has always named them, the switch did not, so they registered as unknown. `.bmp` now decodes as an image through `createImageFromArrayBuffer(buffer, 'image/bmp')` — `DragDropHandler`'s image list has always contained it, so one could be dropped and then registered as unknown. `.mpg`/`.mpeg` get a case, which `sniffFileType`'s own docstring already claimed existed ("returns a canonical extension matching the cases in parseAsset").

- **Fixed `.m4v` video and most audio formats reporting success from a URL while loading nothing** (`2eae1827`; `handleParsedFile`'s upload dispatch in `src/CFileManagerParse.js`). `handleParsedFile` reads the **filename** extension while `parseAsset` dispatches on the **sniffed** type, and that mismatch was the bug. An `.m4v` sniffs as `mp4` (it is the same ISO-BMFF container), parses as dataType `video`, then found no branch under its own name and dead-ended at `console.warn("Unknown video format")` followed by `return true` — success reported, nothing loaded. The same narrow test dropped every audio container except `m4a` and `mp3`, which was the URL path's only route, since a **dropped** audio file never reaches here at all (`importDroppedFile` hands it straight to the video node with the browser's own MIME). `m4v`/`mp4v` now join the `mp4` branch with an explicit MIME from `VIDEO_MIME_TYPES`, because `` `video/${ext}` `` would invent a "video/m4v" that nothing accepts; the audio test is now `isAudioOnlyFormat()` with `AUDIO_MIME_TYPES`, excluding `webm` on purpose since it is in the audio list but is also a video container and has always been handled by the video branch; and `.mpg`/`.mpeg` reaching that dispatch — which means a genuine MPEG **program** stream, one that is really a transport stream having been recognised by content much earlier — now gets the actionable `ffmpeg -c:v libx264` re-encode message that `.m2v` already had, instead of a silent console warning.

## Version 2.131.1 (2026-08-15)

### New Features

- **Place on 3D Objects — control points can land on the scene's own objects, not just the ground and the buildings** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Place on 3D Objects*** (`ab05ad9e`; `objectAlongRay()` and `NEVER_A_LANDMARK` in `src/FitSurfacePick.js`, `useObjects` in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `getUseObjects` threaded through `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`, `userData.is3DObject` in `src/nodes/CNode3DObject.js`, `useObjects` on `pickWorldPoint`, `fitPointsConfigure` and `_fitSummary` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, `docs/FitPointsAPI.md`). Default **on**, serialized with the same `if (v.useObjects !== undefined)` guard as `useTiles`, so saved sitches keep whatever they had. It reaches all three placement paths and only those: a click on the video (`surfaceUnderVideoPixel()`), a handle dragged in a 3D view (`CFitHandleOverlay.onMouseDrag()` → `groundUnderCanvasPoint()`), and the `pickWorldPoint` API — so like *Place on 3D Buildings* it affects where new points are dropped and where dragged handles land, never points already placed.

  Between the object hit and the surface hit, **nearest wins** — deliberately not the strict tiles → elevation → ellipsoid priority the surfaces use among themselves. That priority exists because one surface can be invisible *and* in front: the elevation height field draped over the building being aimed at. An object has no such problem — it is solid, drawn, and occludes what is behind it, so if the ray reaches it first then it is what the clicked pixel shows; and taking it unconditionally would be the opposite mistake, since an object standing behind a building is not on screen at that pixel. Measured on a sitch with an A340 in shot: the same pixel returns altitude HAE 170.58 m with objects on against 138.74 m with them off (the aircraft is the nearer hit), while a pick away from the aircraft is byte-identical either way.

  `objectAlongRay()` collects candidates from `NodeMan.iterate()` — the flat node dictionary, not a scene traverse — keeping any node whose `group.visible && group.userData.is3DObject`, then raycasts just those with `firstHitOnly` and the ray's `MAX_GROUND_RANGE` of 400 km (so an object further off than that is not picked, the same limit the ground pick has always had). The cost is one cheap pass over the node list plus a raycast against the handful of meshes that are actually objects; the terrain is never in that set, which matters because it carries no BVH and costs about a millisecond a ray. The raycaster borrows the view camera's layer mask, for the same reason the tiles pass does — object groups sit on the main/look render layers and a default-masked raycaster matches nothing. `.visible` is tested explicitly because Three.js raycasting ignores it: without that, an object switched off in **Show/Hide** would still catch the pick, which from the user's side is a point landing on nothing at all. The marker is a `userData` flag stamped by `CNode3DObject`'s constructor rather than an `instanceof` at the far end, because `FitSurfacePick` is deliberately a leaf module (see its header — importing back into the view graph closes a cycle through `CNodeViewUI` that Jest's loader trips over), and because `userData` survives minification where a class name would not.

  `cameraObject` is excluded by id through `NEVER_A_LANDMARK`. It is the marker sphere sitting at the camera's own position (a `TrackPosition` along `cameraTrackSwitchSmooth` in `data/custom/SitCustom.js`), so it is not a thing in the world but a picture of the answer the fit is solving for: a control point placed on it would be pinned to a target that moves every time the fit succeeds, and each solve would chase the landmark it had just displaced. Proven with a control — scaling `cameraObject` 200× and parking it halfway along the ray changed the pick by 0.0 m, while doing the same to `traverseObject` changed it by 88 m. The option carries across the whole MCP surface rather than the pick alone: `pickWorldPoint` gains a `useObjects` parameter defaulting to **true**, `fitPointsConfigure` accepts it as an optional boolean, and `_fitSummary` — the state object `fitPointsStatus` and the other fit entries return — reports it alongside `useTiles`, so an assistant can both set the option and see what it is set to. `docs/FitPointsAPI.md` lists it with the other configurable keys and notes that a pick now hits objects. One default does change for existing callers: `pickWorldPoint` answers with the object wherever one stands between the camera and the ground, where it used to answer with the ground.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed a fit switching *Match Video Aspect* back on — *Sync Look Camera* no longer owns that checkbox** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Sync Look Camera***, **Camera → *Match Video Aspect*** (`ab05ad9e`; −70 net in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, the `syncLookCamera` doc string in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). 2.131.0 gave `setSyncLookCamera()` two jobs — routing the look view's wheel and left drag to the video's zoom and pan (`fitViewSyncActive()` in `src/FitViewSync.js`), and forcing `matchVideoAspect` on the `<camera>_Frustum` node through `setMatchVideoAspect()` — and had `runFit()` **re-assert** the sync on every successful solve, specifically so that a hand-unticked Match Video Aspect would be repaired. Between them those two decisions meant the user's own choice could not survive: untick *Match Video Aspect* in the **Camera** menu, press *Fit Now*, and it came straight back on. The two are now separate. `setSyncLookCamera()` sets `this.syncLookCamera` and calls `setRenderOne(true)`, and nothing else; Match Video Aspect is untouched in both directions, on and off. The whole `_restoreMatchVideoAspect` lifecycle goes with it — the constructor field, the `modSerialize` key, its `modDeserialize` restore, both undo halves (`captureState()` no longer records `matchVideoAspect`/`restoreMatchVideoAspect` and `restoreState()` no longer writes them, going through `setSyncLookCamera()` now that one flag is all there is), the `dispose()` hand-back, and the `setMatchVideoAspect()` helper itself. A `restoreMatchVideoAspect` key written by a 2.131.0 save, or carried in a 2.131.0 undo snapshot, is read and ignored: nothing owes that checkbox a value any more, and re-applying one would only reinstate a coupling that no longer exists. `runFit()` still turns the sync on at the end of a successful solve, announced only on the change. `fitPointsConfigure`'s `syncLookCamera` doc string is corrected with it — it told an assistant the setting meant "Lock the look view to the video's framing — Match Video Aspect on, and look-view wheel/drag zoom and pan the video", which was the coupling itself written down, and now describes the gesture routing alone and says explicitly that Match Video Aspect is not touched. The dead `findGuiController()` helper goes too, its only caller having been `setMatchVideoAspect()`.

  Nothing is lost by the separation, because the look view already follows the video without it: the view is built with `syncVideoZoom`, so `CNodeView3D` sets `camera.zoom` from the `videoZoom` node, widens the look camera's vertical field by `1/fovCoverage` (scoped to `id === "lookView"`) and shifts the projection matrix by the video's `panOffsetX/Y` every frame. *Match Video Aspect* decides one thing only — whether the look canvas is letterboxed to the video's aspect so the extra field around the video's frame is cropped away, or left visible as margins. The two pictures stay comparable either way, and judging a fit at a glance often wants the wider field, so that the building being checked is visible along with its surroundings.

- **Fixed the look view's wheel and drag moving the video away from the pointer when the look view is not cropped to the video** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Sync Look Camera*** (`ab05ad9e`; `videoFractionUnderPointer()` and `fitViewSyncPan()` in `src/FitViewSync.js`). Both mapped the cursor through `renderedRect(view)` and assumed the rendered rect spanned exactly `1/zoom` of the video in each axis. That holds only while *Match Video Aspect* letterboxes the look canvas to the video's own frame. With it off, `CNodeView3D` widens the camera by `1/fovCoverage` and the pane spans `1/(fovCoverage*zoom)` of the video on the boxed axis, so the wheel zoomed about a point that was not under the cursor and a drag moved the picture by the wrong amount on that axis. Reachable in 2.131.0 by unticking Match Video Aspect by hand between fits, or by reloading a sitch saved in that state (`modDeserialize` restores `syncLookCamera` as a plain flag and lets the frustum node carry its own value) — and it is the *ordinary* state after the fix above, which is what makes this worth fixing now. Both paths now go through the `mirrorVideo` overlay, which shares the look view's div and whose `canvasToVideoCoords()` **is** the mapping the video was drawn with: `[px/videoWidth, py/videoHeight]` for the wheel, and `(dxPx/dWidth) * (sWidth/videoWidth)` for the drag — the same conversion `CNodeVideoView`'s own left-drag uses at `CNodeVideoView.js:1292`, which is exactly "pixels divided by the displayed image's width in pane pixels". Right in every mode without this module having to know which is in force: letterbox or pillarbox, cropped or filling the pane. Measured before the fix on a letterboxed look view, the vertical mapping put the pointer at 0.2975 of the frame where it truly sat at 0.1287 — 0.169 of the frame out.

  The wheel path calls `mirror.update()` before reading, because `CNodeMirrorVideoView.update()` is where the mirror copies the video's `panOffsetX/Y`, and it runs once per rendered frame while a trackpad delivers wheel events a good deal faster than that: the second notch of a flick would otherwise map the cursor through the pan the first notch had already superseded, and the zoom would walk away from the pointer. `update()` is used rather than re-copying the two fields, being the defined "make the mirror current" operation, cheap and idempotent, and proof against the mirror ever mirroring more state. Measured after: five notches with no rendered frame between them drift 0.00003 of the frame, identical to five notches with frames landing between them. The pan path needs no `update()` — what it reads is the ratio `sWidth/dWidth`, a function of the zoom and the pane and not of the pan (clipping shrinks both terms together), though it does call `getSourceAndDestCoords()` to make those current. The old `renderedRect` computation is kept as the fallback where no `mirrorVideo` overlay exists, where its `1/zoom` assumption remains the best available guess.

## Version 2.131.0 (2026-08-15)

### New Features

- **Free Look Camera — fly the look camera by hand, and keep where you flew** — **Camera → Camera Tweaks → *Free Look Camera***, mirrored as **the Look view's own header menu → *Free Look*** (`cd187efe`, corrected by `09e11208` and `ff0a0b82`; +182 in `src/nodes/CNodeCamera.js`, +94 in `src/js/CameraControls.js`, `misc.freeLookCamera.{label,tooltip}` and `viewMenus.freeLook` in `src/i18n/en.js`, the `freeLook` slot placed first in `lookView` in `src/ViewUIBarMenus.js`). Default off, added only for the node with `id === "lookCamera"`. While it is on the look camera navigates exactly like the main camera — left-drag moves the world, middle-drag orbits the point under the cursor, right-drag looks around, the wheel zooms, WASD walks. Three gates make the hand-flown pose survive the frame it was set in. (1) `applyControllers()` returns early, which suspends every computed source at once — Location, Heading, FOV, Tracking Wobble — *without* touching the per-controller `enabled` flags, which belong to the source switches and are rewritten on every choice change, so a second owner would only fight them. (2) `update()` gates the node's other pose writers on a local `poseIsComputed`: `altAdjust` (which **raises** the current position rather than setting one, so with no controller re-seeding it each frame it would compound and the camera would climb away), the `celestialLock` aim, and `applyGroundTrackSwitch()` — while `updateGroundTrackSwitchFrameRange()` still runs, being GUI upkeep rather than a pose write. (3) A new `getInteractivePTZController()` in `src/js/CameraControls.js` reports no PTZ controller while the mode is on, so gestures fall through to the plain main-camera set instead of the PTZ pan/zoom ones, which would otherwise write az/el/fov into a controller that is no longer being applied. It is deliberately **not** folded into `getPTZController()`, whose other callers want the object whether or not it is currently driving anything — `SitNightSky`'s URL save/restore reads its az/el/fov and asserts it is present.

  The flown pose does not float free. `syncFreeLookPosition()` publishes the camera position back into `fixedCameraPosition` once per rendered frame from `CameraMapControls.update()`, which is downstream of every gesture — drag, orbit, pan, wheel, WASD, touch — and is where the WASD walker already writes that node. So the Location folder's Lat/Lon/Alt track the flight, `CCustomManager`'s `PositionLLA.onChange` listener promotes the Location source to *Manual*, and switching Free Look off leaves the camera where it was flown rather than snapping back; the orientation, which nothing else publishes, is handed to `ptzAngles` via `syncFromCamera()` on the way out, so a Heading of *Manual* keeps looking where the user left it. Measured after a 6.7 km drag: 0 m position drift and 0° orientation drift across a full recalculate. Sub-millimetre moves are ignored so a parked free-look camera does not cascade a recalculate every frame. Altitude follows the WASD walker's rule — written as MSL for an absolute-altitude node (`ECEFToLLAVD_radii` returns HAE, so `meanSeaLevelOffset()` is subtracted before `setLLA`), and via `setFromECEF(pos)` with `changeAlt` left false for an AGL one, which writes lat/lon only, because "N metres above the ground" is a standing instruction that outranks the height flown at. WASD reverses direction under the mode: `updateWASDWalking()` steps the camera itself and rides the 3D tile surface below at `WASD_EYE_HEIGHT`, because a write to the suspended position node would move nothing. A look view built with `noOrbitControls` (the Gimbal pod views) gets `addOrbitControls()` on demand, tracked by `_freeLookAddedControls` and switched back off when the mode is, so such a view navigates exactly as before afterwards.

  Two ordering defects in the original commit were caught by review and fixed before release, both of the same shape — constructor work that assumed it ran before, or instead of, deserialization. `freeLook` was registered with `addSimpleSerial()` inside `addFreeLookGUI()`, which runs *after* the constructor's `applyEarlyMods()` at `CNodeCamera.js:102`; `simpleDeserialize` walks `simpleSerials` as it stands at that moment, so the saved value was silently skipped and the mode did not survive a reload. Registration moved into the constructor ahead of `applyEarlyMods()`, and out from behind `addFreeLookGUI()`'s early return on a missing menu, which had made what a sitch *saves* depend on what GUI happened to be present (`09e11208`). The view wiring then moved into `wireFreeLookView()`, which reports whether a view was there, retried from `update()` until it lands — one boolean test per frame once wired — because restoring a saved sitch drives the setter while the camera node is still in its constructor and its view is not built until later in `SituationSetup`, so a saved Free Look session on a `noOrbitControls` view reloaded with the mode on and no controls to fly it with (`ff0a0b82`). Also in `cd187efe`: `CameraMapControls.update()`'s keyboard zoom (`+`/`-`) and the WASD walker now sit inside `if (this.enabled)`, so a view whose controls are switched off — image-set export, feature editing, point dragging, flood sim, ground overlays, synth clouds — is no longer still walkable by keyboard. The measure-arrow update stays outside the gate, being display upkeep rather than navigation.

- **Sync Look Camera: the fit's view lock is now its own switch, not part of *Enable Fit*** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Sync Look Camera*** (`0cc30e2b`; +109 in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `fitViewSyncActive()` in `src/FitViewSync.js`, `fitPointsConfigure`/`fitPointsStatus` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, `docs/FitPointsAPI.md`). Two things together made the look view a second window onto the video rather than a camera you fly: forcing `matchVideoAspect` on, and `FitViewSync` routing the look view's wheel and left drag to the video's zoom and pan. Both hung off `fit.enabled`, which conflated two decisions that alternate within one session — judging a fit wants the lock, while reading the scene, checking what is behind a building, or lining up the next keyframe wants the 3D camera back, and those happen with the fit still on; equally, switching the fit off is not a reason to unframe a comparison the user is still looking at. Both halves are now gated on one new serialized flag, `syncLookCamera` (default off, since until there is a solved camera there is nothing to compare), through `setSyncLookCamera()`; `fitViewSyncActive()` tests `fit.syncLookCamera` in place of `fit.enabled`. Gating both halves on the same flag is deliberate — released separately they can end up half on, with the gestures redirected to a video the look view no longer frames like. `setEnabled()` no longer touches Match Video Aspect at all, and the whole `_restoreMatchVideoAspect` lifecycle now lives in the one setter (plus `dispose()`, which hands it back).

  A successful fit **re-asserts** the sync at the end of `runFit()` rather than merely flipping it, because *Match Video Aspect* (**Camera** menu) is a checkbox in its own right: unticking it by hand leaves the sync ticked but no longer syncing, and only a re-assert repairs it. The status note is emitted on the change alone, so refits do not keep announcing a lock already in force. Three things now carry across a save and an undo that did not before. **Old saves**: a save with no `syncLookCamera` key predates the flag, and back then the sync *was* Enable Fit, so `modDeserialize` reads it as `!!v.enabled` — without that, a sitch saved mid-fit reloaded with its gesture routing silently gone. **The restore value**: `_restoreMatchVideoAspect` is serialized, so unticking the sync after a reload puts Match Video Aspect back where unticking it before one would have, rather than guessing at a value the user may have chosen. **Undo**: a fit switches the sync on by itself, exactly as it selects the camera switches `captureCameraState()` already records, and with *Fit on Change* one point drag flips it — so all three components are captured (the flag, the `matchVideoAspect` it drives, and the value owed back) and restored component by component rather than through the setter, because the third is not derivable from the other two. Snapshots taken before this was captured leave all of it alone. Also exposed as `syncLookCamera` in `fitPointsConfigure` and `fitPointsStatus`, so the MCP surface can see a setting that fits now change.

### Improvements

- **Off a fit keyframe, the tool now offers to go to one instead of only refusing** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points** (`c1a9dc56`; +137 in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`, `src/FitHandleDraw.js`, `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). Control points belong to the frame they were observed on, so editing or fitting from anywhere else has to be refused — but *"Points belong to frame 214 — go to it to fit"* left the user to find frame 214 when the tool knew the number and could just as well go there. New `offerNearestKeyframe(verb, thenFit)` raises a `showChoice` dialog titled **Not On A Fit Keyframe** offering *Go To Frame N* or *Cancel*, with N from `nearestKeyframeFrame()` (the keyframe closest to the playhead, or `fitFrame` when there are none yet); Cancel falls back to the old status line via `wrongFrameMessage(verb)`. Accepting a refused **fit** also runs the fit on arrival; accepting a refused **point grab** just moves. `_keyframePromptOpen` allows one dialog at a time, so a held press over a handle cannot stack modals.

  The fit after the jump is **deferred one tick** through `_pendingFitAfterJump`, consumed in `update()` the same way `_pendingEnable` already is: `runFit` reads the live camera as its starting state, and the live camera is whatever the controllers produce at `par.frame` — which they have not produced yet at the moment `par.frame` is assigned, so fitting inline would have solved the keyframe's points against the pose of the frame the user was just looking at. On arrival it re-checks the frame rather than assuming it, since the user may have scrubbed away while the prompt was up. The hit test now runs **before** the frame check in all three grab paths (`onMouseDown` in `CNodeFitCameraPoints` and in `CFitHandleOverlay`, plus the new `onWrongFrame` callback threaded through `FitPointHandles3D`): free when the answer is a silent status line, but a dialog raised on every press would have made a 3D view unorbitable and the video unpannable off-keyframe, so the offer belongs only to a press that actually lands on a handle. Nothing is claimed either way, so a press on a faded handle still orbits or pans. Two paths deliberately keep the quiet refusal: a press on **empty video** is as likely to be a pan as an add, and `requestFit` (*Fit on Change*) reaches `runFit` on every point nudge, where a dialog raised by a drag nobody thought of as "attempting a fit" would be an ambush. `runFit` itself still refuses unconditionally, so the rule is enforced in one place and merely offered in the others. `fitPointsSolve` passes the new `fitNow(false)` — a modal on the API surface would put a dialog on screen with nobody in front of it and hand the caller a summary of a fit that had not happened; `runFit`'s own refusal reaches it as a status string, which is what that API already reported, and the tool description now says so. `showChoice` already resolves to its dismiss value under `Globals.validationMode`, so regression runs neither block nor move the playhead.

- **Fitting with Free Look on now offers to clear it, instead of solving into a camera that cannot move** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Fit Now*** (`9c4b1ce1`; +97/−15 in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, the `fitPointsSolve` `doc` string in `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). Free Look makes `CNodeCamera.applyControllers()` return early, which suspends every computed source that writes the camera's pose. A fit still **solves** correctly under it — it reads the live camera, and a hand-flown pose is a real pose — but it cannot **apply** the answer. `applyResult()` selects `cameraTrackSwitch → fixedCamera` (position through `writePosition`), `fovSwitch → userFOV` and `CameraLOSController → Manual`, then writes `ptzAngles.az/el/roll/fov` and calls `ptz.refresh()` to land the FOV in `fovUI` — every one of them a controller source whose output reaches the camera only through the suspended `applyControllers()`. So the tool reports a residual and a *Fitted* status for a camera sitting exactly where it was hand-flown, which is the worst failure this tool can have, because the camera **is** the output.

  New `freeLookOn()` (`!!this.lookCameraNode()?.freeLook`) and `offerClearFreeLook()` split the response the same way the wrong-frame gate does: **enforced** in one place, **offered** in another. `runFit()` refuses unconditionally with *"Free Look is on, so the fit could not move the camera — switch it off and fit again"*, placed after the `enabled` / re-entrancy / `videoSize` gates and before the wrong-frame one, so it covers every path including `requestFit` (*Fit on Change*, which reaches `runFit` directly) and `refitOtherKeyframes`. The **offer** is only on `fitNow()`, the explicit button: a `showChoice` titled **Free Look Is On** reading *"Free Look needs to be off to fit points."* with **Clear Lock, then Do Fit** and **Cancel Fit**; declining leaves the mode on and reports *"Fit cancelled — Free Look is still on"*. `_freeLookPromptOpen` allows one dialog at a time. Accepting goes through `cam.freeLookController.setValue(false)` where the menu exists, falling back to the bare property where it does not — the setter does the real work either way, but going through the controller keeps the **Camera → Camera Tweaks → *Free Look Camera*** checkbox and its `.listen()`ing twin in the look view's header menu from silently disagreeing with the state.

  Accepting is safe because switching Free Look off is not a discard: the setter runs `syncFreeLookPosition()` and hands the orientation to `ptzAngles.syncFromCamera()`, so the flown position is already published into `fixedCameraPosition` and the pointing into the manual PTZ angles. The fit therefore starts from the pose the user chose rather than from wherever the camera was before they began flying — measured on the reference sitch, the fit that follows lands at the same 1.39 px residual as one run with Free Look never touched.

  The two prompts chain, and the rest of the change is the plumbing for that. Free Look is asked **first**, so the user is not moved to another frame only to be told the fit could not be applied there either. `fitNow`'s parameter is renamed `offerFrameJump` → `offerFixes`, since it now gates both prompts; `fitPointsSolve` in `src/CSitrecAPI.js` already passes `false`, so the API path is unchanged — no modal with nobody in front of it, and `runFit`'s refusal reaches the caller as the `status` field of the `_fitSummary` it already returns. Its `doc` string now says so, alongside the off-keyframe refusal `c1a9dc56` added there, so an assistant calling `fitPointsSolve` is told to expect a `success: true` whose status reports a solve that was blocked. `_pendingFitAfterJump` is renamed `_pendingFit` and shared by both prompts, and the deferred resume in `update()` no longer gates on `onCorrectFrame()`: it re-enters `fitNow()` so the remaining gates get another look, which is exactly how clearing Free Look while off a keyframe raises the keyframe prompt in its turn. Dropping that gate costs the case it was added for — a user who scrubs away in the one tick between accepting a keyframe jump and its resume now meets the keyframe prompt a second time instead of a silent no-op.

- **A zoomed video now fills its pane when the aspect is not locked to the video** — **View → *Video Zoom %*** (`f525ecff`; +170/−33 in `src/nodes/CNodeVideoView.js`). `getSourceAndDestCoords()` cropped the **source** by the zoom but computed the destination purely from the two aspect ratios, so the letterbox was a constant: at any zoom the video was drawn into the same centred band and the rest of the pane stayed black, even with plenty of image in hand to cover it. On a 1388×759 photo in an 835×871 pane at 3.54× that threw away 48% of the pane while the source crop it was drawn from sat comfortably inside the image. The displayed image is now modelled as a rectangle of size `(baseW*zoom, baseH*zoom)` centred in the pane and offset by the pan, intersected with the pane, with the source rect following from the same clip; past `zoom = aspectSource/aspectView` (1.91 in that sitch) the bars are pushed off the pane entirely, and the transition is continuous — measured 1.7 px of bar left at 1.90× and none at 1.92×. New helpers `videoSourceSize()`, `videoFitInPane()` and `lockedToVideoAspect()` give the two rectangles and the mode one definition each, and the clip is expressed in **fractions** of the displayed image (`clamp01`) so both rectangles derive from one pair of numbers and land on exactly 0 and 1 when the image is wholly inside the pane — a pane-space subtraction came back a float ULP short, and the fractions keep zoom 1 bit-for-bit what it was.

  Gated on *Match Video Aspect* (**Camera** menu) being **off**. With it on, `CNodeView3D` letterboxes the look view's canvas to the video's aspect and shows exactly the video's centred 1/zoom crop, so the pane has to letterbox identically or the two pictures stop being comparable; that path is byte-identical to before. The 3D side needed **no** matching change: `fovCoverage` widens the look camera's vertical field and `camera.zoom` applies the zoom separately, so the look view's half-tangent `tan(fov0/2)/(fovCoverage*zoom)` is identically the pane's `tan(fov0/2)*heightPx/fullH` — the correspondence was already there and unused, and `fovCoverage` is unchanged by this rewrite (the new `baseH/heightPx` reduces to the old expression term for term). It stays zoom-**independent** for the same reason: folding the zoom in here would apply it twice. `clampPanOffset()` becomes per-axis — the old `(1 - 1/zoom)/2` is only correct on the axis where the image fills the pane, and along the letterboxed axis the pane covers *more* of the image than `1/zoom`, so the symmetric limit let a black bar back in at the far edge of a pan — and the draw holds the image edge from current geometry via `coveredEdge()` rather than trusting the stored pan, since a pane **resize** (or a pan deserialized against a differently-shaped pane) moves the limit with no mouse handler involved; the corrected pan is written back so a later drag carries on from what is on screen. Measured at the new limits, a full pan lands the source rect on the image edge exactly (759.0000000000000 of 759). `fovCoverage` also gains a zero-height guard, where `baseH/heightPx` would be 0/0: the look view divides its camera FOV by this and tests only for `undefined`, so a NaN would become a NaN field of view for that frame; the guard returns 1, which is what the old else-branch returned there. Not changed but worth knowing: `CNodeMQ9UI:481` and `CNodeWescamMXUI:307` size their HUD grid from `dWidth`/`dHeight`, so above zoom 1 that grid now spans the pane instead of a fixed band — identical at zoom 1, which is where those sitches sit.

- **Better starting defaults for *Fit Camera to Points*** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points** (`1225ce4a`; `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `docs/FitPointsAPI.md`). Both are constructor defaults with an `if (v.x !== undefined)` guard in `modDeserialize`, so existing saves carry their own value and only new sitches see the change. **`autoFit` (*Fit on Change*) now defaults off**: placing the first points is the part of the workflow where the solution is least constrained, so fitting as you go spends the time on answers nobody wants and swings the camera between them — place the set, then *Fit Now*. **`useTiles` (*Place on 3D Buildings*) now defaults on**: the tiles are the surface the analyst is looking at, and a rooftop corner placed against the elevation map instead lands at street level. That is not a coverage gamble, because `surfaceAlongRay` is strict priority — tiles, then the elevation height field, then the ellipsoid — so where the tiles are absent or still streaming the pick lands on exactly the surface the old default used, and a landmark on bare ground still lands on bare ground because the tilesets carry their own ground. `docs/FitPointsAPI.md` told MCP callers to pass `useTiles: true` and warned that "with autoFit on, each add re-solves"; both were about to become wrong and are corrected, including when to pass `useTiles: false` (every landmark *is* the ground — a river bend, a shoreline, a track). No scoping was needed for these two: `CNodeFitCameraPoints` is only constructed under `if (Sit.isCustom ...)`.

- **A view's *Effects* now starts off in the custom sitch** — **Effects → *Effects*** (`1225ce4a`, scoped by `09e11208`, made a default rather than an assignment by `ff0a0b82`; `addEffects()` in `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`). An effects chain is an interpretation laid over the scene — blur, focus — not part of it, so a sitch the user is building from scratch should start by showing what is actually there. The first cut turned it off everywhere, which review caught as wrong for the built-in sitches whose effects chain **is** the picture: `SitAguadilla` and `SitJellyfish` declare `isIR`, and the render path gates both the `FLIRShader` pass and the IR ambient-light swap (`lightingNode.setIR`) on `effectsEnabled`, so they would have loaded as ordinary visible-light views. The default is therefore `!(Sit?.isCustom ?? false)` — of the sitches that define an `effects` chain at all (Aguadilla, Chilean, Custom, FLIR1, Jellyfish, Model Inspector, SWR), `SitCustom` is the only one that is `isCustom`, so the rest are untouched; Gimbal, GimbalCustom and Starlink are `isCustom` but define no effects, so `addEffects()` never runs for them, and `isCustom` is never assigned at runtime. It is applied as a **default, not an assignment** (`if (this.effectsEnabled === undefined)`): `CNodeView3D`'s constructor calls `super(v)` at line 111 and `CNodeView`'s runs `applyEarlyMods()` at its line 299, so by the time `addEffects()` runs at line 351 a saved sitch has already had `effectsEnabled` restored, and assigning here would change what that save renders. That hazard predates this branch — the unconditional `= true` it replaces clobbered a saved `false` identically, and was masked for custom saves by a later deserialize pass; relying on that pass is exactly what stopped `freeLook` persisting, so it is not relied on here. `Sit` can be `undefined` for a view built before any sitch loads, which falls through to `true`, the long-standing behaviour. This is not a master render switch: the render path reads `effectsEnabled || useLookViewHDR || effectiveAerialPerspective`, so HDR and aerial perspective are unaffected.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed the video overlay painting black over the whole look view** (`40b953a6`; +45 in `src/nodes/CNodeVideoView.js`, `data/custom/SitCustom.js`, `data/misb/Sitmisb.js`). A video view filled its canvas black before drawing the frame. That is right for a **pane** — the bars are what make it read as a screen — but an overlay is not a pane, it is a layer, and the fill is a sheet of paint over the view underneath: with the video zoomed out to 53% and *Vid Overlay Trans %* at 0.69, the whole look view came back at 31% brightness with one bright rectangle where the video was. `autoFill` now defaults to `!isOverlay` (`isOverlay` being `this.overlayView !== undefined`, set by `CNodeView`'s constructor before this runs) and `autoClear` defaults to `isOverlay` to match — a freestanding view repaints every pixel each frame, but an overlay leaves whatever it did not draw over, so zooming the video *out* would otherwise smear the previous, larger frame around the new one. Clearing is **derived** from the fill (`if (!this.autoFill) this.autoClear = true`) rather than left to the sitch definitions, because `autoClear: false` is baked into every custom sitch **already saved**: it was correct in those saves, and a saved sitch overrides the sitch definition, so correcting `data/custom/SitCustom.js` reaches only new ones. `SitGimbal`, `SitGoFast` and `SitGimbalCustom` have always passed `autoClear: true, autoFill: false` by hand — that *is* this default written out longhand — so they are unchanged. An overlay with **no** video still fills black, which is what the *Vid Overlay Trans %* tooltip documents and the only thing that makes the slider do anything before a video is loaded; that cannot be settled at construction, since `videoData` arrives (and can go away again) long afterwards, so `renderCanvas()` picks between the two, guarded on `_autoFillIsDefault` so a sitch that asks for a particular value still gets it. Verified by sampling the overlay canvas: alpha 0 outside the video rect and opaque inside with a video loaded, opaque black everywhere with none. Also checked through the export compositor (*Render Viewport Video*) and at the alpha-1 endpoint of *Render Fade*, where the bug was worst — a fade **to** the video used to fade the surrounding scene to black.

- **Fixed off-keyframe fit handles looking editable in the 3D views while faded on the video** (`c1a9dc56`; `OFF_FRAME_ALPHA` added to `src/FitHandleDraw.js`, consumed by `CFitHandleOverlay.renderCanvas()`/`drawVideoPlaneHandles()` in `src/FitPointHandles3D.js` and by the video overlay's draw in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`). The 3D ground handles and the video-plane handles drawn in the main view were drawn at full strength off-keyframe while the video's own handles faded to 0.3, so the same point looked live in one view and faded in the other — which read as their being different things, when the fade is the signal that a point is not editable at this frame. The alpha moves to one exported constant so the three call sites cannot drift.

## Version 2.130.1 (2026-08-15)

### Improvements

- **A pin's edit menu is now an edit mode you can drag the pin in** — right-click a pin, or drop one with **right-click the ground → *Drop Pin / Add Feature*** (`2a913f14`; ~+430 in `src/CFeatureManager.js` — `handleContextMenu()`, `showFeatureEditMenu()` gaining a `view` argument, new `startEditing()` / `stopEditing()` / `onPointerDown()` / `moveFeatureTo()` / `featureScreenPoints()` / `screenDistanceToFeature()`; `featureManager.done` in `src/i18n/en.js`; the `dropPin` call site in `src/CustomManagerMenus.js` now passing `ViewMan.get(sourceViewID)`). Right-clicking a pin used to open a plain context menu that any click dismissed. It is now a persistent **Edit: &lt;label&gt;** menu matching the building / clouds / overlay editing menus: clicking elsewhere leaves it up, and it closes on *Done*, Escape, a double-click on its title, or being dragged off screen — closing it is what leaves edit mode. While it is open the pin can be dragged around the view it was opened from, landing on the surface under the cursor via `raycastLocalGround()` — terrain, or a Google 3D-tile roof where those are loaded — and taking its height from the elevation map only when the ray misses everything and `raycastLocalGround()` falls back to its ellipsoid sphere, which sits hundreds of metres off the drawn ground. Grabbing the label rather than the arrow preserves the grab offset, so the pin does not snap to the cursor.

  The pointer handlers are registered on `document` in the **capture phase** and swallow a drag they take, so the view's canvas never sees it. Without that, `CameraControls` reads the press, has its state cleared by the first disabled move, then counts the drag's `pointerup` as a tap — and a click within 300 ms and 15 px of it double-tap-zooms the camera. Presses that are not on a pin propagate as before. The drag also takes pointer capture on the view canvas (wrapped in try/catch, since `setPointerCapture` throws on a pointer the browser no longer considers active) and ends on `pointercancel` or on a move with no button held, so a release outside the window cannot strand it with the camera controls disabled. Also in this change: the menu's location rows update live as the pin moves (they were snapshots that never changed), a drag is undoable through `UndoManager` via `moveFeatureTo()`, deleting a pin or loading a new sitch leaves edit mode, and the menu is re-fitted to the screen *after* its rows are added — it was previously measured while empty, so the new *Done* button landed off the bottom.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed *Fit Camera to Points* control points landing in mid-air over Google Photorealistic 3D tiles** — **Camera → Fit Camera to Points**, with *Place on 3D Buildings* on (`surfaceAlongRay()` in `src/FitSurfacePick.js` now calling `intersectDisplayed()`, which is exported from `src/raycastGround.js` for the purpose). This is the **same defect the 2.130.0 entry above describes, at a second call site that fix missed**: `surfaceAlongRay()` was still using `raycaster.intersectObject(group, true)`, which ignores `.visible`, so the LOD levels `3DTilesRenderer` has stopped drawing stayed in the hit list — and being coarse ancestors interpolated across a whole region, they generally won as the nearest hit. Verified at one Torrance pixel: before, lat 33.7721 / 1677 m altMSL; after, lat 33.8033 / 27.9 m altMSL. Zamperini Field is at 101 ft = 31 m and the elevation-surface control at the same pixel gives 28.2 m, so the old answer was ~3.4 km away from the pixel's actual ground and ~1.65 km above it. Affects `CNodeFitCameraPoints` (placing and dragging a control point onto 3D geometry) and `CSitrecAPI.pickWorldPoint`, the world-point pick the assistant and MCP use. `intersectDisplayed()` is now the exported single entry point for every ray that means "what is the user looking at", locked by a new `tests/intersectDisplayed.test.js` (5 tests). Its central case is a throwing container standing in for `TilesRenderer`'s `TilesGroup`: that class's `raycast()` override runs its own recursive descent with **no** `.visible` prune, so a walk that prunes but still calls `raycast()` on containers puts every hidden tile straight back — which is why only geometry-bearing leaves are raycast, and why the test throws if anyone "simplifies" it.

- **Fixed terrain ground queries returning the top of the quadtree pyramid — ~76 m too high — while Google Photorealistic 3D tiles are the rendered ground** (`getPointBelow()` in `src/nodes/CNodeTerrain.js`: the `raycast` branch is now skipped when `this.UI.suppressMapImagery()` is true, falling through to the existing elevation-map path). The root cause is measured, and is not what it looks like. Under imagery suppression the terrain tiles keep a shared **placeholder** material with no `.uniforms`, so `QuadTreeMap`'s readiness predicates — which require `material.uniforms?.map` — never pass, so the suppression-only reconciler never retires an ancestor tile, so no tile layer bits are ever cleared. The terrain group ends up holding its **entire** quadtree pyramid, all active: one vertical column at Torrance hit 13 meshes with spans from 9,343 m to 12,756,312 m (the zoom-0 whole-globe tile), and 512 of 514 terrain meshes carried the placeholder material. `getClosestIntersect` takes the hit nearest the ray origin and the origin is 100 km **up**, so it returned the **highest**: +70.34 m HAE where the ground, and the finest tile, are at −5.5 m. Verified at five points after the fix: −6.13 / −7.10 / −5.41 / −11.45 / +3.25 m, bit-identical to the elevation-map path, where before it returned +70.34 / +73.45 / +66.54 / +60.33 / +78.54. **This is not a geoid or datum artifact** — ruled out both by source audit (the geoid is added exactly once, at tile decode) and by the finest LOD matching truth. Nor can it be filtered out: 0 of 514 terrain meshes are hidden so `.visible` catches nothing, the camera's layer mask yields the same 13 hits, and `isRenderingForView` fails **closed** (its uniforms gate passes for 2 meshes in the whole terrain). Falling through is contractually safe because the branch already falls through whenever the ray misses. The tile surface is deliberately **not** consulted here: it is a single draped mesh that would answer with rooftops, and this function promises buildings-free terrain.

- **Fixed placing a position at eye level measuring from the elevation map instead of the surface you clicked** (`setFromECEF()` in `src/nodes/CNodePositionLLA.js`; `adjustHeightAboveGround()` in `src/threeExt.js` gaining an options object). Shift-held placement of a non-AGL position drops it 7 ft above local ground, but it passed a bare `true` to `adjustHeightAboveGround()` — which is the `raycast` flag, not a ground selector — so under Google Photorealistic 3D tiles it measured from the terrain elevation map rather than the surface the user had just pointed at (measured in one Athens block, the elevation map sits ~12 m above the tile ground in most columns and up to ~6 m below it in a fifth of them) and, before the `CNodeTerrain` fix above, from a terrain raycast that was itself ~76 m out. `adjustHeightAboveGround(point, height, options)` now takes `{raycast, useVisibleGround}`, with a bare boolean still accepted as `{raycast}` so every pre-existing call is unchanged; the shift path passes `{useVisibleGround: true, raycast: true}`. When `useVisibleGround` is set the tile ground resolves **first**, so on success the terrain is never consulted and `raycast` cannot spend a millisecond raycasting a basemap that is hidden anyway; it remains the fallback for when no tile ground there is acceptable. It is off by default because it costs a tile raycast (~0.2 ms) that bulk callers — which sit on the ground by construction — do not need. "Which surface is the visible ground" is now encoded exactly once, in a new module-private `visibleGroundBelow(point)` in `src/threeExt.js` (returns the tile surface when the terrain basemap is hidden, else `null`), shared with `clampAboveGround()` — a behaviour-preserving substitution there, since that call was already inside the `terrainBasemapHidden()` branch.

- **Fixed hidden 3D objects forcing full shadow-map re-renders** (`hasVisibleShadowCaster()` in `src/nodes/CNode3D.js`, now `traverseVisible()` rather than `traverse()`). The old walk tested the root object's own `.visible` and each child's own `.visible`, but never the intermediate ancestors — and Three.js will not render a child whose ancestor is hidden, so a `castShadow` mesh under a hidden mid-level group still counted as a visible caster. Moving one then reached `markShadowCastersDirty()`, which sets `viewSun.shadow.needsUpdate = true` on every `CNodeView3D`: a full shadow-map re-render per view, for geometry that never reaches the screen. `traverseVisible()` stops at any node with `visible === false` and subsumes the old root-visibility early-out.

- **`groundBelow()` no longer considers tile LODs the renderer has stopped drawing** (`src/nodes/CNodeBuildings3DTiles.js`, now using `intersectDisplayed()`). **Latent** — no failure was reproduced, and the elevation-map arbitration already rejected the gross cases (a hidden hit 4,920 m underground was correctly thrown out). But that arbitration only establishes *plausible* ground, not *displayed* ground: a hidden coarse ancestor that happened to sit nearer the elevation map than the displayed fine tile would win, and within the 40 m `GROUND_TOLERANCE` nothing would catch it. Measured 107 of 618 tiles hidden in the main view and 99 of 407 in the look view. Since what this function returns is the visible surface below, geometry that is not being drawn has no business in its hit list.

### Documentation

- **Corrected two comment claims that were measurably false** (`src/raycastGround.js`, `src/threeExt.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeBuildings3DTiles.js`, `src/nodes/CNodePositionLLA.js`). (1) `intersectDisplayed()`'s header claimed pruning invisible subtrees was "also cheaper than the recursive intersect". It is not: measured over the Torrance tiles (339 displayed meshes, 206 hidden) a ray costs ~0.044 ms through `intersectObject` and ~0.055 ms through the pruning walk, because the BVH rejects a hidden tile about as fast as the traversal skips it. It pays for itself in the answer, not the clock — the same claim has been corrected in the 2.130.0 entry above. (2) Several comments claimed `groundBelow()` "rejects roofs". It does not and cannot: Google photogrammetry is a **single draped mesh**, so a building is a bump in the surface with no street underneath — a straight-down ray returned exactly **one** hit at all 144 Torrance points sampled — so over a footprint the roof is the only hit, the "nearest the elevation map" arbitration degenerates to "return the only hit", and the 40 m `GROUND_TOLERANCE` accepts any structure shorter than that. The function is really *visible surface below*, and its tolerance rejects gross coarse-LOD error, not buildings. That behaviour is correct and deliberately unchanged — the draped surface is the only occupiable surface, and preferring "true ground" would put a WASD walker inside the building's watertight shell — so only the comments changed, plus a warning never to wire it into a query that promises bare terrain.
