The real result is applied **after** the replay, not up front and re-shown: `land()` is handed to `playback.start()` as its finished callback, because `applyResult` selects switches and selecting a heading source re-syncs `ptzAngles` from the live camera, which would fight the playback every frame. Per step, `showTracedCamera` therefore makes only the three writes `restoreCameraState` already makes — `fixedCameraPosition` via `setLLA`, and `ptzAngles`' az/el/roll/fov — with the ECEF→LLA conversion injected by the caller, so the module stays free of Sitrec's coordinate and geoid modules (the caller subtracts `meanSeaLevelOffset`, matching `writePosition`, since the altitude field means orthometric height). Re-entrancy and teardown are covered: `runFit` returns early if a replay is running and this is not the replay's own solve; `stepPlayback` sets `applyingFit` around its writes so the cascade cannot start a second solve inside the first; and pressing the button again, unticking *Enable Fit*, or disposing the node all call `playback.stop()`, which still fires the callback — so the camera lands on the solved fit rather than being abandoned wherever the search had reached. The status line reads e.g. *Descending 7 / 13 · 12.4 px* or *Sweeping FOV 96 / 142 · score 3.21e-3*, and deliberately stops writing progress on the final step, which would otherwise overwrite the real *Fitted* status.
- **Fit Camera to Points: place control points on the 3D tile geometry rather than the elevation surface** (`a3b92a9e`; new exported `surfaceAlongRay` in `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`, `groundUnderCanvasPoint` gaining a `useTiles` argument and `getUseTiles` joining the handles' callback contract; new serialized `useTiles` (default `false`) in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`; new exported `ellipsoidAlongRay` in `src/raycastGround.js`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Place on 3D Buildings***, label hard-coded). The elevation map is a smooth height field with no buildings on it, so a rooftop corner placed against it lands at street level — tens of metres from the thing being pointed at, an error that is invisible at long range and decisive at short range. At short range essentially every recognisable feature stands **up** off the ground, which is why this is what makes a close-range fit possible at all. Measured by the author in an urban window-reflection scene: residual **0.77 px**, `observability` reading *Good (position ±1 m)*, per-point residuals 0.2–1.0 px — against ±84 m on a long-range elevation-based fit. It applies to both placement paths, which is why they now share one function: dragging a handle (`CFitHandleOverlay.onMouseDrag` → `groundUnderCanvasPoint(..., this.owner.getUseTiles())`) and seeding a new point from a video click (`CNodeFitCameraPoints` now calls `surfaceAlongRay` where it called `raycastGroundElevationFast`), so clicking a rooftop seeds on the roof instead of on the street and then jumping the first time it is dragged. `surfaceAlongRay` is **strict priority — tiles, then elevation, then ellipsoid** — and deliberately **not** `raycastLocalGround`'s nearest-concrete-surface. That distinction is the whole point: the elevation surface can sit *above* the tile geometry and win on distance. Measured at one test pixel, the elevation surface was **6.9 m higher and 43 m nearer** than the tiles, so "nearest" hands back the invisible height field draped over the very building being aimed at. `raycastLocalGround` only escapes this when the basemap is hidden — its `terrainHidden` check, which exists because Google Photorealistic 3D tiles hide the basemap. Verified by flipping basemap visibility with everything else held fixed: the tiles answer was unchanged (174.34 m altitude / 8.8166 km range both ways) where nearest-wins would have jumped to the elevation surface (181.28 m / 8.7735 km) — the same 6.9 m and 43 m gap. `raycastLocalGround` itself is left untouched, because nearest *is* correct for orbit, pan and zoom anchors, which want whatever is visibly frontmost. Step 1 raycasts the `buildings3DTiles` group with `firstHitOnly` (the tiles' BVH nearest hit; ignored by non-BVH meshes, where sorted `hits[0]` is nearest anyway) and borrows the camera's `layers.mask`, because the tile meshes live on the main/look layers; `groundUnderCanvasPoint` passes `view.camera` and not the LOD-prepared camera, since `prepareCameraForLOD` changes fov, aspect and offsets but never the layer mask, which is the only thing this pass reads. Step 2 is the fast elevation height-field march (`raycastGroundElevationFast`), **not** the terrain mesh, which has no BVH and costs about a millisecond per ray — unaffordable at one ray per frame during a drag. Step 3 is the ellipsoid, so a ray outside tile coverage or ahead of streaming still lands somewhere defensible, while still returning null for a ray heading at the sky. It is off by default for two reasons, neither of them timidity: the elevation surface is the right one for a landmark that *is* the ground (a river bend, a shoreline, a track), and it is the one that is always there — elevation covers the whole planet at some zoom, whereas the 3D tiles cover a fraction of it and the `buildings3DTiles` node only exists once **Terrain → *3D Buildings*** has been switched on. The setting is serialized with the fit's other options, and governs where new points are dropped and where dragged handles land, not points already placed. Supporting refactor: the ellipsoid intersection was lifted out of `raycastLocalGround` into exported `ellipsoidAlongRay(origin, direction)` so both callers share one copy of the subtlety it carries — the sphere radius is the geocentric ellipsoid radius at the **ray origin's own latitude**, not `Globals.equatorRadius`, because at mid-latitudes an equatorial-radius sphere sits several kilometres above the real ground, a street-level camera is mathematically *inside* it, and from inside a sphere `Ray.intersectSphere` returns the far exit point ~12,700 km away through the opposite side of the planet, poisoning every anchor derived from it. `raycastLocalGround` now calls the extracted function; its behaviour is unchanged.
- **Render Fade: crossfade the sim and the video overlay into a rendered video** (`7991c2a1`; new `createFadeExportPlan` and `findFadeOverlayView` in `src/VideoExporter.js`, `setupFadeMenu`/`exportFadeVideo` and six new settings on `VideoExportManager`, a new `options.plan` path through `CNodeView3D.exportVideo`, i18n block `videoExport.fade.*`; **Video → Video Render &amp; Export → Render Fade**). Renders the view chosen in *Render Video View* (`videoExportView`, default `lookView`) while driving the video overlay's `transparency` — the same 0–1 the ***Vid Overlay Trans %*** slider writes (a `CNodeGUIValue` created by `CNodeViewCanvas` under the **View** menu) — on a schedule measured in **seconds** rather than frames: hold on the starting view for *Initial Delay (s)*, then each of *Fades* crossfades over *Fade Time (s)* and holds for *Hold Time (s)*. Alpha 0 is the sim alone and alpha 1 is the video overlay alone; *Start With* (*Look* / *Video*) picks which end it opens on. Output length is `initialDelay + fades × (fadeTime + holdTime)` (`plan.totalSeconds`), rendered at `Sit.fps`; an even fade count returns to the starting view and an odd one ends on the other (`alphaEnd`). *Hold Current Frame* (`fadeHoldFrame`, default on) makes `frameAt()` return `par.frame` for the whole render, for a still comparison; off, it plays the A-B range from `Sit.aFrame` and wraps with `startFrame + (index % rangeLength)` when the schedule outlasts the clip. Implemented by making the single-view export loop take a **pre-built frame plan**: `CNodeView3D.exportVideo` now accepts `options.plan` and only derives one from A-B (with the duplicate-frame scan) when none is supplied, and `createFadeExportPlan` returns the same object shape `createVideoExportFramePlan` does plus `alphaAt(index)` — so the encoder, compositing, progress and download paths are reused unchanged, with `nameSuffix: "fade"` now appended to the filename by `getVideoExportSpeedSuffix`. The overlay it drives is located by `findFadeOverlayView`: the view whose `overlayView` is the exported view and which carries a `transparency` (the mirrored video over the look view), which is exactly how the export compositor in `exportVideo` identifies overlay children. It is forced visible with `setVisibleRaw(true)` for the duration — necessary because that compositing pass only draws children that are `_effectivelyVisible`, so a fade requested with the overlay hidden would otherwise silently render no fade — and both the transparency and the visibility are restored in the `finally`. The fade writes `view.transparency` directly and never the GUI node, so the slider's own value is left alone; `canvas.style.opacity` is kept in step purely so the on-screen view fades along while rendering. `exportFadeVideo` refuses with a `showError` when the chosen view is not exportable, or when it has no such overlay, the second message pointing at loading a video and exporting the view it is mirrored onto. Audio is omitted (`includeAudio` passed as `false`) because the schedule either holds one frame or wraps the clip, so there is no source timeline for an audio track to follow; for the same reason the fade plan fixes `playbackSpeed: 1`, `pingPong: false`, `loops: 1` and `skippedDuplicateFrames: 0`, so the A-B speed, ping-pong, loop and *Unique frames only* settings do not apply to a fade render. Covered by seven new Jest cases in `tests/VideoExporter.test.js`: schedule length, the alpha ramp in both start directions, an odd fade count ending on the other view, hold-versus-wrap frame selection, the plan fields the export loop reads, and `findFadeOverlayView` picking the overlay child that carries a transparency.

## Version 2.120.1 (2026-08-08)

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed the *Fit Camera to Points* landmark handles staying on screen after the fit was switched off** (working tree; one line in `CFitHandleOverlay`'s constructor in `src/FitPointHandles3D.js` — `this.separateVisibility = true`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Enable Fit***). Unticking *Enable Fit* left the circle-and-crosshair handles and their numbers drawn over the main and look views — and in the main view, the markers showing where each video point falls on the video in the frustum as well. *Clear All Points* could not shift them either. The cause is one flag, and the reason it matters is a genuinely counter-intuitive interaction between visibility and render-on-demand. `ViewMan.updateDOMVisibility()` (`src/CViewManager.js`, run every frame from `src/indexRender.js:479-480`) handles three kinds of view: a non-overlay gets `div.style.display`; an overlay that declares `separateVisibility` gets `canvas.style.visibility`; and *any other overlay is left alone*, its DOM controlled by the parent's div display. The two fit-handle overlays (`fitHandles_mainView`, `fitHandles_lookView`, one per entry in `HANDLE_VIEWS`) were in that third bucket, but their parents are `mainView` and `lookView`, which stay up — so nothing ever touched their canvases. Meanwhile `FitPointHandles3D.setEnabled(false)` sets `visible = false`, which makes `_computeEV` return false and drops the overlay out of the render loop at `src/indexRender.js:500`. The canvas therefore sat in the DOM holding the last handles it had drawn, frozen there *precisely because* the view that would have cleared it was no longer being rendered. Measured before the fix: both canvases still `display: block`, `visibility: visible`, `opacity: 1`, with 61 and 72 painted pixels in an 8400-sample grid. The *Clear All Points* half of the report is the same defect, not a second one — the clear path itself is correct (verified through a real render frame: 0 painted pixels, sight lines gone, `sightLines.group.visible` false); it only looked broken with the fit already off, because there was then no frame in which to erase the stale pixels. Declaring `separateVisibility` puts these overlays on the same footing as the fit's own video overlay, `CNodeFitCameraPoints`, which has set the flag since it was introduced — the 3D handle overlays were the inconsistent ones. Verified by round trip: fit on → both canvases compute `visibility: visible`; fit off → both `hidden`, the video overlay `hidden`, `sightLines.group.visible` false; fit on again → both `visible` and 7 sight lines rebuilt. The sight lines themselves (`FitPointSightLines3D`) were never affected — they are scene geometry and `setEnabled(false)` already called `clear()` and hid the group. One consequence worth knowing when debugging later: these overlays no longer inherit their host view's effective visibility, so an overlay can now be "visible" while `mainView`/`lookView` is hidden. That is the standing behaviour of every other `separateVisibility` overlay (annotation, mask, tracking, grid, mask, lens ghost), and the compositors already account for it — `VideoExporter.js` skips an overlay whose `overlayView` is not itself effectively visible, and `CViewManager.unsuppressView` carries `separateVisibility` children along when a fullscreened parent is re-shown.

## Version 2.120.0 (2026-08-08)

### New Features

- **Fit Camera to Points: a second solver, by plane homography** (working tree; new `src/CameraPlaneHomography.js`, exporting `fitCameraByPlaneHomography`; `FIT_METHODS` and the *Method* dropdown in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, serialized as `fitMethod`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Method***, options *3D points (direct)* / *Plane homography*). The direct solver in `CameraPointFit.js` searches position, pointing and FOV together against each landmark's real terrain position. The homography route is the classical alternative most published photogrammetric reconstructions of oblique video take: assume the control points are coplanar, solve the plane-to-image projective map, and recover the focal length from the fact that two columns of a rotation matrix must be orthogonal and of equal length — the same principle as checkerboard calibration. Having both on the *same* control points is what makes it possible to show that a disagreement comes from the points rather than from the choice of method. Pipeline: work in a local east/north/up frame at the control points' centroid so ECEF curvature does not distort the plane fit; least-squares ground plane (`fitPlane`); normalised DLT with Hartley conditioning (`conditionPoints`, `dltHomography`, using `jacobiSVD` re-exported from `CameraPointFit.js`) followed by a coordinate-descent polish of the eight free entries (`refineHomography`); then a 900-sample log scan of focal length between 170° and 1° horizontal FOV minimising `orthonormalityScore`, golden-section refined, and `decomposeAtFocal` picking the overall sign that puts the camera *above* the plane. Requires at least 4 control points. Two consequences are surfaced rather than hidden. (1) The method solves position, pointing and focal length as one decomposition and cannot hold any of them fixed, so *Lock Position*, *Lock FOV* and *Lock Roll* are greyed out while it is selected (`syncMethodControls()`, called from `_setupGUI`, `modDeserialize` and the dropdown's `onChange`). (2) Its conditioning is set by how the control points are spread in **range**, not by parameter conditioning — camera height is recovered from the near/far differential in depression angle — so it supplies its own `observability` string from the range-spread ratio (≥2.0× *Good*, ≥1.5× *Weak — height poorly determined*, below that *Unobservable*), and `CNodeFitCameraPoints` now prefers `result.observability` over `describeObservability(result)` when a solver provides one. `diagnostics` additionally carries the 5% score band in horizontal FOV, `maxOffPlane`, `heightAbovePlane` and the homography's own RMS, because a sharply peaked focal score is precision, not accuracy. The reported *Residual* still comes from `evaluateCamera` against the real 3D points, so the two methods' numbers are directly comparable — and because the homography never minimises reprojection error, it normally lands slightly worse in RMS than a direct optimum even when it is exactly right. The fit-acceptance guard was therefore made solver-dependent: the direct path keeps its hair's-breadth `current.rms + 0.01` margin (its answer *is* the RMS optimum, so anything worse means a bad basin), while the homography path uses `current.rms * 4 + 20`, which only catches an actual runaway — the tight margin rejected every homography fit attempted after a direct one, which is precisely the comparison the second method exists to support. The rejection message is reworded to match. **Not yet exercised in the browser: this solver and its dropdown are new in this release and have not been run against real footage.**
- **Fit Camera to Points: the sight lines the fit is solving for** (`861027b5`; new `src/FitPointSightLines3D.js`, plus `videoQuadMatrix`/`videoQuadOccluder`/`rayDisplay`/`frustumNode` and `videoPointOnQuad` in `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `behindQuad`/`drawVideoPlaneHandles` in `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`; new serialized toggle *Show Sight Lines* — internal `showRays`, default on — in **Camera → Fit Camera to Points**). Every control-point pair asserts that its ground point lies on the sight line through its video point; the camera is wherever all of those lines are satisfied at once. This draws that assertion in the world: a line from the camera to each ground point in that pair's colour, with the video point marked separately where it falls on the video hanging in the frustum, so a correct camera runs each line straight through its own marker and any visible gap is that point's reprojection residual — the same number the video overlay prints in pixels, here at the scale and direction it has in the scene. Drawn in the **main view only** (`RAY_VIEW`), because in the look view every line would project to a point and every marker would land on the pixel it already occupies; the look view is also the one view the frustum's video quad is not drawn in, since the quad is on `MASK_HELPERS`. The lines are real scene geometry on the helpers layer, not overlay strokes, so terrain occludes them: a line that dives into a ridge and re-emerges past it is saying something true about where that landmark is. Their vertices are held **relative to a `Group` positioned at the camera**, because `Line2` packs positions into a float32 buffer and the world frame is ECEF (~6.4e6 m), where float32 steps about half a metre and every line would visibly crawl; relative to a double-precision group origin the quantisation is millimetres. Rebuilds are gated on a metre-resolution `signatureOf` key, since `LineSegmentsGeometry.setPositions` allocates a fresh instanced buffer per call and `update()` runs every frame. The video-point markers appear only when **Show → *Video in Frustum*** is on, and are placed by putting normalised (u,v) through the quad's own world matrix (composed live from the camera rather than read from `quad.matrixWorld`, which can still describe last frame's camera when the frustum's `update()` has not yet run — a fit moves the camera in one step, and mixing frames would smear the markers off the video for exactly the frame the user is looking at). In the same commit, the ground handles — which stay overlay-drawn on purpose, so a ridge cannot hide a landmark being placed — are now clipped by the video quad in the main view, tested in the quad's local frame where it is the unit square at z = 0 (`behindQuad`: one segment-plane intersection and two comparisons). A marker showing through the *front* of the video would read as a point in mid-air rather than a place on the ground beyond it.
- **Fit Camera to Points: the look view's wheel and drag now zoom and pan the video** (`e28c2538`; new `src/FitViewSync.js` — `fitViewSyncActive`/`fitViewSyncWheel`/`fitViewSyncPan` — hooked into `CameraMapControls`' wheel and mouse-move handlers in `src/js/CameraControls.js`). Placing a control point means finding the same feature twice, once in the footage and once in the world, which needs both zoomed a long way in — but the only way to zoom the 3D was to move the camera, which is the very thing being solved for; nudging it desynchronised the two pictures and changed the answer. The rendering half of the loop already existed and is unchanged: the look view is created with `syncVideoZoom`, so it reframes itself to the video's zoom and pan. What was missing was the other direction. While a fit is being edited, the wheel and the left drag on the look view are forwarded to the `videoZoom` node (**View → *Video Zoom %***) and the video's `panOffsetX/Y`, and the 3D follows because it was already following; middle and right drag keep their normal meaning so the camera remains reachable. Deliberately narrow gating — look view only, `syncVideoZoom` required (without it, driving the video's pan would move one picture and not the other), a `videoZoom` node required (the `pos`-based fallback zoom in `CNodeVideoView` moves the view's own rectangle, which the 3D cannot follow), and the fit must be enabled — so turning the fit off puts every control back exactly as it was. Two details that are load-bearing: the pointer maps through `renderedRect` rather than the pane, because the fit forces *Match Video Aspect* on and that letterboxes the rendered image inside the pane (measured: 2 px inset, 4 px short on a 767×435 look view), and pane coordinates would put the zoom anchor off the feature being pointed at by more the further from centre the user is — which is exactly where they are once zoomed in to place a point; and the drag hook keys off `this.button === 0` rather than `this.state`, because `updateStateFromEvent` forces every button to `STATE.PAN` whenever a PTZ controller drives the camera, which during a fit it always does. Wheel step is the same 10%-per-notch the video view uses, and the pan is expressed as a fraction of the visible region (1/zoom), so the two views move together by construction rather than by a tuned constant. Verified in-browser: over a zoom from 100% to 209.075% the look camera translated 0 m, rotated by 0, and held its fitted FOV at 31.4265°, while the pan followed the zoom-about-the-cursor law exactly (0.25·(1 − 1/z) for a fixed pointer position).
- **Measurements can now be shown in the look view** (`8c979ada`; `measurementLayerMask()`/`refreshMeasurementVisibility()` in `src/nodes/CNodeLabels3D.js`, `Globals.showMeasurementsLook` in `src/index.js`, `globalsNeeded` in `src/CustomManagerSerialize.js`, i18n key `labels3d.measurementsInLook` in all ten locales). Measurements reached the main view through `MASK_HELPERS`, which `MASK_LOOKRENDER` deliberately omits — so a V/B measurement, or any `CNodeMeasureAB` / `CNodeMeasureAltitude` (the built-in camera-to-target distance labels among them), could never appear in the look view at all. They now follow a per-view mask built from two toggles, the same shape *Labels* and *Features* already use: the **Show** menu's *Measurements* becomes ***Measurements in Main*** and is joined by ***Measurements in Look***. The mask is applied in three places, all of them necessary — to the label's `layerMask` (which gates `renderLabels3D`), to the node and root groups, and to the arrow objects directly via `setLayerMaskRecursive`, because `DebugArrow` applies a layer mask only when it *creates* an arrow, so arrows already in the scene would otherwise keep their original mask forever. The group `visible` flag stays the master switch as well as the mask, because `CNodeMeasureAB.update()` early-outs on it and `CNodeMeasureAltitude`'s ground point is a terrain raycast not worth running for a measurement nobody can see. Backward compatibility is exact in both directions: main keeps `MASK_HELPERS` rather than moving to `MASK_MAIN`, the look toggle defaults **off**, and the global keeps its original name `showMeasurements` rather than gaining a "Main" suffix — it is written into every saved sitch, and renaming it would silently turn measurements back **on** in every sitch saved with them off. `CNodeLabel3D` picks up the measurement mask by testing `groupNode.isMeasurement` rather than falling through the generic `else`, which also catches labels hung on unrelated groups — the night sky's celestial arrows among them — that must not start following the measurement toggles.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed the video overlaid on the look view showing a different picture from the video view under Full A-B Echo, Blend or Exposure** (`4859d1b2`, `src/nodes/CNodeMirrorVideoView.js`; **Video → Video Processing → *Full A-B Echo* / *Full A-B Blend* / *Full A-B Exposure***). These three accumulate the whole A-B range into one composite, and that composite is *per-view* state (`_fullABEchoResult`) living on whichever video node actually ran the accumulation — always the main video view, because the Video Processing GUI binds its buttons to the first video node that built it (`addFiltersToVideoNode`), while the flag nodes themselves are shared singletons that every video view reads. So `CNodeMirrorVideoView` saw the flag as on but its own result as `null`, which made `hasFullABOverlay` false in `getAdjustedVideoFrameSource`: it fell into the rolling-echo branch and returned `fullABOverlay: null`. With *Full A-B Echo* — which force-enables *Echo Light* if neither echo flag is set — that meant the look view was overlaid with an *Echo Frames*-deep rolling smear while the video view showed the full range; with *Blend* or *Exposure* and no echo flag set it meant the plain live frame. The two are meant to be the same picture, which is the entire point of an overlay. The mirror's `update()` — the same method that already re-points `videoData` at the mirrored node's and copies its `panOffsetX/Y` so the overlay stays registered with the video view — now also copies `_fullABEchoResult` and `_fullABEchoRunning`, extending the existing "whatever the mirrored view is showing, show that" pattern to the one piece of per-view state it was missing. The second flag matters because it selects between the two ways the composite is shown: while the accumulation is still running the composite **is** the frame, and once finished it is drawn *over* the live frame at *A-B Echo Opacity %*, so copying only the result would render a finished pass as if it were still accumulating. Confirmed by branch probe: the mirror now receives the same composite object as `fullABOverlay` at the opacity the slider names (1.0 at its default), where before it received `null` and a rolling-echo source image.
- **Fixed a crash tearing down Fit Camera to Points when one sitch is loaded after another** (working tree, `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`). `FitPointHandles3D` builds its per-view handle overlays lazily on first *Enable Fit*, and constructs them **with ids** (`fitHandles_mainView`, `fitHandles_lookView`), so they are registered in `NodeMan`. `dispose()` called `o.dispose()` straight on the node, which tears down its DOM but leaves the registration behind; `NodeMan.disposeAll` then reached the same node during sitch teardown and disposed it a second time, and `CNodeViewCanvas.dispose()` — which does `this.div.removeChild(this.canvas)` and then nulls `this.canvas` — threw on `removeChild(null)`, killing the transition. The stale registration was the second half of the same defect: re-enabling the fit tried to build `fitHandles_mainView` when one already existed. Disposal now goes through `NodeMan.disposeRemove(id)` when the overlay is registered (falling back to a direct `dispose()` if it is not), which does both halves.
- **SitrecBridge 1.0.60: single-view screenshots returned flat grey and dropped every overlay** (`6ad025b5`; `tools/SitrecBridge/extension/page-bridge.js`, `manifest.json` 1.0.59 → 1.0.60). Developer tooling — the MCP bridge offered under **Help → Download MCP Bridge**, not part of the Sitrec app itself; no effect on regular user sessions. `sitrec_screenshot({view: "lookView"})` returned a uniform grey image *and wrote that grey to the live canvas*, where it stayed until something else asked for a repaint. Measured: sampling the look-view canvas immediately before the capture gave correct sky and terrain — (100,153,174), (166,121,99) — and immediately after gave uniform R=G=B. The main view was unaffected; the look view is the one carrying the IR/video effects chain. Cause: the handler drove `renderSky()`, `renderCanvas()` and `renderTargetAndEffects()` by hand, but `renderCanvas()` **is** the whole render for a 3D view — it calls `renderTargetAndEffects()`, which calls `renderSky()`. It now makes the single call the frame loop makes; `renderCanvas()` is idempotent, verified byte-identical over two consecutive calls. The mechanism inside the effects chain that produces the grey was not pinned down, and the code comment claims only what is established: that the extra calls cause it and one call does not. Two further corrections in the same handler: capture reads `viewNode.canvas` rather than `renderer.domElement` (for a 3D view the renderer draws into an offscreen target that is composited onto `v.canvas`, which is also the surface the full-viewport path reads); and the view's children are now composited into an offscreen canvas, mirroring the app's own single-view exporter — overlay children **and** `relativeTo` children (the compass, Wescam MX and MQ9 HUDs) — gated on `_effectivelyVisible`, because a hidden overlay's canvas keeps its last pixels and would paint stale handles back onto the image. The output frames the view's **div**, not the 3D canvas, since under *Match Video Aspect* the canvas is letterboxed inside the div and stretching one onto the other misregisters every handle. Previously a single-view capture silently dropped fit handles, measurement labels, tracking cursors and the HUD — usually the thing it was taken to look at.

## Version 2.119.3 (2026-08-08)

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed cursor picks landing away from the mouse pointer under video zoom, video pan or Match Video Aspect — the V/B measurement points most visibly** (`src/mouseMoveView.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeView3DMouse.js`, `src/ViewUtils.js`, `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`; symptom reachable via **View → *Video Zoom %*** or panning inside the video pane, and **Camera → *Match Video Aspect***). Nothing in the measure code was wrong: V and B only copy `cursorSprite.position` into `globalMeasureState.startPoint`/`endPoint`, through `getCursorPositionFromTopView()` in `CameraControls.updateMeasureArrow`. The fault was upstream, in the shared screen→world pick, and it was **two independent defects** that compose — either alone displaces the hit. **(1) NDC was measured across the wrong rectangle.** `screenToNDC` divided the view-relative mouse position by `view.widthPx`/`view.heightPx`, which assumes the 3D render fills the pane. With Match Video Aspect on it does not: `CNodeView3D` letterboxes by resizing and centring the 3D **canvas element** inside its div (`canvas.style.width/height/left/top`, `CNodeView3D.js:2154-2171`) rather than by using a viewport inside a full-size canvas, so the mouse was mapped across more pixels than the scene was drawn into — exact at the centre, drifting toward the edges, and drifting by a different amount whenever the letterbox changed. This is the same defect class `821f6ce5` fixed for the fit handles, measured there on a 572×435 div whose 3D canvas was 572×321 at a 57 px vertical inset, putting one handle 39 px low. `screenToNDC` now maps through `renderedRect(view, view.widthPx, view.heightPx)`, which covers letterbox, pillarbox and neither without the caller knowing which is in play, and reduces to the old expression exactly when the render fills the canvas. **(2) The ray was cast through a projection the user was never shown.** `CNodeView3DMouse._refreshCursorFromMouse` wrapped the pick in `applyDisplayLookAt` alone — one of the eight things `prepareCameraForLOD` applies to turn the stored camera into the displayed one. The other seven are `camera.zoom` taken from the `videoZoom` node, `aspect = widthPx/heightPx`, the look view's `fovCoverage` widening, Match Video Aspect's fov/aspect rewrite, the video pan's off-centre frustum, y-compression, and the camera-tweak offsets — and the video ones all bite exactly when the user zooms or pans the video. The pan term is the reason a rebuild cannot substitute: it is written straight into `projectionMatrix.elements[8]/[9]` (`CNodeView3D.js:1147-1166`), which `updateProjectionMatrix()` will never reproduce, as is y-compress into `elements[5]`. The wrapper is now `withDisplayedCamera(this, …)`, i.e. `prepareCameraForLOD()` / `restoreCameraAfterLOD()`, which applies all eight and subsumes the lookAt the old code did on its own. It is re-entrant — if LOD has already prepared the camera (a pick from inside the render pass) the state is used as-is and left alone, because the paired restore rebuilds from the saved fov/aspect/zoom and a nested pair would restore to the wrong baseline. **Blast radius:** fix (1) lands at all 22 `screenToNDC` call sites at once, every one of them latently wrong the same way whenever the view was letterboxed — the V/B measure points, C/X camera and target snapping (`CNodePositionLLA.js:373`), the orbit/pan pivot and the middle-click spline inserts refreshed on mouse-down, focus-track snapping and command-scrubbing, the LOS-from-mouse debug arrow, the right-click object/track menu, and the handle picking in `C3DSynthManager`, `CNodeGroundOverlayEvents`, `CNodeFloodSim`, `CNodeSynthClouds`, `CNodeSynthBuildingEvents` and `SitFAA2023`. **Scope deliberately left:** fix (2) is applied to the cursor-refresh pick only. `onMouseDown` and `onContextMenu` still wrap their own raycasts in `applyDisplayLookAt` alone, and `CameraControls.onMouseWheel`'s zoom-toward-cursor anchor still builds its NDC with the older `mouseToNDC` (`ViewUtils.js:77`, unchanged), so that anchor keeps the full-pane mapping and gains only the displayed-camera half of the fix. **Supporting refactor:** `renderedRect` and `withDisplayedCamera` were private functions inside `FitPointHandles3D.js`; both now live in `src/ViewUtils.js` and are exported, with bodies unchanged and their doc comments generalised from "the overlay canvas" to "anything working in the div's pixel space". `FitPointHandles3D.js` imports them and behaves identically. `ViewUtils.js` imports neither `mouseMoveView` nor `FitPointHandles3D`, and `mouseMoveView` already imported `ViewUtils`, so no import cycle is introduced.

## Version 2.119.2 (2026-08-08)

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed Fit Camera to Points *still* never adding a control point on click** (`src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `src/mouseMoveView.js`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Enable Fit***). 2.119.1's fix delivered the release to `finishPendingAdd` correctly, but shipped alongside an ownership guard that was itself wrong, so clicking empty video still added nothing and the feature remained unusable in that release. The guard read a newly added `getMouseDragView()` and bailed if any view other than this one held `mouseDragView`. But `mouseDragView` does not mean "the view that claimed the press": the dispatcher (`onDocumentMouseDown`, `src/mouseMoveView.js:168`) sets it for any handler that did not return an explicit `false`, and most handlers fall off the end returning `undefined` — and since `mouseInViewOnly` only rejects a view when a HIGHER-z view covers the point, every video overlay at z=3 gets `onMouseDown` and the LAST one wins. `CNodeTrackingOverlay.onMouseDown` returns `undefined` for an ordinary left click, because its add path is gated on `e.ctrlKey` and its claim path (`return true`) needs a `draggable` hit, so neither fires; and the node is a visible view even with *Show Tracking* off, since `showTracking` only early-returns inside `renderCanvas` and never touches visibility. The manual-tracking overlay therefore silently held `mouseDragView` for every plain click on the video, `owner !== this` was always true, and every add was rejected. The test is replaced with the video view's own existing predicates for "this left click belongs to an overlay rather than to me" — `_isMaskEditing()`, `_isAnnotateEditing()` and `_isOverlayDragging()` (`src/nodes/CNodeVideoView.js`), already the gates that keep left-drag pan away from an overlay mid-edit — called through `this.overlayView` with optional chaining so a sitch without one degrades to "not an overlay's click" rather than throwing. Asking the overlays directly is the point: they are the single place that already answers this question, rather than a second opinion derived from the dispatcher that can drift from it. They are true only while an overlay is genuinely mid-edit, so an ordinary click now commits while an annotation stroke, a mask paint or a manual-tracking keyframe drag still correctly suppresses one. `_isFitPointDragging()` is deliberately not among them — that is this node's own drag, and a press that hits a point claims the gesture by returning `true` and never arms a `pendingAdd` at all. The **capture-phase** `pointerup` registered in `setEnabled` stays load-bearing, but now for a different reason than the comment there gives: `_isOverlayDragging()` samples `trackingOverlay.draggable[].dragging`, which `CNodeTrackingOverlay.onMouseUp` clears, and that runs from `onDocumentMouseUp` — a bubble-phase `pointerup` registered at startup — so a bubble listener would find the flags already cleared and read a genuine keyframe drag as an ordinary click. `getMouseDragView()` is removed from `src/mouseMoveView.js` entirely (nothing else referenced it) and replaced by a comment on `mouseDragView` recording why it must not be reintroduced; the dispatcher's own behaviour is unchanged. One gap is knowingly left: manual tracking adds a keyframe on **ctrl+click**, which sets no `dragging` flag, and `CNodeFitCameraPoints.onMouseDown` does not gate on `ctrlKey`, so with both enabled a ctrl+click on empty video places a keyframe and a fit point.

## Version 2.119.1 (2026-08-08)

### New Features

- **Vertical and horizontal field of view, with the aspect they are quoted against** (`src/nodes/CNodeControllerPTZUI.js`, `src/i18n/*.js`; **Camera → FOV (Zoom)**). Only the VERTICAL FOV is stored — `this.fov`, which is what a three.js `PerspectiveCamera` takes — so `ptzUI.zoomFov.label` is relabelled from "Zoom (fov)" to **VFOV (deg)** in all ten locale files. The node, the key and the serialization are untouched, so saved sitches are unaffected. A new **HFOV (deg)** control is an `hfov` getter/setter pair on `CNodeControllerPTZUI` that reads and writes that same vertical angle through `fovAspect` — `hfov = 2·atan(a·tan(vfov/2))`, and the inverse on write — so it is not a second stored quantity and the two controls cannot disagree; the slider spans 0.0001–179° while the derived vertical value is clamped to the vertical slider's own 0.0001–170°, so neither end can drive the camera somewhere the other could not reach. `fovAspect` resolves in a fixed order: a loaded video wins outright (`videoAspect()`, taken from `originalVideoWidth`/`originalVideoHeight` — the coded pair, so a resolution cap rewriting the working dimensions or a metadata rotation swapping them does not move the number), else `lockedAspect` when Lock Aspect is on, else `liveAspect()` — the pixel aspect of the `ViewMan` view whose `cameraNode` is this controller's `_objectNode`, recorded in `apply()` because the controller is attached after the camera is built — falling back to `lockedAspect` (default 16/9). A read-only **Aspect Ratio** readout (`aspectDisplay`, a plain field rather than a getter because lil-gui assigns to the property it is handed) shows the ratio to four decimals plus what it means: the video's own pixel dimensions when a video owns the aspect (`1.7778  (1920×1080)` — a 1440×1080 clip stretched to 16:9 is a thing that happens, and the pixel pair says so exactly), otherwise a name from `NAMED_ASPECTS` matched within 0.5% (`16:9`, `4:3`, `2.39:1`, …). **Lock Aspect** pins the ratio instead of letting it follow the view pane, which otherwise changes every time the window is resized and makes HFOV wander while nothing about the camera has changed; ticking it freezes the current `liveAspect()`, so the box never moves the camera, it only stops the number drifting afterwards. `updateAspectLockAvailability()` runs from `apply()` (touching the controller only when the state actually changes) and forces the box on and greyed out while a video owns the aspect — a checkbox that stays unticked while the value it controls is overridden reads as the app ignoring it — remembering the user's own setting in `_userLockAspect` and restoring it when the video goes away. `lockAspect` and `lockedAspect` are added to the node's `modSerialize`/`modDeserialize`. This is distinct from `matchVideoAspect` (**Camera → Match Video Aspect**, `CNodeDisplayCameraFrustum`, unchanged here), which governs how the 3D is RENDERED rather than what the FOV numbers mean. The motivation is that a horizontal FOV quoted without stating the frame it spans is not a measurement of anything, so the frame is now shown next to the number rather than left implicit. Note the three new i18n keys (`ptzUI.hfov`, `ptzUI.aspect`, `ptzUI.lockAspect`) exist only in `en.js` and are read with `{defaultValue: ...}` fallbacks, so the new controls read English in the other nine locales until translated; those nine `zoomFov` tooltips still describe the vertical FOV, which remains correct.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed Fit Camera to Points never adding a control point on click** (`src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `src/mouseMoveView.js`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points → *Enable Fit***). A press on empty video deliberately returns `false` from `onMouseDown` — the press is either a click that adds a point or the start of a video pan, and nothing can tell which until the pointer moves or does not, so the node claims nothing and defers the decision to release via `pendingAdd`. But the dispatcher hands `onMouseDrag` and `onMouseUp` only to the view in `mouseDragView`, and since `dc9bf0ca` an explicit `false` means "not mine" and never sets it. So neither half of the deferred gesture was ever delivered: the movement test in `onMouseDrag` never ran, and `onMouseUp` — the only place that committed a `pendingAdd` — was never called. `dc9bf0ca` is *older* than the feature commit `c575f597` and both shipped inside `2.119.0`, so this is not a regression of working behaviour: click-to-add was unreachable in the only release that has ever contained the feature. Dragging an existing point and right-click-to-delete both return `true`, claim the gesture normally, and were unaffected, as were the 3D handles in the main and look views. The node now watches the document directly for as long as it is enabled: `setEnabled` registers a `pointermove` (`trackPendingAdd`) and a **capture-phase** `pointerup` (`finishPendingAdd`) alongside the existing pointercancel/blur cancel listeners, and removes them when disabled. Capture is load-bearing — `onDocumentMouseUp` is itself a bubble-phase `pointerup` registered at startup in `SetupMouseHandler`, and it clears `mouseDragView`, so a bubble listener would find the claim already gone. `onMouseUp` still routes into `finishPendingAdd` when the dispatcher does deliver it; whichever delivery lands first consumes the pending add and the other finds nothing to do. Three correctness guards come with it. **Ownership**: `mouseMoveView.js` exports a new read-only `getMouseDragView()` (purely additive — no change to the dispatcher's behaviour), and `finishPendingAdd` drops the add if any other view claimed the press, because every visible view under the cursor receives `onMouseDown` and so a pending add is armed even when Annotate, the video mask or manual tracking took the gesture; committing it then would drop a camera-fit point into an unrelated edit. Ordinary video pan and zoom are unaffected by this test because `CNodeVideoView` pans from its own canvas-level `CMouseHandler` and never becomes `mouseDragView`. **Path-based slop**: `trackPendingAdd` voids the add once the pointer moves more than `CLICK_SLOP` (4 canvas px) from the press point, which both restores the test `onMouseDrag` could not deliver and is stricter than it needs to be — comparing press position to release position alone would read a pan that wandered away and came back as a click. **Pointer identity**: only a primary pointer arms a pending add (`e.isPrimary !== false`) and it records its `pointerId`; `isPendingPointer` is checked before the add is consumed, so another pointer's release leaves it intact for the one that opened it, and during a pinch — where the second `pointerdown` has already voided it through `cancelGesture` and cannot re-arm — neither finger's release drops a point. A mouse is always primary, so none of this changes on the desktop. `finishPendingAdd` also rechecks `enabled`, `hasVideoGeometry()` and `button === 0` before committing. The **Ownership** guard above was wrong and defeated the whole fix — `mouseDragView` is not the view that claimed the press, and the manual-tracking overlay held it for every plain click — so click-to-add was still unreachable in 2.119.1. `getMouseDragView()` was removed again in 2.119.2, which replaces the test with the video view's own mid-edit predicates; see that entry.

## Version 2.119.0 (2026-08-08)

### New Features

- **Water Reflection — Planar Mirror mode** (`dc2452e4`; new `src/WaterPlanarMirror.js`, plus `src/nodes/CNodeWaterReflection.js`, `src/js/map33/material/SharedUniforms.js`, `src/js/map33/material/TerrainDayNightMaterial.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`; **Effects → Water Reflection → *Method*** = *Planar Mirror (experimental)*, look view only). 2.118.0's reflection sampled a cube map of the celestial sphere only, so water could show stars, Moon and Sun but never the far shore. Planar Mirror re-renders the whole `GlobalScene` from a camera mirrored through the water's surface, so hills, buildings and objects land in the water too. `CWaterPlanarMirror` has three parts. **The plane** (`detectPlane`): there is no water geometry to take a plane from, but the elevation map already holds a perfectly flat lake, so a 5×5 grid of ground raycasts plus an altitude histogram recovers it — measured 1873.788 m HAE at Tahoe with 20 of 25 probes agreeing. The tangent point is the centroid of the agreeing hits, which puts the plane through the middle of the *visible* water rather than under the camera; *Auto Water Level* off plus *Water Level (m HAE)* overrides it for when the largest flat thing in view is not water. **The mirror camera** (`setupCamera`, `applyObliqueClip`): reflected position/forward/up are rebuilt with `lookAt` so the basis stays right-handed and face culling stays valid, plus Lengyel oblique near-plane clipping. That clip is load-bearing — the mirror camera sits below the plane, buried in terrain, and without it the lake fills with the grey inside of the ground. It is safe despite Sitrec's unusual depth setup because it rewrites only the z row, and both depth paths in play (`logarithmicDepthBuffer` and the terrain shader's own `gl_FragDepthEXT`) derive depth from clip-space w; it is applied after the sky passes, which move the camera to the origin where a view-space clip plane is meaningless. **The lookup**: the mirror camera's ray through a point on the plane *is* the ray the real view reflects into, so the base sample is one matrix multiply through `sharedUniforms.waterMirrorMatrix` (bias × mirrorProjection × mirrorView). That matrix is origin-relative via `waterMirrorOrigin`, because cancelling 6.4e6 m in float32 would leave metres of error on a lookup that has to be pixel-accurate. Ripples then sample along the *perturbed reflected ray*, which gets perspective compression right for free and absorbs part of the Earth's curvature with the same term. The mirror camera **copies** the look camera's projection matrix rather than rebuilding it, so FOV override, `matchVideoAspect`, video pan and Y-compress all carry through — rebuilding produced a symmetric frustum and misregistered the reflection. Two supporting changes in `CNodeView3D`: `waterReflectionNode.push(this)` moved *inside* `_enterShadowRenderScope()`, because while shadows are on `Globals.sunLight` is hidden and only the view-scoped sun is visible, so capturing before the scope was entered lit the reflection with ambient alone; and `populateAtmosphereRayUniforms()` gained an optional `camera` argument so the sky gradient can be built for the mirrored camera (`view.camera` is a getter onto the camera node and cannot simply be swapped). Mirror-only controls live in a *Planar Mirror* sub-folder — *Ripple Reach (m)*, *Mirror Resolution*, *Clip Below Water*, *Clip Bias (m)*, *Auto Water Level*, *Water Level (m HAE)* — and `applyMode()` hides the cube-only controls (*Star Boost*, *Moon Boost*, *Env Map Resolution*, *Terrain Occlusion*) in mirror mode. `applyMode()` is also re-run from `modDeserialize`, since restoring `mode` writes the property directly and never fires the dropdown's `onChange`. Costs 1.79× the look view render at Tahoe, draw-call bound; shadow maps are reused and no LOD runs from the mirror camera. Known limits: one plane cannot serve two lakes at different altitudes, curvature leaves ~0.3° of error at the far end of a 35 km lake, and reflected stars are dimmer than in cube mode (which boosts their size to survive a coarse cube face).

- **Fit Camera to Points — recover an unknown camera from landmarks** (`c575f597`, with `de0cba1d`, `821f6ce5`, `1fb91bdb`; new `src/CameraPointFit.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeFitCameraPoints.js`, `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`, `src/FitHandleDraw.js`, plus `src/ViewUtils.js`, `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeVideoView.js`; **Camera → Fit Camera to Points**). A redacted clip arrives with the platform position and the field of view stripped out — the two things every downstream measurement depends on — but the footage still shows *places*, so the analyst can still say "that pixel is that headland", and enough of those pairs determine the camera. A control point is one 2D point on the video plus one point on the ground, drawn as the same numbered circle-and-crosshair handle in the same colour on the video, the main view and the look view. Note the workflow this implies is the opposite of what it looks like: a newly added pair seeds its ground point by casting the current camera's ray through the clicked pixel onto the terrain, so it starts exactly on its own line of sight and contributes *no* information — clicking asks a question, dragging the ground handle to the real feature answers it. `FitPointHandles3D` offers handles in `mainView` and `lookView` (`HANDLE_VIEWS`); dragging casts a ray from *that* view's camera through the cursor and takes the ground hit from `raycastGroundElevationFast`, so the third dimension comes from the terrain rather than the user — a landmark has no vertical degree of freedom to get wrong. This replaced a disc-and-arrows gizmo, which is right for a target in mid-air but only invites putting a landmark underground. The solver in `src/CameraPointFit.js` (pure, 19 tests in `tests/CameraPointFit.test.js`) is Levenberg-Marquardt over ENU metres, az/el/roll in degrees and log focal, minimising rectilinear reprojection error in *original video pixels* through the existing `CameraLens` convention. Steps are taken through an SVD of the column-scaled Jacobian, so a direction the landmarks cannot see gets no step and stays at its starting value: the distant-landmark case, where camera range and focal length trade off exactly, then reports as unobservable instead of returning a confident wrong answer. Huber loss limits one badly placed pair without erasing it. Solving in az/el/roll rather than a rotation vector is deliberate — it is also the write-back target, so what solves is what renders, and *Lock Roll* becomes an exact parameter removal; the cost is a singularity at the camera pointing straight up, so it refuses past `MAX_ABS_EL` (85°). Seeds are ranked by a short LM run rather than by their own residual: measured on the PR043 clip all 42 candidates scored 1288–1365 px (noise), and picking on that returned a camera 9800 km away with a 169° field. Points own the frame they were placed on (`fitFrame`) — mixing observations from different frames into one seven-parameter solve would be silently wrong for anything but a locked-off camera — so editing or fitting on the wrong frame is refused with a status message rather than assumed. The node is a **tool, not a controller**: it writes `fixedCameraPosition`, `ptzAngles` and `fovUI` and then stops existing as far as the render path is concerned; with *Enable Fit* off there is no overlay, no handle, no listener, no solve and no camera write. Write-back order is load-bearing — switches first (selecting Manual syncs PTZ from the live camera), relative off (or angles apply as a delta on themselves), and altitude converted out of both HAE and AGL because `CNodePositionLLA` means MSL and a fit stored as a terrain-relative offset would drift as tiles refine; the applied camera is then re-read, since `TrackPosition` clamps above ground and can move it. Nothing is applied unless it beats the camera already there. Every edit — add, move, delete, clear — is one `UndoManager` entry covering the points and the camera together, restored directly rather than by re-solving (which is not an inverse). Control points are saved with the sitch, so a published camera carries a record of which landmarks it was derived from. The node is created unconditionally in `CustomManagerSetup.js` with id `fitCameraPoints` for `Sit.isCustom` sitches that have a `video` node, for the same reason the annotate and mask overlays are: a node that does not exist when the mods are applied never receives its saved state. GUI: *Enable Fit*, *Fit on Change*, *Fit Now*, *Lock Position*, *Lock FOV*, *Lock Roll*, read-only *Status* / *Residual* / *Observability*, and *Clear All Points*.

- **Right-click arbitration between a view and its overlays** (`c575f597`; `claimRightClick` / `rightClickWasClaimed` in `src/ViewUtils.js`, consumed in `CNodeVideoView.js`; 4 tests in `tests/rightClickClaim.test.js`). An overlay canvas has `pointer-events:none` and receives clicks through the document-level router in `mouseMoveView.js`, while a view's context menu comes from a `contextmenu` listener on the *view's* canvas — two separate DOM events on two different elements, so an overlay that acts on a right-click has no event to cancel. The overlay now leaves a claim and the view checks it. The claim is both **single-use** and **time-windowed** (600 ms) because the failure modes differ: consuming it means one claim suppresses exactly the one context menu it was paired with, so a second right-click still opens the menu normally; the window means a claim that is never consumed — the overlay acted, but that view has no context menu to suppress — expires instead of lying in wait. Right-clicking a fit point deletes it and claims; right-clicking empty video does not claim, so *Video Adjustments* still works while fitting. Separately, `CNodeVideoView._isFitPointDragging()` gates left-drag pan on the **drag**, not on the feature being enabled (unlike the mask and annotate gates) — placing fit points accurately is mostly a matter of panning and zooming to find the landmark, so taking left-drag away for the whole session would break the workflow.

- **Simple Flight Sim: Climb Rate** (`873b2740`; `src/CustomSupport.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeJetTrack.js`; **Physics → Simple Flight Sim → *Climb Rate***, −1000…+1000 fpm, default 0). A `CNodeGUIValue` with id `climbRate` created in `CCustomManager.setupSimpleFlightSim()` alongside `legLength` and `transitionTime`, and patched into the existing `flightSimCameraPosition` JetTrack via `addMoreInputs` (the JetTrack is constructed before these nodes exist, since the sitch object is processed first, so `optionalInputs` left them undefined). `CNodeJetTrack` reads it per frame — so a keyframed or linked climb rate works — and applies `f2m(climbFPM) / 60 * dt` along `getLocalUpVector(jetPos)`, making it a real altitude change on the ellipsoid rather than a nudge in a fixed world direction or a pitch of the flight path. It uses the same `dt` as the airspeed step and the turn integration, so Sim Speed stretches the clock without bending the vertical profile. Deliberately **not** applied when a terrain node is present (AGL / terrain-following): there the clamp at the top of the loop owns the altitude and a climb would just fight it. As an optional input, sitches created before this existed (Gimbal, FLIR1, GoFast) have no `climbRate` node and fly level exactly as before.

### Improvements

- **Planar Mirror: coarse distant tiles stop reflecting instead of going blotchy** (`8b473da7`; `sharedUniforms.waterMaxTileSize`, `TerrainDayNightMaterial.js`, *Effects → Water Reflection → Planar Mirror → **Max Tile Size (m)***, default 4000, 0 disables). The colour-keyed water mask degrades at distance: distant water is drawn by enormous low-zoom tiles that still carry only a 512 px texture, so one texel spans kilometres, the flat OSM water fill is averaged together with the coastline, the test passes in patches, and the reflection breaks into blotches. The shader now fades the **mask** (not just the reflection) where the tile under a fragment is wider than the limit, so distant water simply reverts to plain map colour. Tile width is recovered per-fragment as `(length(vWorldPosition - cameraPosition) / cameraFocalLength) / length(fwidth(vUv))`, since `vUv` runs 0..1 across a tile — deliberately not `fwidth(vWorldPosition)`, because at ECEF magnitudes float32 quantises world position to ~0.4 m and its derivative is pure noise. The 4000 m default is measured, not guessed: Tahoe's far-shore water sits on 470–1882 m tiles, which stay at full strength, while its distant 7658 m tiles and Santa Monica's 16 km ones are dropped. Mirror mode only — the sky cube reflects a smooth sky that hides the blotches anyway.

- **Planar Mirror: terrain skirts that would stand across the water are hidden** (`8b473da7`, refined by `f8770248`; `QuadTreeTile.js` tags `skirtMesh.userData.isTerrainSkirt` and back-references `userData.tile`; `CNodeWaterReflection.hideSkirts()` / `restoreSkirts()`, *Hide Waterline Skirts*, default on). Terrain tiles carry a skirt — geometry extruded straight down from every tile edge by a *tenth* of the tile's width — to cover the cracks between detail levels. Looking down at terrain you never see one; at eye level over water you see little else, because a distant tile is kilometres across, so its skirt is a wall hundreds of metres deep standing across the view and hiding the water behind it. They also share the tile's material, so the water shader runs on them and paints the reflection onto a vertical wall of 1-D smeared texture, which reads as a band of vertical streaks. Nothing in the shader can fix that, because whatever is painted there is occupying screen space where the water should be visible; dropping skirts from the water mask leaves pale bands, keeping the darkening without the reflection leaves dark bands, and sliding the fragment up onto the mirror plane brings the streaks back (a vertical wall collapses to one plane point per column, sampled where the reflection varies fastest). Skirts are therefore hidden for the duration of the look view's render, scoped to `push()`/`pop()` so it covers both the mirror capture *and* the main draw while `mainView` keeps its skirts — hiding them only inside the mirror capture changes nothing. `f8770248` narrows the exposure: a skirt is hidden only if it can actually **reach** the water (`tileAltitude - tile.size * 0.1 < waterLevel + SKIRT_HIDE_MARGIN_M`). Gating on tile altitude was tried first and is wrong — a 16 km tile on a 500 m ridge trails a 1.6 km wall that ends a kilometre under the sea, and you see it, because the water curves away and a sightline aimed just below the shoreline passes over the near water and strikes the wall hanging below the far waterline. Honest about the benefit: in a lake or coastal view nearly every visible skirt does reach the water (401/401 at Santa Monica, 531/531 at Tahoe), so the rule earns its keep only where terrain stands well above the water on small tiles; what it buys today is that the exposure is correct by construction rather than a blanket sweep.

- **Planar Mirror: mountain streams and rivers are no longer treated as reflectable water** (`ee55d4fd`, enabled by `b101543c`; `CNodeWaterReflection.tileWaterAllowed()` / `applyTileWaterGating()` / `restoreTileWaterGating()`, per-material `tileWaterAllowed` uniform in `TerrainDayNightMaterial.js`, instrumentation in `src/TextureColorProcessor.js`). OSM draws streams and rivers in the same fill colour as the sea, so a mountainside threaded with watercourses was classified as water and reflected in a plane fitted to sea level hundreds of metres below — every valley lit up as a bright line, reading like a crack in the terrain. Decided per **tile** rather than per fragment, because that is the only level at which the evidence exists: a fragment cannot know its tile's elevation range or how much of the tile is water. Two tests, either one disqualifying — the tile's lowest point is more than `WATER_TILE_ALT_MARGIN_M` (20 m) above the water, so whatever is blue on it belongs to some other elevation; or under `WATER_TILE_MIN_FRACTION` (2%) of it is water, which is a watercourse rather than a body of one (this catches valley floors near the water level, which the altitude test lets through). Unknowns count as allowed, so a tile whose `altitudeBounds` are not measured yet, or whose texture came from an ancestor and carries no match count, behaves exactly as before. The gate is a **per-material** uniform the shader multiplies into `waterMask`, deliberately not in `sharedUniforms` since the whole point is that it varies per tile; it is set each frame and restored in `pop()`, so nothing leaks into `mainView` or into cube mode. Gated tiles also **keep** their skirts — a tile with no reflectable water has nothing to get out of the way of, and that is the half that stops LOD seams opening in the hills. Measured: Santa Monica excludes 470 of 789 tiles by altitude and 29 more by fraction; Tahoe excludes 21 of 941, leaving the lake untouched — that asymmetry is the check that matters. The second test is only possible because `b101543c` made `compositeWaterFromOSM` record `osmMatched` / `osmTotal` / `osmSrcRect` / `osmImageSize` on the returned `CanvasTexture`'s `userData`: the function builds its canvas before the matching loop and returns it unconditionally, so a composite that matched *nothing* was indistinguishable from one that stamped a whole lake — "the tile texture is canvas-backed" proves the composite ran, not that it found anything. That count is also what a caller would key off to stop caching an empty result under the `'_osmwater'` key, which currently means "combine requested", not "valid mask obtained".

- **Main-view terrain is now selected against the field of view actually rendered** (`947c2919`; `CNodeView3D.prepareCameraForLOD`). Consequence of scoping the `fovCoverage` widening to the look view (see the picking fix below): in any sitch with a letterboxed video, main-view terrain tiles come out ~8% finer than before. That is the correct answer rather than a new one, but it is more tile loading and memory in a view that previously got away with less.

### Bug Fixes

- **Fixed Google Photorealistic 3D tiles dropping out of the look view under video zoom and pan** (`947c2919`; `src/nodes/CNodeBuildings3DTiles.js`). Symptom: correct imagery in a band at the top of the look view, nothing below a straight horizontal line, while the loader was perfectly healthy (1889 tiles loaded, 0 failed) — not the LRU dropout fixed previously; nothing was being evicted or refused. Video pan is an asymmetric frustum shift written into `projectionMatrix` `elements[8]`/`[9]`, and `PerViewTiles` handed `setCamera()` the **live** camera, whose shift was 0/0 while the displayed frustum was −0.425/−1.209 — a vertical displacement of 1.21 half-heights, about 263 px on a 435 px view. Tiles were being culled against a frustum that had slid off the one being rendered. The buildings updater now runs inside `prepareCameraForLOD()` — which applies zoom, letterboxing, pan, y-compress, the display-only `lookAt` and the camera tweak, and is what terrain subdivision already used — **replacing** the bare `applyCameraOffset` rather than wrapping it, since the helper applies that rotation itself and doing both would rotate twice. This is a widening of an earlier, narrower fix of the same bug class, whose own comment already said that culling against the wrong frustum means "the tiles actually on screen never load (gaps)". Scoped to views whose displayed projection actually differs (`syncVideoZoom || syncPixelZoomWithVideo || yCompress > 1.0001`), so a plain main view keeps its previous behaviour exactly, and bracketed on `view._lodSavedZoom` because `prepareCameraForLOD` is not re-entrant and does not guard itself.

- **Fixed terrain and tile detail not refreshing after a video pan** (`947c2919`; `CNodeTerrainUI.js`, `CNodeBuildings3DTiles.js`). Both settle fingerprints summed matrix and camera terms that a pure pan does not touch — a pan sliding the frustum from −1.209 to −1.906 left the fingerprint identical to the last digit — so once the grace period expired, panning could not wake subdivision at all and the terrain stayed at its pre-pan LOD until something else disturbed the camera. The frustum shift (`p[8]`, `p[9]`), the vertical scale (`p[5]`) and the render resolution are now compared **exactly and per view** rather than folded into the sum, because a sum cancels: pan right and up by matching amounts, or pan one view and counter-pan another, and the total does not move. The terrain fingerprint is now taken from the **prepared** camera, which closes the same hole for the camera-tweak rotation and the display-only `lookAt` (neither of which reaches the live `matrixWorld`); this requires preparing every frame rather than only inside the grace window, costing a handful of matrix operations per view while the expensive tile-tree traversal the gate protects is still skipped. The terrain prepare/restore pair also gained the `try`/`finally` it lacked — an exception anywhere in subdivision would otherwise strand every view's camera in the prepared projection, quietly corrupting the rendered view rather than just failing the pass.

- **Fixed screen-space handles landing off-target in the main view when a video is loaded** (`947c2919`; `CNodeView3D.prepareCameraForLOD`, affecting `TreeManualBrush` and `FitPointHandles3D`). `prepareCameraForLOD` applied the video's `fovCoverage` widening unconditionally, while the render path computes it inside `if (this.id === "lookView")`. At a 0.918 coverage the main view's 30° came out of the helper as 32.54° — 8.47% wide, a widening its render never applies. Benign for LOD (a wider frustum is a superset, so nothing on screen was culled; it just picked slightly coarser tiles), but this helper also places and picks screen-space handles, so an inflated field put a handle where the thing it represents is not: measured 20–29 px out near the edges of a 709×603 main view and zero at the exact centre, meaning a fixed ground point appeared to **slide** as the camera turned and its screen radius changed — 41 px of error at one heading becoming 69 px a tenth of a radian later. Now guarded to the look view, and the error is 0. Two smaller divergences from the render remain, both currently harmless: the pan block gates on `syncVideoZoom || syncPixelZoomWithVideo` while the render gates on `syncVideoZoom` alone (equivalent while every video-synced view sets both), and the `matchVideoAspect` block is self-scoping via a per-camera `<cameraNode>_Frustum` node the main camera does not have.

- **Fixed manual-tracking keyframes not being draggable on the video** (`dc9bf0ca`; `src/mouseMoveView.js`). Every view under the cursor gets `onMouseDown` and the **last** one won `mouseDragView`, because `mouseInViewOnly` only rejects a view when a *higher-z* view with an `onMouseDown` covers the point — overlays sharing a z-index (all the video overlays sit at z=3) never exclude each other. So a handler that **declined** the click by returning `false` was still handed the drag, stealing it from the view that actually took it. That is how manual-tracking keyframe dragging broke: `trackingOverlay` started the drag (and jumped to the keyframe's frame, which is why it looked like a seek), then `annotateOverlay` — not in editing mode, returning `false` — overwrote `mouseDragView`, so the `mousemove` never reached the overlay and the point never moved. An explicit `false` is now treated as "not mine"; anything else (`true`, or the `undefined` most handlers return) keeps the previous behaviour, so this only changes views that already opted out on purpose.

- **Fixed Fit Camera to Points corrupting the rest of a saved sitch on load** (`de0cba1d`; `CNodeFitCameraPoints.modDeserialize` / `update`). Enabling the fit builds two overlay **views**, and `modDeserialize` called `setEnabled` directly — so on any sitch saved with *Enable Fit* on, new views appeared in the middle of the loop that was still applying mods to the existing nodes. Measured on a real save: 17 other nodes silently lost their restored state, among them the camera position, which reverted to the `SitCustom` default off California while the save plainly contained 11.391280, 43.179771; also the FOV and the target position. Applied mods went 74 with 17 mismatched, against 83 and 0 once the enable was deferred. That is the worst shape of bug this tool could have, since the camera *is* its output. `modDeserialize` now records the wish in `_pendingEnable` and `update()` grants it once `Globals.deserializing` clears — one frame late is invisible, the wrong camera is not. The overlays that predate this feature (annotate, videoMask) sidestep the question entirely by being built in `CCustomManager.setup()`, before any mod is applied.

- **Fixed Fit Camera to Points ground handles not staying over their terrain features** (`821f6ce5`; `renderedRect()` in `src/FitPointHandles3D.js`). Handles slid as the letterbox changed and moved when *Match Video Aspect* was toggled. `projectToCanvas` converted NDC straight across the overlay's full rect, which assumes the render fills it — but with *Match Video Aspect* on, `CNodeView3D` letterboxes by resizing and centring the 3D **canvas element** inside its div via CSS, rather than by using a viewport inside a full-size canvas, and the overlay these handles are drawn on is a *separate* canvas that still covers the whole div. Measured on a 572×435 div: the 3D canvas was 572×321 at a 57 px vertical inset, so handles were spread over 435 px of a scene drawn into 321 of them — correct at the centre, wrong everywhere else, wrong by a different amount whenever the letterbox changed, and one point placed 39 px low. Both `projectToCanvas` and `groundUnderCanvasPoint` now map through the canvas's real rect relative to the div, which covers letterbox, pillarbox and neither without this code knowing which is in play, and reduces to the previous formula exactly when the render fills the canvas. Note the earlier "the projections agree so the handles must be right" reasoning was only half the mapping — matching projection matrices say nothing about how the rendered image is then *placed* on the canvas.

- **Fit Camera to Points now holds Match Video Aspect on while fitting** (`1fb91bdb`; `CNodeFitCameraPoints.setMatchVideoAspect`, `findGuiController`). The fit is solved entirely in video-pixel space, so this does not change the answer — residual and solved camera are byte-identical either way. It changes whether the **preview** is worth looking at. With *Match Video Aspect* off, the look view renders the 3D at its own aspect while the video has another; `fovOverride`/`fovCoverage` nearly compensates for the video sitting letterboxed inside the view, but not exactly. Measured against where each control point's own video pixel actually lands, at a fit residual of 1.77 px: match on gave 0.2 / 0.2 / 0.7 / 1.1 px, match off gave 0.6 / 6.6 / 9.8 / 10.9 px, with the error growing away from the view centre — so a point sitting exactly on its landmark can appear a third of a frame's worth of error away from it, and judging a sub-2 px fit through an 11 px preview means chasing errors that are not there. Enabling the fit turns it on and disabling restores whatever was there (if it was already on it is left alone), and the change is made through the lil-gui controller so the checkbox follows rather than silently disagreeing. The status line says it happened rather than letting a checkbox appear to tick itself. This is a different alignment from the sibling `821f6ce5` fix: that one is about handles tracking the **terrain** (correct in either state); this is about the 3D tracking the **video**.

## Version 2.118.0 (2026-08-06)

### New Features
- **Water Reflection — the sky reflected in map-detected water, day and night** (`a9433056`, `4a87a4ca`, `5ad6b389`, `85ea10ba`; new `src/nodes/CNodeWaterReflection.js`, `src/js/map33/material/TerrainDayNightMaterial.js`, `src/js/map33/material/SharedUniforms.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayNightSky.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeTerrainUI.js`, `config/config.js.example`; **Effects → *Water Reflection***, default off, look view only). Water is detected **in the terrain fragment shader** by matching the raw map texture against the active source's declared `waterColor` — the flat OSM water fill `#AAD3DF` / `[170, 211, 223]`. That is a deliberate hack: it needs no vector tiles, no extra geometry and no extra data, and it tracks whatever the user is actually looking at. It is gated on the source *declaring* a colour, so satellite/debug imagery cannot invent lakes out of similarly-coloured pixels. `config/config.js` is per-install and gitignored, so the colour is added to `config/config.js.example` **and** backfilled in `CNodeTerrainUI` for the `osm` / `osmHighlight` sources, or existing installs would silently lack it (a config that sets `waterColor` itself always wins). The node is created by `addNightSky()` with the stable id `waterReflection`, so every night-sky situation gets it (including `custom`) and the id exists before saved mods deserialize; a sitch with no night sky has no node at all.
  - **Sky capture.** A `CubeCamera` at the **origin** captures the celestial sphere — which works because the sphere is always rendered from the origin, so there is no parallax and the cube inherits the EQJ→ECEF orientation already applied to the group. **Both** `GlobalNightSkyScene` and `GlobalSunSkyScene` are rendered: when a day scene exists `CPlanets` hides the night-scene Sun/Moon and draws visible copies in the sun-sky scene, so a night-scene-only capture would produce a starfield with **no Moon in it** — the one thing you most want to see in a lake. Verified by cube pixel readback: the captured Moon lands 0.03° from its true direction, and by day the brightest texel lands 0.16° from the Sun's. The target is `HalfFloatType` with mipmaps so the Moon's disc is not clamped to the same value as a saturated star. Captures are cached on **sky content** (orientation, coarse observer position, settings) rather than a frame counter, because one timeline frame can be rendered from several camera poses.
  - **Surface shading.** Reflection uses **geodetic** up, not the geocentric radial — on WGS84 they differ by up to 0.19°, which would tilt the whole reflected sky by twice that — with analytically-differentiated ripples and a Schlick Fresnel term. The reflection is added **after** the shader's closing `sRGBTransferEOTF`, since sky radiance is linear. The flat map fill is pulled towards real water colour first (*Water Darkening*, default 0.9) so the reflection carries the surface instead of competing with map blue.
  - **Look-view scoping.** `push()` / `pop()` bracket the actual `GlobalScene` draw inside `CNodeView3D.renderTargetAndEffects` rather than living in a `preRender` hook: the terrain uniforms are shared **by reference** with mainView's per-view material clones, and `ExportImageSet` / `CFileManager` call `renderCanvas()` without ever running `preRender`, so anything looser would leak the reflection into mainView. Sitting after `renderSky()` also means the Sun and Moon are already synced to this view's observer.
  - **Terrain Occlusion** (default on). The sky cube holds the whole celestial sphere including the part standing behind a hillside, so the lake happily reflected stars invisible from it. A **second** cube holds the terrain skyline as seen from the observer — white for open sky, black where terrain blocks it — and the shader multiplies the sky sample by it; both cubes are indexed by direction, so they line up even though the sky is captured from the origin and the mask from the observer. Kept separate rather than punched into the sky cube because the skyline only changes when the observer moves while the sky cube re-renders as the sky rotates: measured, 8 ms for the terrain pass (1626 tiles × 6 faces) against 0.2 ms for the sky, so merging them would have put the 8 ms on every frame of playback. Only landscape occludes — everything else in `GlobalScene` is hidden for the pass, or track markers and LOS lines would carve black streaks across the reflection. The occluder is a flat black basic material with depth testing off over a white clear (a silhouette needs no depth, which sidesteps the sky cube's 100 m frustum versus terrain's tens of kilometres), and it gets **no** mipmaps, since minifying a hard ridge line bleeds terrain into the sky either side of it. Both capture passes disable and restore `renderer.shadowMap` — Sitrec leaves three's `autoUpdate` on, so six renders of `GlobalScene` were dragging six shadow-map updates along with most of the scene hidden.
  - **Daylight.** The effect originally gave up as soon as the Sun was up (`push()` returned false once the night factor hit zero), leaving daytime water with the flat pale fill the map paints it and no reflection at all. `waterReflection` is now **purely the master on/off gate**, with a separate `waterNightFactor` carrying time of day — that split is what lets it run around the clock. Water attenuates towards a *colour* (`mix()` onto the new `waterDayColor` uniform) instead of a scalar multiply towards black, so daytime water goes deep-water dark blue and night water still goes to black where only reflected light remains; the colour is exposed as *Daylight Water Colour* (default `[0.06, 0.13, 0.20]`) since what reads as "deep water" is a judgement call. The Sun needed no capture work — it was already in the cube via `GlobalSunSkyScene`; only the daylight gate stopped it being sampled. The night-factor weighting was also dropped from the reflection add: the cube already holds whatever suits the hour, so weighting it again by time of day was wrong once the effect ran by day.
  - **Env Map Resolution** — a dropdown of 256/512/1024/2048, default 1024. A dropdown rather than a slider because a slider fires `onChange` on every drag step, each one disposing and rebuilding the render target — at 2048 that is a ~270 MB texture per step.
