Capture time is flat across resolutions (both passes are geometry-bound, not fill-bound), so this trades video memory alone: ~6 MB at 256 up to ~281 MB at 2048, with the occlusion mask following but stopping at 1024 (it is a silhouette, not a starfield, and it is a whole extra cube). Every label carries a non-digit (`"512 (low)"`, not `"512"`) because object keys that look like integers are hoisted to the front in numeric order by the JS engine, which scrambled the menu.
  - **Star Boost / Moon Boost** (1–3, default 1.4, step 0.01). A 90° cube face at 1024 resolves ~0.09°/pixel, so stars at true size land sub-pixel and vanish once the water shader samples them; `starBoost` enlarges them. Because boosting size raises flux by roughly its **square**, `moonBoost` keeps the moonglade dominant instead of being out-glared by the boosted starfield, and both ranges are deliberately small — the earlier 1–30 range was almost entirely unusable. *Reflection Strength* is 0–2 (1.0 being the physical Fresnel amount).
  - **Cost control.** Ripple animation only keeps the render loop awake while the effect is enabled and waves are actually moving; the wave-phase origin re-anchors only past `WAVE_ORIGIN_REANCHOR_M` (50 km), beyond which float32 world positions stop resolving a wavelength, so the pattern never visibly swims during normal camera movement.
  - **Not covered:** terrain/object planar reflections; the twilight sky gradient and the daytime sky itself (both screen-space quads, absent from the cube — so daylight water is dark blue plus Sun rather than sky-blue at grazing angles); satellites (they live in `GlobalScene`); and Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles mode, which hides the map-textured terrain entirely. **Diagnostic gotcha:** terrain occlusion correctly suppressing a Sun grazing a ridge reads as a "missing" reflection — in one test the skyline was 0° at azimuth 291 but 3.5° at 297 with the Sun at 3.7°.
- **Combine Terrain with OSM — stamp OSM's water fill into other imagery** (`5f4e7288`, ownership moved in `5ad6b389`; new `src/OSMWaterTileMapping.js` + `tests/OSMWaterTileMapping.test.js`, `src/QuadTreeTileMaterial.js`, `src/TextureColorProcessor.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeWaterReflection.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeTerrainUI.js`; **Effects → Water Reflection → *Combine Terrain with OSM***, default off). Satellite photography has no flat colour for water, so colour-keyed detection could not find a lake on it and Water Reflection simply did nothing under MapBox or ESRI. With this on, each terrain tile also fetches the OSM tile covering it, finds the pixels matching OSM's water fill, and writes that exact colour into the loaded imagery — the photography survives everywhere else, and only water is overwritten, which is what gives the shader something to match. Water Reflection falls back to OSM's `waterColor` when the combine is active, or it would still be reading the source's own (absent) colour and staying off with combined tiles right in front of it. The flag and its serialization live on `CNodeWaterReflection` (`combineWithOSM`) because the combine exists to serve that effect; only the compatibility test `canCombineWithOSM()` stays on `CNodeTerrainUI`, which owns `mapSources`. The tile pipeline reads the flag straight off the node (`osmWaterSourceForTile`), so a sitch with no night sky has no node and no combine.
  - **Gating.** Compatibility requires sharing OSM's tile grid, tested via the existing `mapping: 4326` flag that already selects GoogleCRS84Quad over Web Mercator elsewhere: `NRL_WMTS` is rejected, MapBox and ESRI allowed, OSM itself rejected as a no-op. The control disables when unavailable **and clears the flag**, rather than reading as on while doing nothing. Availability is re-checked each frame in `updateCombineAvailability()` rather than wired to change notifications — the terrain node may not exist yet when this node is built, and the map source can change at any time; it is a couple of property lookups and it correctly enables the control the moment the source becomes compatible.
  - **Caching and correctness.** Cache keys gain an `_osmwater` suffix: the tile URL is identical either way, so without it every already-cached tile would ignore the toggle. Toggling takes the same reload path as switching map source (`loadMapTexture` + `requestSubdivisionPass`). Image smoothing is off when rescaling the OSM tile — OSM serves 256 px and satellite sources often 512 px, and interpolating between them blends shoreline pixels into colours that no longer match the flat fill, eating the edge of every lake. OSM stops at zoom 19 while MapBox reaches 20 (in practice, not just in theory), so deeper tiles fall back to the deepest OSM ancestor and crop to the sub-rectangle they occupy; because a wrong crop would paint water in the wrong place *silently*, that arithmetic lives in its own three.js-free, state-free module (`osmTileForTile` in `src/OSMWaterTileMapping.js`) with tests — including one asserting all 16 children of a tile map to distinct, non-overlapping quadrants inside their ancestor.
  - **Loading.** Costs one extra tile fetch per tile while enabled; a failed OSM fetch is non-fatal (the tile keeps its own imagery and simply has no detectable water). The OSM fetch was originally chained **after** each tile's own texture, so every tile waited on two round trips back to back against a slow public tile server, which showed up as tiles filling in seconds late after a camera sweep; both fetches now start together under `Promise.all`. *(Verified structurally, not by measurement — the browser had these tiles cached at ~1 ms each, so parallel and sequential were indistinguishable in the resource timings.)* In-flight OSM fetches are additionally deduplicated by URL in `osmWaterImageLoads`, because past OSM's max zoom the several terrain tiles cropping from one OSM ancestor each issued their own request and `loadTextureWithRetries` has no dedup of its own; the shared load deliberately gets **no** abort signal, since the result is shared and one tile being pruned must not cancel the fetch out from under its siblings. Repeat loads after one settles are left to the browser's HTTP cache rather than held in memory.
- **SHF: the results compass rose is a live magnetic compass** (`2b2ac333`; `tools/shf/app.js`, `tools/shf/skyview.js`, `tools/shf/style.css`, `tools/shf/sw.js`; standalone Starlink Horizon Flares PWA under `tools/`, not part of the webpack bundle). Everything on the rose that carries an **azimuth** — the tick ring, the flare-density arc, the flare-dot sprinkle and the direction arrows — now lives inside a single `.rose-dial` group that the page rotates so N points at **true north**; the two backing circles and the hub are rotationally symmetric and stay outside it, and the eight cardinal letters are moved separately by the new exported `roseLabelXY(azDeg, headingDeg)` so they **orbit the ring while staying upright** and readable. Heading comes from the shared `tools/src/DeviceOrientationCompass.js` — the same library `tools/compass` and `src/ARMode.js` already use — imported **lazily** on the first results screen, so the app still boots and runs offline on a device with no sensors. Raw headings are smoothed exponentially along the short way round (so the dial neither jitters with the magnetometer nor spins the long way through the 360°/0° wrap) and redraws are coalesced to one `requestAnimationFrame`; `applyRoseHeading()` writes one transform attribute plus eight label positions and never rebuilds the SVG. Sensors run **only while the results screen is showing** (driven from `renderScreen`), since an orientation listener left attached in the background is pure battery drain. On by default (`compassOn = true`), with one unavoidable platform exception: iOS gates orientation behind a permission prompt that must originate in a user gesture, so `startCompassSensors()` bails there until the toggle is tapped once — and inside `toggleRoseCompass` the `DeviceOrientationEvent.requestPermission()` call goes **first**, before the awaited module import, because awaiting the import would end the user-gesture window and the prompt would be refused. The toggle chip (`.rose-compass`, top-right of the rose, same round-chip idiom as `.hv-toggle`) is only emitted where `window.DeviceOrientationEvent` exists at all, lives **outside** `.rose-wrap` because `paintRose()` replaces that element's `innerHTML` wholesale, and lights up only when headings are actually arriving, so it never claims to be live while iOS is still waiting for its tap. `tools/shf/sw.js` gains a `SHARED` scope (`../src/`) alongside its own `SCOPE`: the shared library sits outside the worker's registration scope but the worker still *observes* those fetches, so caching it there is what keeps the live compass working offline. `tools/shf/tools/verify-browser.mjs` now maps `/src/...` to the real `tools/src` directory, mirroring how the deployment serves both under `/tools`. The rose's viewBox also became **square with uniform padding** (`ROSE_PAD = 46` around `R = 84`, so the rim spans ~65% of the box; the old adaptive box put the rim at ~93% of its *width*) — this supersedes the adaptive `compassViewBox(arrows)` framing shipped in 2.111.0, which biased the spare room to the flare side, a distinction a rotating dial makes meaningless. `compassViewBox()` still accepts and ignores its argument so existing callers are unchanged.
- **SHF: a "use my current location" button on the Origin field** (`2b2ac333`; `tools/shf/index.html`, `tools/shf/app.js`, `tools/shf/style.css`). A crosshair button (`#origin-locate`, `.locate-btn`) sits to the **left** of the Origin input inside a new `.input-row` flex wrapper; the autocomplete dropdown still anchors to `.field`, so it spans button + input underneath both. Leaving Origin blank already geolocated at submit time — this does it up front via `locateOrigin()` so the user can *see* where they were placed, and correct it, before searching. While the fix is in flight the button goes amber and spins (`.busy`) and is not clickable again; failures land on the form's own status line (`formError`) rather than the results screen, which is where the user is still looking. A geolocated point carries no IANA zone, so `formTz` is cleared and the time-zone button re-synced by hand — writing `.value` from code fires no `input` event — while the UTC/local toggle, being the user's own choice, is left alone.
- **BOTBench: a *Probe* column — data quality by attempting the extraction** (`114f6816`; `src/analysis/BotBenchUI.js`, `src/analysis/BotBenchRunner.js`, `src/TraverseAnalysis.js`, `src/TraverseHypotheses.js`; **File → File Analysis → *BOTBench…***). CV rcond grades one method family's entry conditions and demonstrably does not track the pipeline's Truth column. What *does* answer "could a path be extracted from geometry alone" is an actual attempt — and the battery already makes one on every file: the Minimum Acceleration fit's stage-1 pure-smoothness gate (the P1-hardened valley machinery). Its verdict now rides every row as the new Probe column, at zero extra cost, **added alongside** the existing CV rcond column rather than replacing it. Three states, because the gate has three: **`geom N`** (green) — pure geometry pinned the range at N nautical miles, no speed assumption involved; **`geom→spd`** (amber) — geometry *did* pin a range but the speed it implies exceeds twice the fit's target, so the fit deliberately fell back to its prior, which for data quality reads as RECOVERABLE (a fast object at pinned range is a finding, not an ambiguity); **`prior`** — geometry left range genuinely ambiguous. `fitPlausibleBestRange` now exposes the pre-sanity verdict (`geometryDecisive`) and the fallback flag (`speedSanityOverride`) — `usedSpeedTarget` is unchanged for all existing consumers — and the plausible hypothesis carries the valley diagnostics in its params. Cell tooltips carry decisiveness, valley width, residual, and floor-shaped / boundary-limited caveats, plus the scope rule: **the probe speaks for geometry only**, and physics and stationary methods may still succeed on a `prior` file. Five probe fields (`probeGeometryPinned`, `probeSpeedOverride`, `probeRangeM`, `probeDecisiveness`, `probeValleyWidthLog`) join the CSV export for correlating Probe against Truth across a run, and `TABLE_MIN_WIDTH_PX` rises 1600 → 1660. Codex review APPROVEd only after the speed-sanity state was split out — a decisive-but-fast input must not read as "ambiguous".
- **BOTBench ingests any pointing-bearing track CSV, through the same dispatch the app uses** (`7546e7bf`, `a6d84def`; new `src/TrackFiles/TrackCSV.js` + `tests/botbench/genericCsvIngest.test.js`, `src/CFileManagerParse.js`, `src/ParseUtils.js`, `src/ParseFeaturesCSV.js`, `src/analysis/BotBenchIngest.js`). `TrackCSV.js` becomes **the** single source of truth for track-CSV importing: `detectCSVType` moves there to sit beside the shared type→parser→class dispatch it feeds (`trackFileFromCSVType`) plus each format's `trackCSVConventions` (`pointing`, `multiRole`). `CFileManagerParse`'s former eight-branch CSV dispatch now calls it and re-exports `detectCSVType` for existing importers, so a new CSV format added in one place is loadable in the app **and** analysable in BOTBench in the same commit. `ingestGenericTrackCSV` runs Airdata drone logs (`boresight` pointing convention — the platform frame *is* the pointing, with sensor-relative angles left empty on purpose) and MISB-column CSVs through that path and then the same sightline/clock pipeline as FMV; the type is judged **before** parsing, because several parsers legitimately touch scene state that a file about to be refused must not trigger. Position-only tracks and multi-role (platform/target/ground) files refuse with the specific reason rather than being analysed anyway. Timestamps normalize **per value** via `epochStampSeconds`, not per format: the MISB CSV importer passes the file's numbers through verbatim, so the unit is a property of the *file*. A number is accepted only when exactly one of its s/ms/µs readings lands in a 1980–2100 era window — the era is ~13× wide but the units are 1000× apart, so the three windows cannot overlap and anything falling between them (e.g. any 1971 stamp) returns `NaN` and refuses loudly instead of ingesting 1000× wrong. Pinned against the real µs-stamped `MISB_FULL` fixture (~5 Hz, not 0.005 Hz — a static "CSV = milliseconds" declaration had turned its 0.2 s cadence into 200 s). `isFeaturesCSV` moved to `ParseUtils` as a pure header sniff so headless consumers can import detection without dragging in the `FeatureManager` render chain, and the `detectCSVType` spec-guard test points at the function's new home. `a6d84def` additionally has the generic ingest return **the file's own truth track** from the `truth_lat` / `truth_long` / `truth_alt` columns, in the exact shape the BOT ingest returns — feet assumed for the unit-unlabeled `truth_alt` (matching `CTrackFileMISB`, with a warning stating the assumption) and the same hold-last plus leading back-fill treatment of truth gaps.

### Improvements
- **BOTBench shows meaningful scenario names from answer-key sidecars** (`1e3110b7`; `benchmarks/botbench/lib/exportInterchange.js`, `benchmarks/botbench/lib/interchangeRelease.js`, `src/analysis/BotBenchIngest.js`, `BotBenchRunner.js`, `BotBenchUI.js`). A sealed release's `All/` (answer-key) sidecar copies now carry `descriptiveName`, the human-meaningful scenario name behind the opaque id. `All/` contains the answers by definition, so the name leaks nothing that folder does not already hold, and the challenge-side sidecars stay name-free — the sealed-release leak scan continues to enforce it and the reidentification suite passes untouched. BOTBench reads the field when present: the File column shows the meaningful name with the path moved to the tooltip (challenge files keep showing their path), and `displayName` joins the CSV export. Regenerating a sealed set with its stored salt (`answers/seal-salt.txt`) preserves the opaque ids, so an existing folder simply gains names on the next run — `bot-0011`, for instance, turns out to be the 20 g pulse anomaly.
- **Self-hosted installs are told when a release adds new server settings** (`1019c479`, documented further in `05299b19`; new `scripts/sharedEnvVersion.js` + `tests/sharedEnvVersion.test.js`, `config/shared.env.example`, `.githooks/pre-commit`, `webpack.common.js`, `webpack.copy-files.js`, `docs/dev/Installing-and-configuring.md`). Operators previously had no way to know when `shared.env.example` gained settings their live `shared.env` lacked. The example now carries a date-based `SHARED_ENV_VERSION` stamp and **builds refuse to run** when the local `shared.env` is older. The check runs from `webpack.common.js` (all bundling builds) *and* from `webpack.copy-files.js`, which does not load common but still copies `shared.env` into `shared.env.php` — so `npm run copy` would otherwise have deployed a stale config through an open door. On failure it prints both versions, the commits and diff for `shared.env.example` since the user's version (via git, with GitHub links as a fallback for zip installs), and the steps to get current. The pre-commit hook stamps the example whenever a commit changes its content, restages it, and syncs the committer's own gitignored `shared.env`; a manual stamp is accepted only if it parses and moves forward, and a file with staged changes *plus* further unstaged edits blocks the commit rather than shipping settings under the old version (bypassable with `--no-verify`, like the existing lint gate). Version comparison is **parsed, not lexical**, so `.10` sorts above `.2`; a generated "today" that trails the existing stamp (contributors straddling midnight in different time zones) increments the existing one instead of going backwards; a newer local version passes, so building an older branch is never blocked; a missing stamp in the example means a branch predating the mechanism and is allowed, while a malformed one is an error, since silently skipping the comparison would disable the gate everywhere. git is invoked with **argument arrays rather than shell strings** — the version comes out of the user's own config and the version regex excludes only whitespace, so a value such as `$(...)` would otherwise be executed by the shell during an ordinary build; a regression test covers it. Fresh installs are unaffected: CI, the Dockerfile and the install scripts all copy `shared.env.example` over `shared.env` and inherit the current stamp. `05299b19` then expands the docs from a description of the gate into a walkthrough of what an admin actually *does* when it fires — the report they will see, reading the diff to find settings that matter, merging them, setting the version line, rebuilding — plus the never-blocked cases and the standalone `sharedEnvVersion.js --check`, with a matching pointer in the Docker update section where the same "a new release added options" problem applies to `.env`.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed refraction being applied as if every camera stood at sea level, tearing a seam across the sky from high altitude** (`a686d912`; `src/atmosphere/refraction.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayNightSky.js`, `src/nodes/CPlanets.js`, `src/nodes/CPointLightCloud.js`, `tests/refraction.test.js`; **View → Atmospheric Refraction**). Saemundsson is a sea-level formula and was applied regardless of observer height, which failed twice from a camera at 493 km: the full ground-level bend was applied to light that never enters the atmosphere, and the formula's −5° floor landed **inside the field of view**, because from that altitude the horizon is 21.8° down rather than just below the horizontal. A 7.62° view spanning −2.58° to −10.20° got 0.65° of bend at the top tapering to nothing 35% down — a visible seam across the sky, with the Moon lifted off the LOS cone that pointed at it. `refractionDeltaDeg` now scales its result by the air density at the **lowest point the sightline reaches** (`densityFactor` → `rayMinHeight`): the observer's own height looking up, the tangent height looking down, via `exp(-zMin / REFRACTION_SCALE_HEIGHT_M)`. That is the same physical quantity as the pressure setting, evaluated where the light actually travels instead of always at sea level. The factor is **exactly 1** for an observer at or below sea level and for any ray that reaches the ground, so ground sitches — including the −3.54°→−5° taper, which is entirely below-horizon — are bit-for-bit unchanged, and all 111 pre-existing refraction tests pass without edits. The scale height is 7500 m, not the 8.4–8.5 km isothermal value, because the real atmosphere has a lapse rate: against the US Standard Atmosphere 7500 gives 0.264 at 10 km where the truth is 0.261, while 8500 would be 19% high. `uObserverHeight` / `uEarthRadius` join the shared uniform block, set per-view in `_updateRefractionUniforms` from the render camera — the same per-view discipline the zenith already had, which matters when two views have different observers (main at 493 km, look at 730 m). The tangent height is written `h·cos(a) − 2R·sin²(a/2)` rather than the algebraically identical `(R+h)·cos(a) − R`, because the latter cancels two numbers near 6.4e6 down to one near 1e4, which the shader's float32 cannot hold; both CPU and GPU paths use the stable form so the CPU result still lands on the disk the shader drew. `applyRefractionFromObserver` derives the height from the observer ECEF it already has, so `CSatellite` needs no change, and the four hand-copied uniform lists become `Object.assign`/spread of the whole block — a material missing `uObserverHeight` silently reads 0, which is indistinguishable from the behaviour this corrects. Measured with refraction on: main view now under 1e-28° across the whole frame and continuous through the old seam; look view (730 m) 0.438° against the sea-level 0.479° at the horizon. **Still unmodelled:** grazing rays with tangent heights of 0–100 km, the ~1.1° bend behind the refracted eclipse ring — from orbit that is only within ~2.4° of the geometric horizon. +22 tests.
- **Fixed the SHF geolocated Origin dropping its coordinates and being re-geocoded from its display label** (`2b2ac333`; `tools/shf/app.js`). Predates the new locate button and also affected the existing blank-origin → Edit → resubmit path. `resolveBrowserLocation()` wrote a place **name** (or a `"40.000°, -105.000°"` string) into the Origin field and returned coordinates that were then discarded, so any later submit sent that *label* back through the geocoder — landing on some arbitrary airport in the same city, or failing outright on a label that is just a pair of numbers. The browser's actual fix is now pinned to the field as `input._geoOrigin` and returned **verbatim** by `resolveField()` before any geocoding is attempted. It is cleared in exactly the three places where the user means something else: on `input` (typing means they want *this* text), on picking an autocomplete suggestion (an explicit pick supersedes the fix), and in `restorePendingRealSearch` (only the text survives a reload, so a restored label must resolve normally or re-geolocate if blank).
- **Fixed the SHF results compass changing size and position the instant a scan finished** (`2b2ac333`; `tools/shf/app.js`, `tools/shf/style.css`). On a 375×667 viewport the rose went 0 → 300 px → 177 px, dragging the wide view 123 px up the moment results appeared, because the live scanning scaffold left three things empty that the final screen fills: the rose itself, the wide view, and the trailing button + data-source note. All three now reserve their final height — the rose is painted empty immediately, the wide view carries an empty SVG with the real one's `viewBox` so it reserves the same aspect, and a new `.results-tail-reserve` block holds a `visibility: hidden` copy of the *Open in Sitrec* button and note (height reserved, nothing drawn, `pointer-events: none` so the invisible button is untappable). The layout measured **during** the scan is therefore already the final layout, and the width that measurement yields is frozen in `_roseW` and reused by every later repaint including the 10 Hz live one, instead of being recomputed against whatever is on screen at that moment. `fitResultsCompass` is replaced by `paintRose(arrows, flares, live)` — the single path every render now goes through — with `unfreezeRose()` on `resize`/`orientationchange` unfreezing for exactly one recompute, so the rose still adapts to the viewport. Two long-standing CSS reserves that existed for this same reason were also 4–5 px short of the inherited 1.45 line-height and are corrected: `.r-dir` `1.2em → 1.45em`, `.r-meta` `1.05em → 1.45em`.
- **Fixed the "UNIC Time Stamp" MISB CSV family importing with no timestamps at all** (`a6d84def`; `src/MISBUtils.js`, `tests/botbench/genericCsvIngest.test.js`). One client family (the `data/misb/misb2.csv` shape) heads its epoch-stamp column **`UNIC Time Stamp`** — a typo baked into the exporting tool — beside a `UNIX Time Stamp date` column holding a spreadsheet day serial. `parseMISB1CSV` matches headers by strip-spaces/lowercase equality, so **neither** column mapped to `UnixTimeStamp`: every record imported with a null stamp and fell to the unhandled-column warning. BOTBench refused the whole folder with "Neither UnixTimeStamp nor KLV PES PTS gives a usable, advancing timeline"; in the app the breakage was masked, because custom-sitch tracks index by frame. `parseMISB1CSV` now aliases the typo header (`"unictimestamp": "UnixTimeStamp"`) and converts the day-serial date column — Excel serial in the 20000–80000 range (1954–2189), a bare number outside it passed through untouched, or a date string — as a **fallback applied after the column loop that fills only rows whose stamp is still null**, so a real stamp column always wins regardless of column order. The no-timeline refusal also diagnoses itself now: when stamps were present but not classifiable as epoch s/ms/µs it says so with a sample value, instead of implying the column was missing.
- **Fixed Celestial Lock aiming at the GEOMETRIC direction to a body while the sky is DRAWN refracted, so the camera pointed off whatever it was locked to** (`b7e245d8`; `src/atmosphere/refraction.js`, `src/atmosphere/refractionSettings.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeCamera.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeControllerVarious.js`, `tests/refraction.test.js`; **Camera → Heading → *Camera Heading* → *Celestial Lock***). `getCelestialDirection` / `getCelestialDirectionFromRaDec` / `getStarDirectionECEF` return the geometric direction — `Astronomy.Equator` with `ofdate=false` and aberration on, no refraction — but every body is bent toward the observer's zenith before it is rendered: `CPlanets` for the Sun, Moon and planets, `REFRACTION_VERTEX_GLSL` for the star field. Aiming down the geometric direction therefore missed the drawn body by the **full refraction amount** — `refractionDeltaDeg(0)` = 0.483° at the horizon at the default 1010 hPa / 10 °C, tapering to zero at the zenith. Latent until `a686d912` (above): with the old flat sea-level bend the error was a constant offset that a fixed camera never revealed; making refraction depend on observer height made it move with the camera, and in the saved *Moon terminator test* regression sitch the Moon's top was clipped off the frame edge because the drawn Moon sat higher than the camera aimed. It is now fully framed. The fix is a new `applyRefractionToDirection(dir, observerECEF, opts, target)` — the direction-at-infinity variant of the existing finite-position `applyRefractionFromObserver`. The bend is a function of apparent altitude and observer height **only, not of range**, which is why a direction needs no distance: the implementation pushes a sample 1e9 m along the ray (well clear of the `dist < 1` early-out, small enough that float64 keeps the subtraction exact), bends that through the same routine the satellites use, and re-normalizes; writing into a `target` aliased to the input is safe because both output writes happen after the input has been read. Both lock paths go through it: `CNodeControllerCelestial.apply()` — the *Celestial Lock* option on the Camera Heading switch, which is the path every custom sitch takes — and the `this.celestialLock` branch in `CNodeCamera.update()`, which `lockOnObject` / `lockOnRaDec` (the assistant/API `lockCameraOnObject` / `lockCameraOnRaDec`) use only as the fallback for sitches that have no Camera Heading switch to drive. Because the height comes from the observer ECEF each is given, the bend scales with the **camera's own** height: a camera in orbit gets almost none, one on the ground gets the full amount. `currentRefractionOpts()` is added to the existing `refractionSettings.js` (which owns **View → Atmospheric Refraction**) so the two new call sites don't each rebuild the options block; it reads `Sit.refractionEnabled` — the master *and* the Sky checkbox — so with refraction off the lock stays geometric exactly as before, and it deliberately carries no `observerHeight` since the helpers derive it themselves. `CSatellite` predates it and still builds an identical block inline. +8 tests: the horizon lift matches `refractionDeltaDeg` and is toward the zenith, the zenith is unbent, the result stays unit length, it agrees with the satellite finite-position path to <1e-6°, it is range-independent, an observer at 492.8 km gets under 1/100th of the ground bend, and an aliased output is safe.

## Version 2.117.0 (2026-08-06)

### New Features
- **Master/scene script tabs via *include*** (`20708dba`; `src/scriptedVideo/ScriptCommands.js`, `ScriptJSRunner.js`, `ScriptRunnerClient.js`, `src/workers/ScriptRunnerWorker.js`, `src/CScriptedVideo.js`; **Video → Scripting → *Scripting Window…***; documented in `docs/ScriptedVideo.md`). `include "Tab Name"` compiles the named tab's script against the same record-only API and runs it at the current clock, so its events land on the master timeline and the clock advances through the scene — a master tab can be nothing but a list of scene tabs run in order. Registered in `COMMANDS` with `runnerSpecial: "include"` and handled inside the runner: sequential only (awaiting the returned promise is what serializes it; the docs warn against attaching `&` lines to an include, which would anchor at t = 0). `CScriptedVideo.parse` passes the other tabs as a `{name: text}` map, excluding the ACTIVE tab so a self-include reads as an unknown tab, and poisoning duplicate names to `null` so `include` refuses the ambiguity instead of silently running whichever copy came last; the runner additionally refuses circular includes via an `includeStack` and caps nesting at 8 (`MAX_INCLUDE_DEPTH`). Events from an included tab are tagged `includedFrom` with blanked `spans`/`offSpan` — their character spans index the included tab's text, so leaving them live would let the timeline's wheel editing rewrite the wrong characters in the master; they edit in their own tab. The included tab's parse and syntax errors are reported against the master's `include` line, prefixed `[TabName]`. A new `included()` predicate is true while running inside an include, so a scene tab that occupies later world time in the master can pad itself for standalone preview (`if (!included()) sleep(90)`) without the padding leaking into the master timeline. The tabs map is threaded through the sandboxed runner worker; covered in `tests/scriptJSRunner.test.js`.
- **Walkers can be built-in 3D models, and a new *TR-3B (lit)* model** (`20708dba`; `src/CSitrecAPI.js`, `ModelFiles` in `src/nodes/CNode3DObject.js`, new `data/models/tr-3b-lit.glb`). `createWalker` — the API command (AI assistant, scripts, MCP) that moves a marker through lat/lon waypoints — gains optional `model`/`modelLength`: `model` must be a `ModelFiles` registry name (validated up front, listing the valid names in the error, so a walker spec can never serialize a model reference the deserialize pass cannot load) and builds the walker as a `CNode3DObject` model instead of parametric geometry, overriding `geometry` and the color/material/size params. `modelLength` is metres at the API boundary; the node's `modelLength` GUIValue stores the current SMALL display unit, so it is converted with `Units.m2Small` at creation while `Globals.walkerSpecs` keeps the metres value — a reload under a different unit system re-converts correctly. Doc fixes in the same pass: walker altitudes are ellipsoidal (HAE — the datum of tile raycasts and `getGroundAltitude`'s `altHAE`), NOT MSL; and walker names must avoid the script-target aliases (`object`, `target`, `witness`, `camera`, `observer`), which the scripted-video system resolves to other nodes. The new **TR-3B (lit)** registry entry is the tr-3b with full-emissive corner lights, a black metallic hull, and a KHR_lights_punctual centre light at the origin that the existing `extractLightsFromModel` pipeline turns into a distance-boosted `CNode3DLight` billboard — the craft stays visible as a point of light at long range, which is what night-sighting recreations need. Available everywhere models are: any 3D object's model dropdown, `createWalker`, `listModels`.
- **BOTBench user guide with glossary** (`7ee3a608`; new `docs/BOTBench.md` + `docs/images/botbench-results.jpg`; registered in `src/docsRegistry.js` with label `menus.help.documentation.botBench` in `src/i18n/en.js`, section *analysis*, `menuId: "file"` — so it appears under **Help → Documentation**, in the **File** menu's *Help* folder, and in the AI assistant's reading list). The page walks the window top to bottom — every control, summary tile and table column, split into the SOURCE quality measurements (baseline, sweep, rcond, the pointing-noise estimate vs the declared sigma) and the ANALYSIS verdict columns — plus what a bulk run deliberately cannot do, how results are scored against truth, the BOT interchange CSV format and its `scenario.json` sidecar, and how the sealed scenario releases are generated (`bench-bot-interchange`). Technical terms are anchor-linked to a glossary at the end of the page. Accuracy fixes from review are folded in: *Cancel Run* aborts the in-flight file rather than waiting for it, and sidecarless BOT files take their sample rate from the CSV's own Time column (only the origin falls back to the default site). The stale-cased `docs/BotBench.md` index entry was replaced so case-sensitive deploys build the same `BOTBench.html` the registry links to.

### Improvements
- **Star Tracker frame analysis runs in parallel: detection in a worker pool, decode pipelined ahead** (`39966b4b`; new `src/starTrack/StarDetectPool.js` + `src/workers/StarDetectWorker.js`, the detect pass of `runStarTracker` in `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`; *Full Analysis* in **Video → Star Tracker**). The Analyze scan runs `detectSources` once per frame, and on real clips that is nearly the whole pass — tens to hundreds of milliseconds of pure computation per frame, previously serialized on the UI thread behind the decode of the frame before it. Every frame is independent, so the scan is now split: decode stays sequential on the main thread (the decoder, the canvas readback and `par.frame` all live there) and feeds frames to a worker pool, so decode and detection overlap AND detection uses the cores. Pool size is min(cores − 1, capped at 8), further bounded by memory — `detectSources`' transient working set is ~48 bytes/pixel, so a ~1.5 GB budget keeps 1080p-class footage at the full core count while 12-megapixel stills get fewer workers; idle workers are kept 60 s so consecutive runs reuse them. Determinism: `StarDetectWorker` is a transport shim that imports the REAL `detectSources` from `StarDetect.js` — same source, same bytes, identical results (rendered-pixel regressions compare star overlays) — and each frame's pixel buffer is TRANSFERRED, never copied. `finalizeFrame` — the rejection tally (judged with the same `maxArea` the detector used), mask filtering, `perFrame`, live preview — runs strictly in frame order however completions interleave, and the playhead follows the FINISHED frames (`framePixels(..., drivePlayhead = false)` decodes without moving `par.frame`) so the preview circles stay on the frame they were measured on while the decode frontier (pool size + 2) stays inside the decoder's 30-frame GOP-cache window. Stills, single frames and no-Worker environments take the old synchronous loop; a failed worker job is re-decoded and detected on the main thread, a broken pool degrades the rest of the run to the synchronous shape with a console warning, and abort/stale tears the pool down immediately (a frame inside `detectSources` cannot be interrupted any other way), failing queued jobs rather than leaking their transferred buffers. The per-frame canvas readback also reuses one shared canvas, and the pass logs its wall time and worker count.
- **Sync Scale is computed from what is still in play, governs the magnified views — and starts OFF** (`573481b4`, `63ca6023`; `applySyncScale` + the bounds accumulators in `hypothesisVolumeScene` in `src/AnalyzeTraverse.js`, `Chart3DGroup.setSyncScale` in `src/Chart3D.js`; *Sync Scale* in the gallery of **Traverse → Analyze Traverse Methods...**). Previously the shared scale was anchored to whichever chart was last SELECTED — it changed with every click, a set-aside outlier kept stretching every graph after being excluded from consideration, and it stopped at the zoom boundary: a magnified chart (setZoom's per-candidate box) ignored it entirely. Now the shared full box is the component-wise UNION of every in-play (non-set-aside) candidate's bounds, and magnified views share a window SIZE — the component-wise MAX of in-play zoomBounds spans — while each stays centred on its own tracks, so candidates compare at one scale without losing their framing. Per-axis aggregation is load-bearing: one candidate's whole box copies its narrow axes along with its long one, and an east-west outlier's window would clip a north-south candidate to a sliver (pinned as a unit test). Setting a tile aside re-tightens every graph immediately; restoring widens them back. `Chart3DGroup.setSyncScale(on, sharedBounds, sharedZoomSpan)` now takes the computed box and span rather than reference charts. Underneath, `hypothesisVolumeScene` grows its bounds from EVERY frame of every series — sensor path, candidate track, family-band members, truth (valid frames, ungated by the drawn count), both ray families' endpoints — regardless of drawing decimation, which is untouched: tiles (360-sample) and the detail view (720) previously reported different extents for the same candidate, so a tile-aggregated shared scale could clip an extremum only the denser view sampled (truth windows small enough to vanish under tile decimation; ray endpoints extending 6% past the track). Measuring and drawing are now separate concerns; 17 Chart3D unit tests cover the group/activeBounds geometry. And the toggle now starts OFF (`63ca6023`): each chart opens at its own natural scale, with the shared largest-in-play scale one click away instead of imposed — the button, its aria-pressed state and the group's syncScale flag all start false together.
- **Co-leaders are named instead of crowning the first tile** (`22861e0f`; `markCoLeaders` + `coLeaderBadge` in `src/TraverseRanking.js`, badge/detail wiring in `src/AnalyzeTraverse.js`; the gallery of **Traverse → Analyze Traverse Methods...**). BOT Bench measured what the gallery's implicit "first tile = the answer" presentation costs: on the 19-scenario interchange set, the blind ranking put the closest available candidate first on only 3 of 18 scenarios. Everything the flat comparator decides above the tie-breakers — screen pass, eligibility, completeness, fit tier, bound-pin count — is sound and comparable across categories; everything below that line is heuristic (category priority, a `secondaryScore` that is not commensurable across fit kinds, raw residual). A candidate that matches the flat leader on every DISCRETE key is therefore marked a CO-LEADER on its rating (`item.r.coLeader`): the analysis genuinely cannot order it against the leader, and tile order among co-leaders is presentation, not a finding. The *Co-leader* badge shows on gallery tiles and both report-card surfaces, and the detail panel appends a plain-language line ("the ranking cannot order this against the other co-leading candidates; their tile order is presentation, not a finding"). With a truth track selected, truth separation soundly orders candidates, so differing truth scores break co-leadership — claiming "cannot order" right after truth ordered them would be false (the quadcopter/lantern pair at 23.6 m vs 273.1 m truth separation is pinned as a test). Marking happens on the flat order inside `groupAndRankHypotheses`, so the gallery path (`rankAllHypotheses`) and the report's fresh regrouping both carry it; a lone leader gets no mark. Scope, honestly measured on the replay: the badge tempers false precision on 13 of the 15 miss cases, but identifies the materially closer candidate on only 3 — finding the right candidate is a calibrated selector's job, which remains future work. No reordering, no verdict-wording changes; six new unit tests.
- **BOTBench naming, plain-language strings, and self-describing window titles** (`7ee3a608`; `src/analysis/BotBenchUI.js`, `BotBenchIngest.js`, `BotBenchRunner.js`, `VideoFolderAnalysisUI.js`, `src/showTimingAnalysis.js`, `src/AnalyzeTraverse.js`). The feature is BOTBench and BOT is Bearings-Only Traversal: the dialog title (*BOTBench — Bearings-Only Traversal bulk analysis*), the **File → File Analysis** menu item (*BOTBench...*), the Help label, the doc title and the report/provenance strings (`BOTBench: <label>` in `situation`/`sitName`) all say so, with the acronym expanded at first contact. "CV family" is spelled out as Constant Velocity (CV) family everywhere it faces the user, and the ingest's OTHER CV — coefficient of variation in the timing warnings — no longer shares the abbreviation ("intervals vary by N% of their mean"). A naive-reader audit of every UI string drove the rest: plain-language rewrites of the Noise/Decl/rcond/Base tooltips (no bare "second-difference", "LOS", or "effective rank"), FMV glossed at first contact, an internal function name removed from a user-facing warning, and the white-residue report paragraph rewritten in words. Windows now title themselves from the result they show, not from leftover or global state: `showTimingAnalysis` takes a `title` parameter — the FMV analyser's summary is headed *FMV Data Summary* instead of *MISB Timing Analysis* — and the traverse gallery title prefers `results.manifest.situation` over `Sit.name`, so a gallery opened from a BOTBench results row names the file it analysed rather than whatever sitch happens to be open (the live path is unchanged: it sets `manifest.situation` to `Sit.name`).

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed the stage-1 geometry gate measuring the grid instead of the valley — slow/close scenes dragged to ~3.6× their true range** (`23959cc6`; `fitPlausibleBestRange` in `src/TraverseAnalysis.js`; **Traverse → Analyze Traverse Methods...**). The gate that decides geometry-vs-speed-prior counted sweep cells under a family threshold (`famCount <= 3`), so the same physical smoothness valley read "decisive" on a 5-cell grid and "flat" on a 72-cell one — and at fine grids the 300 kt prior dragged slow/close scenes to ~3.6× their true range (the BOT Bench P1 finding, independently reproduced at 3.40× in review). The decision now measures the valley itself, at a resolution that never changes with `coarse`: the floor is localized by parabolic bracket-shrink refinement between the winning cell's neighbours (a discrete minimum always lies between them), with up to five bisection probes toward an edge cell when the winner sits on the grid boundary; walls are a fixed rise of `decisiveMargin` above the refined floor, measured by walking outward in fixed 0.26-nat log-range steps (`VALLEY_WALK_STEP`, cap 4/side, `VALLEY_WALK_MAX`) — THROUGH the caller's `[rangeMin, rangeMax]` if that is where they stand. The range bracket constrains the answer, never the measurement: a genuinely interior minimum near a boundary proves its wall just beyond the bracket, while noisy range-unobservable data that parks its closer-is-smoother minimum on the boundary keeps descending out there and never shows one (two rounds of in-bracket "squeezed wall" heuristics were defeated by noise-scale constructions before this simpler principle replaced them). Geometry decides only when decisiveness clears its margin, BOTH walls cross, total width ≤ 0.6 nats (`VALLEY_WIDTH_MAX` — what `famCount <= 3` intended at the default grid), and no sweep cell under the wall threshold sits outside the measured valley (a second range family means genuine ambiguity). When geometry decides, the refined floor seeds the final ±1.5× range refine — previously the returned range could not escape the bracket around a coarse cell a full grid step from the floor it had chosen. `famCount` is still reported as `flatFamilyCount`; `valleyWidthLog`, `valleyMultimodal` and `valleyWalls` join the diagnostics. Verified: six decisive orbit scenes (truth 0.60–19.2 NM, two hugging the bracket's edges) at `coarse` {4, 5, 7, 8, 18, 72} all come out geometric within 35% of truth; three straight-sensor controls (clean, plus two adversarial jitter constructions that previously forced a ~13.5 NM target to 0.5 NM) hold on the prior; the full 980-record physics bench shows zero drift. Codex adversarial review converged over seven rounds — five constructible defects found, fixed, and pinned as tests.
- **Fixed the fixed-wing fit converging on the wrong basin with all three restarts agreeing** (`50f2ea1d`; `fitAircraft` in `src/TraverseAnalysis.js`; regressions in `tests/botbench/fitAircraftBasin.test.js`). The three deterministic default runs (pop 60 / gens 150) can all converge on the same wrong basin — bench scenario bb-2af6154e returned cost 13.69 while a ~10.0 basin existed in-bounds — and denser search, not more restarts, is what finds it. One escalated run (pop 120 / gens 300, deterministic seed) now fires when the default runs disagree (cost spread > 10%: different basins means coverage is incomplete) or when the best cost is mediocre but not hopeless (6..300 in cost units dominated by angular residual — room to be wrong, but a hopeless fit stays hopeless at any budget). It is a latency-bounded recovery pass, not full basin verification — 180/500 recovers more (8.83 vs 10.10 on the reference case) at ~1.6× the added time — and `escalatePop`/`escalateGens`/`escalate: false` let a caller choose. Progress reporting stays monotonic: the default runs share [0, 0.85] and escalation owns the reserved tail. On the physics bench the two recoverable fixed-wing cells transform (aircraft-turn median relSep 0.571 → 0.193, bird 0.493 → 0.030) at ~+16% solver time; nothing else moved. The bb-2af6154e escalation is pinned as a regression (cost < 10.5).
- **Fixed the valley gate reading the optimizer's own range floor as geometric evidence** (`50f2ea1d`; `traversePlausible` + the valley-wall walk in `fitPlausibleBestRange`, `src/TraverseAnalysis.js`). The stage-1 gate could read the optimizer's 120 m soft range floor as a genuine near wall, certifying forced-close results on noisy scenes — the floor stops the closer-is-smoother descent, and the stump reads as a valley. `traversePlausible` now reports `floorActive`, requiring BOTH that the soft-floor rows engaged during the solve AND that the final RAW solution rides the floor (`lam ≤ minDist × 1.02`): rows alone over-report (a transient dip on an early iterate leaves them set while the final answer is genuinely floor-free), and smoothed-lambda proximity over-reported from the other side — B-spline overshoot dips below the raw closest approach and falsely condemned a legitimate ~130 m flyby — which is why the check runs on the raw solve, before smoothing rewrites `lam`. The gate uses it twice: a valley whose own refined floor is floor-active is never geometric (`valleyFloorShaped`), and a floor-active low-wall crossing must pass a DESCENT test — the crossing is re-scored with `rangeFloor: false`, and a bare score BELOW the valley floor's own means the supposed wall only exists because the floor stopped a descent (penalty-built walls collapse: bare 1.2 vs floor ~3.3), while a real close-pass wall's bare solve, even cheating through the physically-excluded region, stays worse than the true minimum (0.578 vs 0.122 on the 121 m flyby) and the crossing stands. The formulation is setting-independent — review defeated a `rangeMin`-edge proxy by simply moving the bracket. Regressions pin six bench cells across both floor-defect classes (floor-shaped centers 112.9–117.9 m; penalty-built walls at ~424 m), the movable-bracket variant (bb-a0e148d4 at rangeMin = 400), the reviewer's exact 121 m flyby fixture (truth 1731.70 m, fits 1775.53 m — the class the guard must not harm), and a rows-only `floorActive` unit. Full suite 3266 passed; Codex adversarial review ALLOW after six rounds, every blocking finding constructible, fixed, and pinned.

## Version 2.116.3 (2026-08-05)

### New Features
- **Auto detect threshold reads the detection level off the footage** (`d5cd40c3`; `chooseDetectionSigma` in `src/starTrack/StarDetect.js`, `params.autoSigma` + the probe in `detectStarSize` in `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`; *Auto detect threshold* in **Video → Star Tracker → Star Tracker Tweaks**). Opt-in, default off: `threshSigma` is the one pixel-space parameter `calibrateDetection` cannot derive from a single measurement, because it defines which blobs exist to measure — and it is not safe to guess: the 42-frame sweep clip solved at thresholds 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 but not the default 5, and at sigma 1 the threshold sank into airglow structure and the detector destroyed the real stars themselves (blobs merged into clouds, centroids 12–37 px off), which no downstream stage can undo. `chooseDetectionSigma` detects once at a permissive 1.5 sigma with `minArea` 2, recording each blob's `peakSNR`, then walks the survivor count N(t) upward in 0.25 steps from t = 2 and stops at the PLATEAU ONSET — the smallest t where raising the threshold a full sigma keeps at least 80% of the blobs (below that the count is halving per sigma: noise; on the plateau the survivors are stars). Guards: fewer than 40 probe blobs refuses outright (a plateau read off a handful of blobs is an anecdote — the caller's value stands); a dense sky with no plateau raises the threshold until at most ~120 blobs survive so the tracker is not flooded; hard clamp [2, 6] (2 is the measured damage line, 6 the top of the reference clip's solvable zone). Measured on the reference clip's frames it picks 3.5–3.75, inside the solvable zone with margin on both cliffs. The UI runs the probe before each run — at the start of *Full Analysis* and on *Detect Star Size (current frame)* — over up to three spread frames of the analysed range, taking the median so one atypical frame (a cloud, a person, a flare) cannot drag the pick; when every probe refuses, the slider's value stands. The chosen value is written to the *Detect threshold (sigma)* slider (its range widens from 3–10 step 0.5 to 2–10 step 0.25, reaching the clamp's floor), and the calibration status is prefixed *"auto sigma N (k frames) - "* (or *"auto sigma: unreadable frames, keeping N - "*).

### Improvements
- **A density-matched middle tier joins the identify cascade** (`d5cd40c3`; `STAR_IDENTIFY_DEFAULTS.tiers` in `src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`). A new tier {magLimit 5.5, maxAngleDeg 22°, neighbors 8} sits between tier 0 (mag ≤ 5.0, 22°) and the deep tier (mag ≤ 6.5, 8°). The 8-nearest-bright-neighbours rule couples magnitude depth to quad size, so a sparse ~15–30° field detecting stars to mag ~5.5–6.5 could fall between tier 0's mag-5 cut (no representable quad at all) and the deep tier's far-too-small quads. The tier costs 101,524 quads and ~126 ms to build, and changed no other corpus case's result. Corpus-validated: it solves two sparse ranges (10–11 stars) of the sweep clip that refused at every other tier, with every matched star verified real; lifts a degraded pan capture from 1 to 4 surviving windows; and solves the occluded flare-lapse this investigation began on — people repeatedly crossing the lens — where every prior configuration refused.
- **Identify failure retries the most persistent tracks, certified against the full input** (`d5cd40c3`; the failure ladder in `identifyStars` (`src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`), `certifySolve` in `src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`). A knife-edge input — one or two marginal tracks the solver cannot digest — can starve quad generation while the field remains perfectly solvable from its reliable core (measured: inputs that failed outright solved from their 11–12 most persistent tracks). When the normal cascade fails, identify now retries capped views of the 12 then 11 most persistent stars (sorted by observation count, then magnitude), each through the full tier cascade with solve bounds from the capped view. Capping shrinks every consensus denominator, which makes acceptance structurally EASIER — so a capped view's solve may not ship until `certifySolve` has re-projected its pose against the UNCAPPED star set with the full set's own bounds, tolerance, and chance arithmetic; `finishSolve` now returns the raw plate model (`model: {T, c0, b0, mirrored}`) so certification uses the same projection the solve itself used, not a reconstruction. The shipped matches, rms, and matched fraction come from the certification, so a rescued solve names every star the pose explains, not just the capped view. The status reports *"identify failed - retrying with the N most persistent stars"* during the ladder, and a rescued result appends *"(rescued from a N-star retry, certified)"*.
- **The Star Tracker Status row carries its full text as a hover tooltip** (`5294207f`; `setupStarTrackerMenu` in `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`). The status readout truncates anything longer than the row (*"identify failed: round-0 rematch collapsed"* showed as *"identify failed: round-..."*), leaving failure reasons unreadable. The visible menu rows are MenuMirror twins of the controller, not its own DOM, and twins only copy a tooltip at creation — so a 500 ms `setInterval` stamps the current status onto the `title` of every `.controller.string` row named *Status* whose input currently shows this status text (an unrelated Status row can only collide when its text is identical, making the stamp a no-op in meaning). A timer rather than `requestAnimationFrame` because rAF pauses in hidden tabs, and a hover tooltip needs half-second freshness, not frame accuracy. The loop retires when the folder's own row leaves the document; a menu rebuild spawns a fresh one.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed star identification failing at the default detection threshold: image quads now out-reach catalog pollution** (`d5cd40c3`; `imageNeighbors` and the banded quad order in `solveFieldInner` (`src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`)). A detection-threshold sweep showed identify failing at sigma 5 (the DEFAULT) and 6 on a 42-frame clip that solves at 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 — a knife edge, not a tuning error. Root cause: the catalog index builds quads from each catalog star's 8 nearest BRIGHT neighbours, but the image side searched only 7 (`imageNeighbors`), and the image list mixes in stars the tier's index cannot contain — real stars past the magnitude cap, junk — each of which displaces a bright partner from the list. With the two such stars the detector admitted at sigma 5, the one quad family the index shared with the image fell out of reach and NO true hypothesis was generated at any tier. `imageNeighbors` is now 9: the same input solves on tier 0 with 17/18 matched (depth 8 fixed only one of the two failing inputs; 10 behaves identically — 9 is validated margin, not a knife edge), and three neighbouring inputs that previously slipped through to a confidently WRONG wide-field solve now refuse or solve true instead. The quad try-order is BANDED by neighbour reach (a new `reach` on each image quad): quads drawn purely from each anchor's 7 nearest neighbours keep exactly the sequence every solved clip was calibrated against, and the depth-9 extension quads follow — unbanded, the extension's larger quads sorted ahead by diameter and pushed the old ones past the hypothesis budget, turning two wide-field solves into refusals. The 2.116.2 round-0 rematch-collapse rule is untouched and revalidated by this sweep: with it disabled, the sweep accepts a wrong Cassiopeia-region field — its third confirmed impostor kill on a third clip.

## Version 2.116.2 (2026-08-05)

### Improvements
- **Star identification solves long pans in wall-aware time windows** (`df470bdc`; `src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`, `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`; *Full Analysis* in **Video → Star Tracker**). A pan's reference chart is stitched from per-frame similarities, and the stitching drift accumulates over time — measured at 1.3° end to end on a 671-frame superzoom pan, against a 6 px verification tolerance — so one plate model can only fit one stretch of it: the full-chart solve of that clip matched 42 of 123 stars, all from the late pan, and the frames the video opens on (Vega among them) got nothing. Worse, drift re-enters broken tracks as duplicate chart entries (~17% of that clip's identify set), permanently inflating a single model's consensus denominator. Clips whose chart robustly extends beyond the video frame — `chartSpansBeyondFrame`, 3rd-lowest-to-3rd-highest star coordinate beyond 1.25× the frame on either axis, so a lone mis-tracked outlier cannot trigger it — are now identified per time window and the labels merged; everything else takes the single whole-chart solve exactly as before, and if no window solves the whole-chart solve is still tried (*"no window solved - trying the whole chart"*). Windows are cut at "walls" — blur bursts break every track at once, splitting the chart into two drift regimes, and a window straddling a wall generates zero correct-field quad hypotheses (measured: solving windows ride on exactly one viable quad each; the straddling window had none). `detectTrackWalls` bins the identify-eligible tracks' observation-span starts and ends into 20-frame bins, flags bins holding at least max(4, 3× median), and merges adjacent flagged bins at their mass-weighted centre; walls move between analyses of the same clip (~80 frames between the two captured runs), so boundaries come from the run at hand, never fixed frames. `planIdentifyWindows` cuts at the walls and splits long spans into 220-frame windows overlapping by at least half (`STAR_WINDOW_DEFAULTS`, parameter-swept: any width in [160, 220] labels 100–106 of 123 with a clean audit; ≥300 breaks the rigid-fit assumption and collapses to 71 with outright mislabels). A track joins a window by its *actual* observed frames (new `obsF` on the identify set — tracks are gappy, and span-based membership admits stars a window barely saw), needing ≥15 in-window observations; a window under 8 stars is skipped. Each window's solve bounds come from where the video actually looked during it (the frame rectangle's corners taken back through the inverse per-frame similarities, unioned with the member stars), never the frame-0 rectangle, and each window runs the ordinary `solveField` tier cascade with every gate applying. `quarantineWindows` then rejects windows contradicting the consensus: windows pair when they label ≥3 of the same tracks, a pair is compatible when agreements outnumber disagreements, the largest connected component of compatible windows is the chain (needs two windows — a lone disagreeing pair is never arbitrated), and a window conflicting with any chain member is quarantined. This catches what per-window gates cannot: a wide-tier hypothesis once passed every gate with a wholly wrong field and would have shipped five labels up to 134° wrong, two of them on tracks no other window matched — but 13 of its 13 labels shared with neighbours disagreed. `mergeWindowLabels` decides one label per track lexicographically — most in-window observations first, then residual normalised by that window's own verification tolerance (`tolPx`, newly returned on the solve result, since it scales with field width and residuals only compare across solves through it) — never a weighted score and never a vote: correlated windows repeating one fragment mislabel would outvote the single window that had it right, while the coverage-first rule resolved every measured cross-window disagreement correctly. Cross-window disagreements are recorded in a returned `disputes` list rather than voted away (data-level only; not currently surfaced in the UI). Validated on two independent captures of the same clip: 100/123 labeled (from 42) with a 25/25 per-label audit on the healthy capture; on a degraded capture whose full chart does not solve at all, the one healthy window still labels Vega + 27 with a clean audit, where the single-model path delivers nothing. The status line reports *"matching window k/n"* during the run and *"identified N/M stars in S/W windows"* after, appending the calibrated frame ranges when coverage is partial and *"zoom varies across the pan"* when the surviving windows' plate scales spread by more than 2%.
- **Sync Camera follows windowed solves per frame, bridges uncalibrated stretches, and bakes a per-frame FOV** (`df470bdc`; `starTrackPose`, `CNodeControllerStarTrack`, `attachStarTrackCamera`, `windowVfovDegAt` in `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`/`StarIdentify.js`; *Sync Camera* in **Video → Star Tracker**). Each surviving window calibrates its own stretch of the chart, so the pose comes from the window(s) covering the frame; in overlaps the poses are blended as unit vectors with triangular weights (distance to the window edge), fading each model in from zero so the camera path stays continuous across every boundary, and a near-cancelling blend (the windows disagree wildly) refuses rather than emitting a meaningless average. Frames no surviving window covers extrapolate from the flanking calibrated windows weighted by proximity — refusing them entirely was tried and punishes exactly the honest case of a clip whose blurred middle broke the chart — except when an interior gap's two flanks disagree by more than 5°, which refuses rather than steering the camera through a fictitious average; the sync status discloses the bridging (*"camera synced - frames a–b, c–d calibrated, the rest approximate"*), and when the flanks disagree the bake refuses with *"identify calibrated frames … only, and the calibrated stretches disagree - cannot bridge the gap"*. The FOV is baked per frame into a new serialized `vfovTrack` (the scalar `vfovDeg` remains the fallback), blended across overlaps with the same weights as the pose via `windowVfovDegAt`, with uncovered frames taking the nearest calibrated window's plate scale — a zoom-during-pan clip has no single plate scale, and baking one window's constant would render the sky at the wrong framing everywhere else. `attachStarTrackCamera` now fills the *Star Track* option of `fovSwitch` (`starTrackFOV` node) with the per-frame array instead of a constant.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed re-identification leaving a synced camera split across two solves** (`df470bdc`; `refreshSyncedCamera` in `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js`). A previously-synced camera drives from its *baked* pose track, but re-running identification (say, after toggling stars off) only refreshed the live `starTrackFOV` array: the heading and the serialized `vfovDeg` stayed on the previous solve, so zoom and heading came from two different solves in the live session, and a save then froze the stale pair for every reload. Re-identification now re-bakes the controller whole (`bakeFrom` + `attachStarTrackCamera`) for both the windowed and single-chart paths; when the new solve cannot bake (a windowed identify with partial coverage whose flanks disagree), the old bake is left intact rather than half-updated, and pressing *Sync Camera* explains why.
- **Fixed two wrong-field acceptance paths in the solver, found while stress-testing the pan windows** (`df470bdc`; `finishSolve` in `src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`). First, a round-0 rematch collapse now disqualifies the candidate (`rej.rematchCollapse`): a first refinement rematch that cannot re-find even half the provisional matches under its own refit is not a failed refinement to roll back from — it is the provisional count confessing to being chance. Both wrong-field acceptances measured on the Giddierone pan windows worked exactly this way: a dense wide-tier projection scraped past the gates, the rematch collapsed 26→5 and 25→8, and the rollback let the final gate judge the unrefined arithmetic. Disqualifying the candidate (not the solve — the caller tries the runners-up) closes that path; a genuine field re-found its matches in every healthy solve of both captured runs. This check alone now blocks the original 2.116.0 southern-sky impostor even with the chance gate disabled — the control test flipped from documenting the acceptance to asserting rejection (its rematch re-found 1 of 44). Second, a final judged on provisional arithmetic alone — no refinement round ever recommitted the match set (`committedAny`) — must clear the chance bar with margin (+2 over max(`chanceMarginMin`, `chanceSigmas`·√expected)) rather than by a fraction of a match, which is precisely how the measured wide-tier impostors survived (clearances of 0.34 and 0.46 matches; `rej.provisionalFinalMargin`).
