## Version 2.116.1 (2026-08-04)

### Improvements
- **Eclipse Path geometry is cached, and re-clamps on elevation and zoom changes** (`89a9f404`, re-measured in `4d06920f`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; *Eclipse Path* in **Show → Celestial**). `update()` calls `rebuild()` every frame, and 2.116.0 dropped the path lines along with everything else in `removeCircles()` each time, so the whole terrain-clamped polyline was rebuilt at frame rate — ~13,000 clamped points at the new 32× subdivision, which would have been ~20 ms/frame. `removePathLines()` is now split out of `removeCircles()` (the circles depend on the current instant; the path depends only on the eclipse and the ground under it), and the built geometry is keyed in `_pathGeomKey` as `path.key + ":" + clearance`, so `buildEclipsePath` returns immediately when nothing relevant has changed. The key is cleared by an `elevationChanged` listener registered in the constructor and removed in `dispose()` — the lines are terrain-clamped, so they go stale as elevation tiles stream in — and it changes when the camera crosses a ground-clearance octave (see the buried-lines fix below). Every `rebuild()` early-out (`!visible`, `!showEclipsePath`, no `Globals.moonPos`/`fromSun`, Moon within 100 km, no eclipse within 24 h) now calls `removePathLines()` explicitly, because keeping lines across frames means nothing else removes them. `_pathCache` (the swept path itself) survives all of this, as before. Measured per frame: 2.1 ms in 2.116.0 → 0.94 ms (`89a9f404`) → 0.80 ms (`4d06920f`). The sweep itself is 9 ms (`89a9f404`) and 29 ms (`4d06920f`), once per eclipse and behind the cache; a worker is not warranted at 29 ms, and pre-serialised path assets are not either, since Sitrec takes an arbitrary date and finds whatever eclipse is within 24 h — an asset set would have to cover every eclipse or silently fall back.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed the limits of totality ending ~290 km short of the published maps** (`4d06920f`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; *Eclipse Path* in **Show → Celestial**). For 2026-08-12 both limits stopped near the Spanish coast instead of running out past the Balearics — not a thin tail, since the corridor is still ~300 km wide there, so Mallorca (the subject of the sitch this was found on) rendered sitting on the terminal closure rather than in the middle of the path. The cause was the question being asked. Taking the umbra outline at one instant and picking its extreme point ACROSS the track is exact mid-path and useless at the ends: the footprint is by then hundreds of km long and lying almost ALONG the track, so cross-track distance over its edge is nearly flat, the position of the maximum is decided by noise, and it jumps hundreds of km between neighbouring samples — measured, a 287 km discontinuity in the northern limit and 345 km in the southern. Rejecting those jumps by demanding a genuine turnover, which is what `89a9f404` shipped, is what ended the limits early instead. So the limits are no longer read off the shadow at all: `shadowGroundAt` and `limitPoints` are deleted, and each limit is found by asking a GROUND POINT directly. `totalityDepth(P, t)` returns the Moon's apparent radius less the Sun's less their separation, in radians — positive means the Sun is completely covered from there; `deepestNear(P, t0)` finds that point's deepest moment with a 20-iteration ternary search over ±5 min (depth is smooth and single-peaked, so no derivatives are needed); `seesTotality` reports both that verdict and the Sun's altitude there, deliberately kept apart because the first bounds the corridor sideways and the second bounds it lengthways; and `limitEdge` bisects across the track for where the verdict changes — a warm-started seed (`seedN`/`seedS` carried from the previous sample, falling back to a 25 km scan across ±500 km), then 14 steps from 500 km down to 30 m. There is no extremum anywhere in that question, so neither failure mode exists. Two supporting pieces. `buildEphemeris(key)` caches Sun and Moon ECEF positions per eclipse at 60 s over ±2.5 h and `ephemAt` reads them back QUADRATICALLY into preallocated scratch vectors (`_vSun`/`_vMoon`/`_vUp`, since the inner loop runs a few hundred thousand times and must not allocate): the fast-moving thing is not either body but the ECEF frame turning under them at 15°/h, and a parabola through three samples of that is good to ~2 m against ~100 m for a straight line, which is what makes a 60 s grid enough — ~0.09 µs per evaluation against ~8 µs for a fresh ephemeris pair. And `axisPointAt(t, allowMiss)` replaces `shadowCenterAt` inside the sweep, with the coarse pass narrowed from ±4 h to ±2.5 h to match the ephemeris grid. WHERE A LIMIT ENDS is decided afterwards rather than sample by sample (`trimLimit`), and this took two goes: the Sun's altitude at the edge sits within a tenth of a degree of zero for the whole last stretch — it IS the sunset curve, so of course it does — and wobbles across the sign, so the first negative ends nothing; and past the true end the reference point the probe measures from stalls and retreats, so the edge doubles back over itself and a gate cannot see it should have stopped either. Each limit is therefore collected whole, cut to its furthest points along track by RUNNING TOTAL of advance (not first sign change — near the ends the samples are seconds apart and real motion is a km or two), then trimmed for daylight, which only ever removes a point or two because the tips land on the sunset curve by themselves, at +0.12° and −0.12°. Verified against `Astronomy.SearchLocalSolarEclipse`, an entirely independent implementation: corridor WIDTHS agree to within 1 km at the longitudes tested (327/327, 310/311, 299/299 km), and the north limit now runs to lon 5.98 and the south to 4.38, from 3.58 and 1.05. A city test settles it past any interpolation error — Madrid is NOT total, missing by 1.3″ of angular margin, and Barcelona is NOT total by 6.0″, while Palma (+28.6″), Valencia (+7.1″), Ibiza (+8.6″) and Mahón (+10.1″) are: six for six against astronomy-engine, including both hairline misses. **Nothing here corrected an accuracy defect beyond the path's length.** An earlier draft of the commit message claimed a 21 km offset against astronomy-engine; that was an error in the COMPARISON, not in the shadow. Path points were being read as GEOCENTRIC latitude and compared against `Observer()`, which takes GEODETIC; the two differ by at most 0.19° — 21 km — and the difference is flat across 37–44°, hence an apparently rigid, longitude-independent offset that left corridor width untouched, since a constant latitude bias cancels in a difference. Converted properly (tan φ_gd = tan φ_gc · a²/b²) the offset is 0.0–0.1 km at every longitude tested, and nothing in the drawing path ever carried a latitude at all: the lines are built from ECEF vectors and `sunAltitude` already uses the true ellipsoid normal, which is geodetic up. Aberration was re-checked on that clean baseline — `aberration=true` agrees to ~0 km and `aberration=false` is ~18 km out, so the existing setting is right rather than merely the better of two poor options.
- **Fixed the ends of the Eclipse Path crossing over themselves, leaping in long straight lines, and stopping in open water** (`89a9f404`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`). Three separate causes, none of them the one it looked like. STEPPED IN TIME: `computeEclipsePath` sampled a fixed ±4 h / 2 min grid, but the shadow's ground speed diverges as the axis flattens towards the limb, so 2 minutes is ~150 km of track over Spain and ~525 km over the Balearics — the most curved part of the whole path drawn as a single straight chord. The coarse grid now only BRACKETS the eclipse; `bisect` pins first and last contact to `EDGE_TOL_MS` = 1 s, and `split` then places samples by GROUND distance, recursing on any interval longer than `MAX_STEP_M` = 80 km to `MAX_DEPTH` = 8 (~0.5 s at the ends). LIMITS READ OFF A CLIPPED RING: near the ends the footprint hangs off the limb and the umbra ring is an open arc, so the extreme among the surviving points is wherever the arc was CUT — a point on the terminator, not an edge of the shadow — which is what crossed the two gold limits over each other. `shadowGroundAt` was changed to return the ring SPARSE (one entry per position angle, `null` where that cone generator misses the Earth) plus an `at(theta)` that re-traces a single generator anywhere, and `limitPoints` required a genuine local turnover (`d[i] >=` both neighbours, both of which must exist) and refined the winner sub-grid with a parabola through it and its two neighbours, since half a step of position angle — 3.75° at 48 segments — is tens of km ALONG track near the ends, a visible stair-step. **Both functions were superseded within this same release**: `4d06920f` deleted `shadowGroundAt` and `limitPoints` outright, so neither exists at 2.116.1; the mechanism is recorded here because the ill-conditioning it describes is the whole reason the limits are no longer read off the shadow. STOPPED AT THE AXIS: the umbra is ~100 km across, so it goes on standing on the Earth after its AXIS has left — at 2026-08-12 the last stretch of the corridor happens entirely then. `extend()` now walks on from each end in 5 s steps for up to 5 minutes (`EXT_STEP_MS` / `EXT_SPAN_MS`, bounded by the ephemeris window), using `nearestSurfacePoint` — where the axis comes closest to the ellipsoid, the same construction as `intersectEllipsoid` continued past tangency, and exact at tangency — purely as a reference to measure cross-track offsets from. Those samples carry their travel direction IN rather than differencing one out, because that reference point stalls and then retreats once the axis is past, and differencing it reverses travel mid-extension, which flips cross-track and swaps north for south partway along. They also contribute no centreline point (`if (s.axisHit)`), since with no axis intersection there is no centre — which is why the centreline is the SHORTEST of the three lines at the ends rather than the longest. In the same pass the old `samples[i + 1] ?? samples[i - 1]` fallback was replaced by a central difference that is always forward in time: at the last sample the fallback reversed the travel direction, swapping north for south on the one sample that ends the path. Finally the corridor is CLOSED at each end: `capBetween` takes the two limits' end points and `addPathLine` draws that chord in gold, while `clipToCaps` cuts the centreline against the plane through each closure and the Earth's centre, interpolating the crossing rather than snapping to a sample (samples are up to 80 km apart there). The closure is deliberately a chord between the LIMITS and not routed through the end of the centreline: the centreline runs on to axis tangency, which is later than either limit ends, so routing through it puts a ~90 km kink in the closure. After `4d06920f` each limit ends on the sunset curve by construction, so the closure is a short arc of the terminator — a few hundred km of great circle, which is what `groundLineBetween` traces between two points to within a couple of km.
- **Fixed the eclipse path and the shadow outlines breaking up into dashes wherever they crossed land** (`89a9f404`; `groundClearance()`, `groundLineBetween`, `addPathLine`, `buildSegmentedCone`, `rebuild()`). It was not resolution: line vertices were quadrupled first (`addPathLine`'s `SUB` 8 → 32, `groundLineBetween`'s default `samples` 40 → 160, and the centre segment's 4 → 16) and the dashes survived that unchanged at 550 m vertex spacing. The line was BURIED. The elevation map `clampAboveGround` reads is FINER than the terrain MESH rendered at map scale, so the coarse mesh stands above the fine clamp height and swallows a line held only 100 m up — the giveaway being that it broke the instant it crossed onto land and stayed solid over the Bay of Biscay. The mesh's error against the real ground is a screen-space budget, so it grows with viewing distance and the clearance has to grow with it: `groundClearance()` returns a thousandth of the main camera's altitude — about a pixel at any zoom, enough to sit on top of the mesh and too little to read as floating — floored at 100 m, capped at 20 km, and quantised in octaves so zooming rebuilds the cached path geometry about ten times over the whole range rather than continuously. It is threaded through every ground-clamped line the node draws: the eclipse path and its caps, the centre cross, the umbra and penumbra ground outlines, and the cone bases in `buildSegmentedCone`, so they all lift together.
- **Fixed the *Moon Shadow Center* along-track line being a straight chord instead of the real track** (`7d8fbf0a`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; *Moon Shadow Center* in **Show → Celestial**). The line through the shadow centre was drawn straight along the direction of travel — correct to first order, and visibly wrong against the Eclipse Path's real curve right next to it. It is now sampled from the shadow axis at other times, exactly as the path is, so there is one definition of where the shadow lands rather than two that can disagree. `shadowTravelDir` returns `{dir, speed}` instead of a bare direction (from the same 30 s finite difference), the axis/ellipsoid intersection at an arbitrary time is factored out into `shadowCenterAt(date)`, and the new `centerPathSegment(date, travel, loD, hiD)` samples 24 points over `t = extent / speed` — the along-track extent through the umbra is already known in metres, so the time span to cover is a division rather than a search, with no stepping until a sample leaves the shadow — joining consecutive pairs with `groundLineBetween(..., 16)`. `spanAlong` becomes `extentAlong`, returning the scalar `{loD, hiD}` rather than endpoints, so the along-track case can rebuild its span in time while the cross-track case still builds a straight chord out from the centre — which is correct, since that one IS a chord through a footprint. The along-track segment is skipped entirely when `showEclipsePath` is on, because that path already contains it and drawing both just doubles a line onto itself; the cross-track line is drawn either way.
- **Fixed the Sun rendering as a hard yellow disc inside its own white glare** (`7d8fbf0a`; `src/nodes/CPlanets.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeAtmosphericOptics.js`). Three places carried a warm tint and all three are now neutral. `CPlanets._createSunMaterial`'s `uColor` was `Vector3(1.0, 0.9490, 0.4784)` — `0xfff27a`, carried over from the `MeshBasicMaterial` that preceded the per-vertex refraction `ShaderMaterial` — and is now `(1, 1, 1)`; this is the one that colours the drawn disc, via `_createSunDisk` for both the night scene and its day-sky copy. The sun-glare gradient in `CNodeAtmosphericOptics._buildSunGlare` returned `[b, b * 0.96, b * 0.86]` and now returns `[b, b, b]`. And `CPlanets.planetColors[0]` went from `"#FFFF40"` to `"#FFFFFF"`. The glare tint failed for a second reason worth recording: the glow is drawn additively, so the red channel saturates first in the core and the green/blue shortfall only shows up where the glare is brightest — inside the Sun — with the disc's own yellow sitting in the middle of it and NARROWER than the glare, because the drawn core is smaller than its quad. Together they read as a small yellow dot inside the Sun rather than as the Sun. **One correction to the commit message**: `planetColors[0]` is not what coloured the disc. The Sun branch of `addPlanets` builds a mesh with `_createSunMaterial` and never applies the table colour to its material; the entry is only stored as `planetSprites["Sun"].color`, which `CNodeDisplaySkyOverlay` uses for the "Sun" name label and `CNodeDisplayNightSky.addCelestialArrow` uses for the *Sun Vector* arrow (**Show → Celestial**). So that one line whitens the label and the arrow, and the disc is fixed by `uColor`. The physics behind all three: the photosphere is very nearly white, and the warmth of a low Sun comes from the air it shines through, which the atmosphere and refraction paths already put in the frame.
- **Fixed *No Lighting in Main View* still going dark during a solar eclipse** (`7d8fbf0a`; `src/nodes/CNodeLighting.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeSunlight.js`; *No Lighting in Main View* in **Lighting**). That switch flattens the main view to pure ambient (`ambientIntensity = 1`, `sunIntensity = 0`) so the geometry can be read, and an eclipse dimming that flat light is exactly what the switch exists to defeat. `CNodeLighting.recalculate(isMain)` now forwards `sunNode.suppressEclipse = isMain && this.noMainLighting` alongside the other per-pass flags; because `recalculate` runs per render pass, it is set only for the main view's pass, so the look view keeps its eclipse lighting. It is honoured inside `CNodeSunlight.calculateEclipseLightFactor` as an early `return NO_ECLIPSE` rather than at the call sites, because all three consumers read the eclipse through that one function: the direct sun and ambient in `calculateSunlight`, the sky brightness in `calculateSkyBrightness` (and through `calculateEclipseSkyFactor` the atmosphere-shader path in `CNodeView3D.populateAtmosphereRayUniforms`), and the 360° warm horizon glow in `calculateSkyColor`. Only the LIGHTING is suppressed — `CNodeEclipse`'s visuals (the Moon's silhouette on the Sun, corona, prominences, beads and diamond ring) still draw in the main view.

## Version 2.116.0 (2026-08-04)

### New Features
- **Eclipse Path** (`2a1b82cd`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; `showEclipsePath`, *Eclipse Path* in **Show → Celestial** — the node's `gui` is `celestialGUI`, a folder of `guiShowHide` — default off, `addSimpleSerial`). Draws the ground track of any solar eclipse whose peak is within 24 h of `GlobalDateTimeNode.dateNow`: the umbra's northern and southern limits (`path.umbraN` / `path.umbraS`) in gold via the existing `umbraMaterial` (`0xFFD700`) and the centreline (`path.centerLine`) in white via the new `centerMaterial` (`0xFFFFFF`, width 1.5). `findEclipseWithin24h` steps back a full day before calling `Astronomy.SearchGlobalSolarEclipse` — that search only looks forward, so an eclipse that peaked this morning would otherwise be missed — then walks with `NextGlobalSolarEclipse` under a 4-iteration guard. The path is SWEPT, not derived from Besselian elements: `computeEclipsePath` samples `shadowGroundAt` over ±240 min at 2 min steps and keeps only samples where the shadow axis actually intersects the ellipsoid (46 for 2026-08-12), and `shadowGroundAt` reuses the same cone-to-ellipsoid intersection `rebuild()` already performs, just at other times — so there is one definition of where the shadow lands rather than two that can disagree. Limits are the cross-track extremes of each umbra ring, and cross-track needs the direction of travel, which needs the NEXT sample's centre; hence the two-pass loop over `samples`. Results are cached in `_pathCache` keyed on the eclipse peak time because `update()` calls `rebuild()` every frame — 8.4 ms to build against 2.1 ms cached — and `disposeGeometry` disposes `pathLines` while deliberately preserving `_pathCache`, since the sweep is still valid for the same eclipse. `addPathLine` subdivides each ~150 km two-minute segment 8 ways through `groundLineBetween` and re-projects every interpolated point onto the ellipsoid before `clampAboveGround`; without that the straight chords sink below the surface and the path renders as a row of dashes. Penumbra path limits are neither drawn nor computed (`shadowGroundAt` traces only the umbra ring): thousands of km across, their edges sweep most of a hemisphere and read as clutter, and omitting them halves the sweep's ray casts.
- **Moon Shadow Center** (`2a1b82cd`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; `showShadowCenter`, *Moon Shadow Center* in **Show → Celestial**, default off, `addSimpleSerial`). Draws a cross ON the ground through `axisHit` — the point where the shadow axis meets the ellipsoid — spanning the umbra's own footprint and terrain-clamped like the shadow outline, via `groundLineBetween` (each sample pushed back out to the ellipsoid radius along its own direction, then `clampAboveGround(surface, 100)`). Axes are ALONG-TRACK and CROSS-TRACK from `shadowTravelDir`, a 30 s finite difference of the axis/ellipsoid intersection flattened into the local horizontal — not from the outline's shape. Two earlier approaches were wrong and are worth recording: deriving the axes from the outline's widest separation flickered badly once the shadow ran off the limb, because the footprint is then an open arc and the farthest-apart pair jumps between unrelated chords frame to frame; and joining the two extreme outline points yields a tilted chord rather than an axis, since on an ellipse those points are tangents offset sideways. `spanAlong` therefore takes only the scalar extent along each fixed axis and rebuilds the endpoints from the centre, which fixes both and puts one line straight down the centreline. `rebuild()` now retains the pre-clamp MSL umbra ring in `umbraGroundMSL` so the cross derives its extent from the same points the ring is drawn from, and only builds when `axisHit` is non-null (the shadow actually reaches the Earth). **This REPLACES the *Show Moon Center* look-view crosshair shipped in 2.115.0, which is removed**: `showMoonCenter`, `drawMoonCenter()` and `MOON_CENTER_CROSSHAIR_PX` are all deleted from `src/nodes/CNodeDisplaySkyOverlay.js`, along with its GUI control and `addSimpleSerial`. The extracted `buildSkyCamera()` helper from that work stays and is still used by `renderStarNames`. Note the two features mark different things — the old one marked the Moon's refracted centre on screen in the look view; this one marks the shadow's centre on the ground in the main view — so a sitch saved in 2.115.0 with *Show Moon Center* ticked simply loses that setting.
- **Ground-derived observer placement in the client API** (`06ccb9b0`; `src/CSitrecAPI.js`). Two new entries in `this.api`, both advertised to the chatbot's tool builder (neither sets `llmCallable: false`, so `getLLMDocumentation` includes them) and both reachable from `window.sitrecAPI` for scripting/MCP. `getGroundAltitude(lat, lon)` — both optional, defaulting to `fixedCameraPosition`'s `_LLA` — returns `{success, lat, lon, altHAE, altMSL, geoidOffset, source}`. `setCameraToEyeLevel(eyeHeight)` (default 1.6 m) calls it for the camera's own lat/lon and does `camera.setLLA(lat, lon, ground.altMSL + eye)`; `CNodePositionLLA.setLLA` takes MSL (its `recalculate` adds `meanSeaLevelOffset` before `LLAToECEF`), which is why `groundAltitudeAt` reports both data. The shared helper `groundAltitudeAt` casts straight down from `LLAToECEF(lat, lon, 100000)` along `getLocalUpVector(high).negate()` — 100 km clears the tallest tile geometry, and running along the ellipsoid normal makes the hit land directly beneath the point rather than on a slanted neighbour — through `raycastLocalGround` (`src/raycastGround.js`), handing it `ViewMan.get("lookView")?.camera ?? ViewMan.get("mainView")?.camera` because that function widens the raycaster's layer mask to the camera's and the Google tile meshes sit on the MAIN/LOOK layers; pass no camera and the tiles are skipped entirely. `raycastLocalGround` tests the `buildings3DTiles` group first and takes the nearest hit overall, except that a hidden basemap — which is exactly what happens under Google Photorealistic 3D tiles — is consulted only when the tiles miss, so in the case that matters the tile surface wins and the elevation map is the fallback. `altitudeHAE(hit.point)` gives HAE and `meanSeaLevelOffset(lat, lon)` converts to MSL. A miss on both returns `source: "ellipsoid-fallback"` (from `hit.isTerrain === false`) rather than passing the bare ellipsoid off as ground — outside tile coverage, or before tiles stream in, there is no answer and the caller should know it. This exists because a photograph's EXIF altitude is not interpretable and the error is not a correctable bias: measured, a Samsung phone wrote height above the ELLIPSOID while tagging it "Above Sea Level" (105 m read as MSL → 144.7 m HAE, 44.9 m in the air over a residential street; read as HAE → 5.2 m up, a balcony — correct), while a Nikon Z 9 wrote true MSL (53 m read as MSL → 103.5 m HAE, 15.0 m up on a clifftop — correct; read as HAE → 35 m underground). Each rule is catastrophic on the other photograph. The horizontal GPS is reliable, so deriving altitude from the ground beneath that position uses only the trustworthy half and cannot produce an impossible observer. The tile surface rather than the elevation map matters for the same reason: a 30 m grid smooths away the cliffs and buildings people stand on to photograph a distant horizon — at Dunnottar's cliff edge the tiles give 88.5 m HAE against the elevation map's 81.1 m, the difference between a valid observer and one buried in the hillside. Nothing in the import path changed: dropping a photo still does not place the camera by itself, this is a call you (or the assistant) make. The commit also gitignores `/alignment-tests/`, a local-only 155 MB set of third-party reference photographs with known camera position and time used to check refraction and celestial positions against real images.

### Improvements
- **The Moon's shadow is drawn in the main view only** (`2a1b82cd`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; *Show Moon's Shadow* in **Show → Celestial**). `v.layers ??=` changed from `LAYER.MASK_LOOKRENDER` to `LAYER.MASK_MAIN`. The old default was wrong twice over: it named the look view, and because `MASK_LOOKRENDER = MASK_WORLD | MASK_LOOK | MASK_TARGET` includes `MASK_WORLD` — which `MASK_MAINRENDER` also carries — the shadow was actually drawn by BOTH cameras. So it was neither look-only nor main-only; it was everywhere, under a name suggesting otherwise. `MASK_MAIN` appears only in `MASK_MAINRENDER`, making it the one mask that means what it says. The cones stretch hundreds of thousands of km and the ground outlines tens of km: geometry for looking AT the Earth from outside, which in the look view is either invisible or a wall of colour across the sky.
- **The penumbra cone is off by default, behind its own switch** (`2a1b82cd`; `showPenumbraCone`, *Show Moon Penumbra* in **Show → Celestial**, default off, `addSimpleSerial`). `rebuild()` now calls `buildPenumbraCone` only when the flag is set. The penumbra diverges from the Moon and encloses the umbra, so at any useful zoom it laid a translucent wash (`opacity: 0.1`, `depthTest: false`) over the very thing the umbra cone exists to show — visible in the annular fast-regression baseline, where it was tinting the whole sky and the stars with it. **This gates the outer CONE only**: the penumbra's ground OUTLINE (`penumbraLine`, orange `0xFFA500`) is built in a separate ungated block and is still drawn whenever the shadow is, since that is what a partial-eclipse footprint is read off. Being a default change it moved two eclipse fast-regression baselines, which the commit regenerated. All three new controls here (*Show Moon Penumbra*, *Moon Shadow Center*, *Eclipse Path*) only draw when *Show Moon's Shadow* is on, because `update()` calls `rebuild()` solely when `this.visible`; and all three use hardcoded English labels with no i18n keys, so they are outstanding for translation, as the *Solar Eclipse* and *Atmospheric Optics (Halos)* folders already were.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed EXIF Orientation being applied twice, so portrait phone photos imported a quarter-turn out with their width and height swapped** (`66fe46f6`; new `src/imageOrientation.js`, `src/CVideoImageData.js`, comment correction in `src/HEICUtils.js`). The stale assumption was stated outright in `HEICUtils`' header — "JPEG, where `new Image()` does not auto-rotate and the EXIF rotation IS applied downstream by `CVideoImageData`". That was true once. Browsers have honoured EXIF Orientation on decode since Chrome 81 / Safari 13.1, because `image-orientation: from-image` is the INITIAL value of that CSS property and so applies even to a detached `new Image()`; `CVideoImageData` then turned the pixels again. Measured on a Berlin Funkturm frame: EXIF Orientation 6, stored 4000×3000, decoded by the browser as 3000×4000, rotated by Sitrec back to 4000×3000, mast on its side. Rather than swap one assumption for another, `decoderAppliedOrientation(decoded, meta)` measures: EXIF records the STORED dimensions, so a decoded image whose `width`/`height` come back swapped relative to `exifImageWidth`/`exifImageHeight` has already been turned. That is decisive for 90° and 270°; for 180°, a square image, or unusable dimensions the axes do not swap and there is nothing to measure, so the decoder is trusted — the safe direction, since being wrong the other way reinstates the double rotation. `residualExifRotation(decoded, meta)` returns the EXIF angle only when the decoder left the pixels as stored, and `CVideoImageData`'s constructor now assigns `this.metadataRotation` from it instead of taking `importMetadata.image.rotationDegrees` at face value. Half-turn (Orientation 3) photos were affected too — browser 180° plus Sitrec 180° left them upside down — and are fixed by the same change. The new module is deliberately dependency-free so it can be unit-tested without the app graph (`EXIFUtils` pulls in `threeExt`, which Jest cannot load); `tests/imageOrientation.test.js`, 10 tests. HEIC is unaffected: libheif applies the irot/imir boxes while decoding and the callers already call `stripImageRotationMetadata`, which sets `rotationDegrees = 0`.
- **Fixed dropped photographs setting the sim time in the viewer's timezone rather than the camera's** (`4ae21211`; new `src/exifCaptureTime.js`, `src/EXIFUtils.js`). EXIF `DateTimeOriginal` carries no zone, so `exifr` builds its `Date` by reading the wall-clock numbers as local time on whatever machine is running, and `extractJPEGImportMetadata` handed that straight to `capture.date` and thence to `setStartDateTime`. A Berlin moonrise at 19:49:28 +02:00 (17:49:28Z) opened on a US Pacific machine became 2026-04-02T02:49:28Z — nine hours out, Moon on the other side of the sky, and nothing about the scene looking wrong. `pickExifUtcOffset(raw)` now takes the first parseable of `OffsetTimeOriginal`, `OffsetTime`, `OffsetTimeDigitized`, and `applyExifUtcOffset` reinterprets the naive date at that offset. The recovery is exact because `exifr`'s misreading is invertible: it took the wall-clock as local, so the local getters hand those same numbers back whatever the machine timezone, and `Date.UTC(...) - minutes*60000` gives the true instant. `parseExifUtcOffset` accepts `"+02:00"`, `"+0200"`, `"Z"`, rejects anything past +14:00 (Kiritimati) as corrupt, and returns `null` — meaning "no zone information", not "UTC" — for absent or unparseable input. The metadata now carries `capture.utcOffset` and `capture.utcOffsetSource: "EXIF"`, and `applyImportedImageCaptureDateTime` logs `[EXIF] <file>: no OffsetTime tag — capture time assumed to be in this computer's timezone (<IANA zone>)` when the offset is missing, so the fallback is stated rather than presented as fact. Verified on two cameras from different hemispheres: Berlin +02:00 → 2026-04-01T17:49:28Z, and Dunnottar −04:00 → 2025-10-26T07:29:10Z — a Nikon left on US Eastern time while in Scotland, which is precisely why this keys off the recorded OFFSET and not the GPS location. `tests/exifCaptureTime.test.js`, 13 tests, dependency-free for the same reason as `imageOrientation`. Applies to HEIC drops as well, since `DragDropHandler` runs `extractJPEGImportMetadata` on every dropped image before the HEIC decode branch.
- **Fixed satellite names being destroyed when a dropped OMM CSV was imported** (`6a1a2b97` / merge `d87c2170`; `src/CFileManagerParse.js:762`). A `.csv` whose first line passes `isOMMCSV` is kept as RAW TEXT with `dataType = "tle"`, because `CTLEData` parses the text itself. The generic CSV branch further down then ran `parsedFile = parsedFile.slice(1)` to drop a header row — on a string, `slice(1)` removes the first CHARACTER, so `OBJECT_NAME` became `BJECT_NAME`, the column lookup missed, every satellite fell back to `"NORAD <number>"`, and name-based Starlink classification never fired. The guard is now `if (!(parsedFile instanceof CTrackFile) && Array.isArray(parsedFile))`. Only dropped `.csv` files were affected; the fetched CelesTrak/Space-Track feeds register as `.tle` (e.g. `starLink_current.tle` in `CSatellite.js`) and take the raw-decode path, which never reached this line.
- **Fixed star identification accepting a match count without regard to how dense the projection producing it was** (`0654ec99` / merge `eec423de`; `src/starTrack/StarIdentify.js`; reached from *Full Analysis* and *Identify Stars (catalog)* under **Video → Star Tracker**). A 671-frame pan of a clip whose true field is 15.6° around Cygnus/Lyra was identified as a 96° field at RA 160.5 / Dec −40.5 — far-southern sky, below the horizon from the camera site — claimed at 44/123 matched. The fraction gates were blind to projected-catalog density: the correct tier-1 solve refined 36 → 43 matches against a 142-star projection (~1.4 chance matches) and was rejected because `43 < 0.35 * 123 = 43.05`, short by five hundredths of a match; the solve then fell through to the wide phone-lens tier, where the impostor projected 3,495 catalog stars into the bounds — dense enough that coincidence alone matches ~30 of 123 image stars within the 6.1 px tolerance — and its 44 matches cleared the same bar. `projectAndMatch` now returns `expected` alongside `matches` and `nProjected`, computed from the projection those matches actually came from: `pChance = 1 - exp(-nProjected * π * tol² / area)` over the projection bounds, times the image-star count. The new `chanceOK(O, nMatches, expected)` requires `nMatches >= expected + max(chanceMarginMin, chanceSigmas * sqrt(expected))` with `chanceMarginMin: 5` and `chanceSigmas: 4` — deliberately generous at 4σ rather than 3, because thousands of hypotheses each get a shot at this gate and a per-test tail probability that looks safe in isolation is not safe across a sweep. It is enforced at the provisional stage in `verifyHypothesis` (new `rej.provisionalChance` diagnostic) and inside `consensusMet`, and `expected` now travels with the match set through `verifyHypothesis` → `finishSolve`, including the per-round rollback triple and `consensusDetail` (which also reports `chanceOK`), so no gate ever judges a match set against another projection's expectation. With the chance gate doing the discriminating, `strongMatchFraction` drops from 0.35 to 0.30 — on this clip the correct solve tops out at 34% matched, because the longer integration detects real stars fainter than anything the projection pools offer and they all sit in the denominator. The commit adds `tests/StarIdentifyLongPan.test.js` (5 tests) with `tests/fixtures/giddieronePanSegments.json`, two live captures of the same video differing only in the analysed In/Out window: a CONTROL test re-creates the old density-blind arithmetic and machine-checks that it still accepts the southern-sky impostor, and the rest pin the corrected long-segment solve, the unchanged short-segment Vega solve, and their agreement at the shared reference frame 1235.

## Version 2.115.0 (2026-08-04)

### New Features
- **Solar eclipse circumstances engine** (`cbdad5f7`; new `src/CEclipseCalc.js`). `getEclipseState(position, date)` returns the topocentric eclipse geometry for an arbitrary observer: `obscuration` (two-circle lens area of the Moon's disk over the Sun's, `sunDiskObscuration`), `lightFraction` (limb-darkened remaining photospheric flux, `eclipseLightFraction(O) = 1 - O + sin(2πO)/(4π)` — slope −0.5 at both ends and −1.5 mid-eclipse, so flux falls slower than area early and faster than area near totality), `exposedFrac` = `(separation + sunRad - moonRad)/sunRad` (0 at second/third contact, negative through totality, 2 at first/fourth), plus `separation`, `sunRad`, `moonRad` and `ratio`. It calls `Astronomy.Equator(body, date, observer, false, true)` — the same flags and the same physical radii `CPlanets` uses for the rendered disks — so the lighting curve and the drawn limbs agree about the instant of contact. Away from an eclipse it returns the shared frozen `NO_ECLIPSE` object, a hard no-op that every consumer tests with `state.obscuration === 0`. Results are memoized on (time, ~1 km-quantized position) mirroring `getCelestialDirection`'s cache, because `CNodeSunlight` probes it several times per frame per view; the cache clears past 128 entries. Atmospheric refraction is deliberately omitted: both bodies sit within a solar diameter of each other, so differential refraction between their centres is a few arcseconds at worst, far below the ~1% obscuration resolution the lighting needs. `getEclipseState` asserts on a non-finite time — letting `undefined` leak through is how "the sky stayed bright through totality" originally hid (astronomy-engine threw, the `catch` silently returned `NO_ECLIPSE`), so the date defaulting belongs to the `CNodeSunlight` entry points.
- **Annular-aware visual gating** (`eclipseVisualGates` in `src/CEclipseCalc.js`). Kept as pure math outside the render node so the annular/total distinction is unit-testable against real ephemeris events. For total-capable geometry (`ratio > 1`) corona and prominences ramp in as the last ~3.5% sliver of photosphere vanishes, and beads/diamond live in a ±0.45%-of-radius window around `exposedFrac ≈ 0` — the tallest limb-roughness bump. For annular geometry (`ratio <= 1`) corona, prominences and the diamond ring are hard-zero forever, because the leftover photospheric ring stays blinding; beads fire only at the INTERNAL contacts via `annularGap = 2*(1 - ratio) - exposedFrac`, which is 0 there and grows to ≈0.046 at maximum annularity for the 2023 Albuquerque event — far outside the ±0.006 bead window.
- **Eclipse visuals** (`cbdad5f7`; new `src/nodes/CNodeEclipse.js`, singleton node `"theEclipse"` created in `addNightSky`; *Solar Eclipse* folder under **Lighting**). Architecture mirrors `CNodeAtmosphericOptics` (`"theHalos"`): meshes live in `GlobalSunSkyScene`, drawn by `renderSky()` with the camera at the origin after the daytime sky quad, so the effects sit over the sky but are occluded by terrain and objects in the main pass; `CNodeView3D` re-calls `syncToObserver` per view (both the look-camera and main-camera render paths) so each view renders the eclipse for its own observer. Everything is analytic in a quad-local angular frame: two tessellated quads (`EXTENT = 8` Sun radii, `GRID = 40`, 1681 vertices) centred on the geometric Sun direction and refracted per-vertex on the CPU with `applyRefractionECI` and `refractionOptsFromUniforms()` — the same model the Sun/Moon disk shaders use — so the limbs stay aligned near the horizon. `darkMesh` (normal blending, `renderOrder` 3) paints the Moon's silhouette near-black only where it overlaps the photosphere, so the dark new Moon stays invisible against the sky off-disk exactly as in real partial-phase photographs. `glowMesh` (additive, `renderOrder` 4) carries the corona (angle-dependent streamers under an r² gaussian envelope, chosen over a windowing band because a band alone leaves a visible Mach contour), opaque prominences that locally suppress the corona behind them (`1/(1 + 6*promDensity)`, without which additive clipping bleaches them white) plus a chromosphere rim that flashes at contact, Baily's-beads glare and the four-point diamond-ring starburst positioned diametrically opposite the Moon's centre. The Moon's centre is placed in quad space through a GNOMONIC projection (divide by `moonDir·S`), matching the tan-space the vertices use, so the analytic mask agrees with the rendered disks to sub-milliarcsecond rather than the ~0.1″ a bare sine projection leaves. Bead structure comes from a deterministic lunar-limb roughness profile (`limbR`, sum of incommensurate cosines, ±0.4% of radius ≈ ±4″ — slightly exaggerated from the real ±2–3″ so beads read on screen, but small enough that the shallow Mallorca 2026 totality, with ~6″ of margin at peak, still covers them). There is no time-based animation anywhere: the whole node is deterministic per (date, observer), which regression capture requires. GUI controls are `enabled` (*Eclipse Effects*), `intensity` (*Intensity*), `corona` (*Corona*), `prominences` (*Prominences*), `beads` (*Baily's Beads / Diamond Ring*) and `affectLighting` (*Affect Lighting*), all in `addSimpleSerials`. Note that `affectLighting` is plumbed through module state (`setEclipseLightingEnabled` / `isEclipseLightingEnabled` in `CEclipseCalc`) rather than a node reference, so `CNodeSunlight` needs no dependency on the visuals node; `modDeserialize` re-pushes it. `syncToObserver` returns immediately with `group.visible = false` when `obscuration === 0` — nothing is computed or rebuilt outside an eclipse.
- **Obscuration-driven lighting** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CNodeSunlight.js`, `src/nodes/CNodeView3D.js`). `calculateEclipseLightFactor(position, date)` defaults the date to `GlobalDateTimeNode.dateNow` — callers such as `calculateSkyBrightness(position)` omit it, and without the default the eclipse silently no-ops on those paths. Direct sun scales linearly with the limb-darkened flux (`result.sunIntensity *= eclipse.lightFraction`); ambient falls more gently and is floored (`Math.max(lightFraction^0.6, 0.05)`) so totality reads as deep twilight rather than a black scene. `calculateEclipseSkyFactor` returns `Math.max(lightFraction^0.3, 0.22)` and is shared by `calculateSkyBrightness` and the sky-gradient path: the 0.3 exponent makes the sky LAG the direct light, because skylight scatters in from a wide region much of which is outside the umbra — at 90% obscuration the sky is dimmer but still clearly daytime, and stars only emerge in the final minute (star visibility rides `Globals.sunTotal`, which is `sunIntensity + ambientIntensity`). `calculateSkyColor` gains a 360° warm horizon ring — the classic all-round sunset of totality, from sunlit air beyond the shadow — ramping in as `lightFraction` falls from 0.05 to 0.005, with `glow = max(sunTotal, 0.28)` so it reads as a glow rather than haze. On the atmosphere-shader path `CNodeView3D.populateAtmosphereRayUniforms` now scales its fixed daylight blue-zenith lerp target (`_atmosphereBlueZenithScaled`) by the same sky factor; without that the gradient path stayed bright straight through totality.
- **Show Moon Center** (working-tree change to `src/nodes/CNodeDisplaySkyOverlay.js`; `showMoonCenter`, *Show Moon Center* in **Show → Celestial**, look view only, default off, `addSimpleSerial`). Draws a 20 px (`MOON_CENTER_CROSSHAIR_PX`) 1 px green `#00ff00` crosshair on the Moon's APPARENT centre. It reads `nightSky.planets.planetSprites["Moon"].equatorial`, which is the REFRACTED position — `CPlanets.updateMoonMesh` builds it with `applyRefractionECI` (`CPlanets.js:530`) and stores it at `:576` precisely so overlay labels track the visible disk, and `syncPlanetSpritesToObserver` re-runs per view so it reflects the rendering view's observer. The mesh itself is a different thing: `moonMesh.position` is set from `equatorialGeometric` (`CPlanets.js:552`) and bent per-vertex in the shader, so using the mesh position would miss the drawn disk by the entire refraction — about 1′ at 45° altitude and ~0.48° (most of a lunar diameter) at the horizon, per `refractionDeltaDeg` at the default 1010 hPa / 10 °C. The draw is placed BEFORE the `showStarNames`/`showSatelliteNames` early-out, because the crosshair is its own toggle and must not depend on either being on, and it gates on `pos.z` since points behind the camera project to plausible-looking x/y. The star-name camera setup was extracted into `buildSkyCamera()` (clone, `renderedFOV`, `zoom = 1`, position at the origin, aspect, `applyCameraOffset`, matrices) and is now shared by the crosshair and `renderStarNames`, so the two project through an identical camera instead of two copies of twelve lines. Behaviour-preserving — the extracted block is line-for-line the code it replaced, and the fast regression suite returned byte-identical diff pixel counts across the extraction, with the "Orion in Both views for Label Check" sitch (which exercises exactly this path) passing throughout.
- **Test coverage** (`tests/CEclipseCalc.test.js`, 21 tests). Pins C1–C4 contact times to within 500 ms of `Astronomy.SearchLocalSolarEclipse`'s own solution for the Mallorca 2026-08-12 total, checks the frozen-`NO_ECLIPSE` identity (`toBe`, not `toEqual`), the memo cache returning the same object, monotonicity of both obscuration and flux, the annular area cap, and sweeps the 2023 Albuquerque annular to confirm no corona/prominences/diamond ever fire and that beads appear only at the internal contacts.

### Improvements
- **Sun glare is independent of the halos master toggle and defaults on** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CNodeAtmosphericOptics.js`; *Sun Glare* in **Lighting → Atmospheric Optics (Halos)**). `sunGlare` flipped from `?? false` to `?? true`, and the gating changed from `this.enabled` to `anySun = this.enabled || this.sunGlare` in `update()`, `syncToObserver()` and the build path — the glare is forward-scattered light, not an ice-crystal optic, so it does not belong behind *Show Halos*. Every other Sun optic, the Moon optics and the Brocken build are now explicitly re-gated on `enabled` (including `_syncBrocken` and the `getCelestialDirection("Moon", …)` call, which is skipped entirely unless a Moon optic is on). **This is a visible default change for existing daytime sitches** — they now get a soft aureole around the Sun where they previously got nothing; untick *Sun Glare* for the old look. During an eclipse the glare dims linearly with the remaining photospheric flux: `syncToObserver` caches `_eclipseLight = getEclipseState(...).lightFraction`, a change of more than 0.001 counts as movement so the geometry rebuilds, and `_buildSunGlare` scales its base by it and early-outs below 0.001 — so the glare is gone at totality. Note that neither the *Solar Eclipse* nor the *Atmospheric Optics (Halos)* folder has i18n keys; both use hardcoded English labels, so both are outstanding for translation.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed the Moon's shadow cone being drawn off-position and undersized** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayMoonShadow.js`; *Show Moon's Shadow* in **Show → Celestial**). Three separate errors. (1) The shadow axis used `Globals.fromSun` — the GEOCENTRIC antisolar direction — instead of the Sun→Moon line (`moonCenter.sub(Globals.sunPos)`); they differ by the Moon's offset from the geocentre as seen from the Sun, about 9″ at the 2026-08-12 eclipse, displacing the umbra ellipse ~15 km along the ground, roughly a fifth of that eclipse's umbra width. (2) The cone half-angle came from the Sun's angular size alone (`atan(Rs/d)`), but the umbra converges at the rate the Sun's limb closes behind the Moon's, `tan(halfAngle) = (Rs − Rm)/d`, so `umbraTipDistance = d·Rm/(Rs − Rm)`; the old form put the tip 0.25% short, which — because Earth sits near the tip — made the 2026-08-12 umbra cross-section ~4 km (5%) too small. The penumbra now correspondingly diverges at `(Rs + Rm)/d`. (3) Cone generators started at the Moon's CENTRE; they now start at the Moon's limb at each position angle (`rayOrigins` in `buildSegmentedCone`, and the same treatment in both ground-outline loops), removing a Moon-radius of parallax worth 1–2 km of ground-track error at grazing incidence. `SUN_RADIUS` also moved to the IAU nominal 695,700 km.
- **Fixed Earth's shadow cone using a fixed Sun distance and slightly wrong cone angles** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayEarthShadow.js`; *Show Earth's Shadow* in **Show → Celestial**). `EARTH_SUN_DISTANCE` is now the live `Globals.sunPos.length()` (falling back to 1 AU), and the umbra length scales with it — the real distance varies ±1.7% over the year. The tip formulae changed the same way as the Moon's: `umbraTipDistance = Re·d/(Rs − Re)` and `penumbraTipDistance = −Re·d/(Rs + Re)` instead of the Sun's angular size alone, which had overstated the umbra's convergence by about 1%. `SUN_RADIUS` moved to 695,700 km here too.
- **Fixed a sitch preset for Earth's shadow being discarded on load** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CNodeDisplayNightSky.js:321`). The default guard tested the misspelled `Sit.showEathShadow`, which is always `undefined`, so it unconditionally wrote `Sit.showEarthShadow = false` before the node was created with `visible: Sit.showEarthShadow` — a sitch asking for the shadow got it hidden every time. Now reads the correctly-spelled property.
- **Fixed the rendered Sun disk using the pre-2015 solar radius** (`cbdad5f7`; `src/nodes/CPlanets.js:656`). `_getAngularDiameterRad("Sun", …)` now takes 695,700 km (IAU nominal) instead of 696,000 km, matching `CEclipseCalc.SUN_RADIUS_M` so the drawn limbs touch at the instant the computed contact times say they do. With the old value the computed contacts sat ~0.7 s off astronomy-engine's own eclipse solution and totality came out ~1.3 s short — outside the 0.5 s tolerance the new tests hold it to.

## Version 2.114.0 (2026-08-04)

### New Features
- **Point Track skips masked pixels when centring** (`36370c8f`; `src/CObjectTracking.js` `calculateWeightedCentroid`, `ObjectTracker.useMask`, i18n `tracking.useMask`; *Use Mask* in **Video → Point Track**, default on). All three centroid rules — bright, dark and colour — take a weighted average of the pixels inside the cursor, so a bright patch of masked ground drifting into the track radius does not merely add noise, it DRAGS the tracked point towards itself and the tracker walks off the object into the trees. The mask test is applied in the single ROI pass that serves all three rules, so they cannot disagree about what is off-limits. The `"videoMask"` node is resolved ONCE per pass rather than per pixel, and coordinates are rescaled into the mask canvas (`maskCanvas.width / imgWidth`) rather than indexed directly: the mask is in VIDEO pixels (invariant 2 in `CNodeMaskOverlay`) and the image being tracked need not be that size, so direct indexing would reject the wrong region on any capped decode. Default on, which changes nothing for anyone without a mask — and someone who has painted one has already said those pixels are not to be used.
- **Contextual Help folders, a sectioned Help menu, and eighteen newly reachable documentation pages** (`0b005576` and `36370c8f`; `src/docsRegistry.js`, `src/index.js`, `src/i18n/en.js`, `sitrecServer/chatbot.php`, `webpack.common.js`, `tests/docsRegistry.test.js`). Eight user-facing docs existed but were in neither the Help menu nor the AI assistant's list, including the only page explaining where to get flight data (`KMLDataSources.md`) and `Nimitz.md`; `36370c8f` had already added `Masking.md` (new) and `StarTracker.md` (existing, unregistered). `helpDocs` goes from 14 entries to 32. Nine pages are new: `Masking.md`, `Refraction.md`, `Terrain.md`, `Video.md`, `PointTrack.md`, `TraverseAnalysis.md`, `DefensibleAnalysis.md`, `KeyboardShortcuts.md`, `Glossary.md` — `DefensibleAnalysis.md` carries the verdict wordings, the four invalid uncertainty inversions and the sensitivity-sweep protocol, previously reachable only through the 221 KB changelog. Registry entries gain `section`, `menuId` and `role` fields. `DOC_SECTIONS` drives seven folders under **Help → Documentation** (*Start Here*, *Data and Tracks*, *The World*, *Video Tools*, *Analysis*, *Worked Examples*, *Advanced*), skipping any section with no docs; a second loop in `index.js` builds a *Help* folder at the top of each menu named by a `menuId`, reaching nine menus — **File**, **Video**, **Objects**, **Satellites**, **Terrain**, **Physics**, **Camera**, **Traverse**, **Contents**. `getHelpDocContent` in `chatbot.php` truncated AI-facing docs at 20000 chars, which hid two thirds of `TraverseMethods.md` — the entire Analyze/verdict half, from byte 43777 — with no notice to the model at all; the limit is now `AI_DOC_CHAR_LIMIT` = 60000, mirrored in `docsRegistry.js`, the notice tells the model its answer may be incomplete, the cut is `mb_substr` so a split multibyte sequence cannot make `json_encode` fail outright, and `TraverseMethods.md` is split at its natural seam into `TraverseMethods.md` + `TraverseAnalysis.md` so both fit. Docs stay FLAT in `docs/` — `chatbot.php`'s name regex, webpack's hard-coded stylesheet path and `chatDocName()` all break on subfolders. `tests/docsRegistry.test.js` is the anti-drift guard: every entry resolves to a real file, every label key resolves, no orphaned help strings, README matches the registry, and no AI-facing doc exceeds the truncation limit — README and the registry had ALREADY drifted, the exact failure the registry exists to prevent.

### Improvements
- **Refraction is on by default** (`REFRACTION_DEFAULTS.enabled` false → true in `src/atmosphere/refraction.js`; `docs/Refraction.md`). That one constant is the fallback every consumer reads — `CPlanets` (`opts.enabled`, and its own defaults block), `CSatellite`, `CNodeDisplayNightSky`, both `applyRefraction*` functions, the shared `refractionUniforms.uRefractionEnabled`, and `ensureRefractionSettings` — so the single flip reaches both halves: `ensureRefractionSettings` sets `Sit.refraction = Sit.refractionEnabled ?? REFRACTION_DEFAULTS.enabled` with `refractionSky` and `refractionTerrain` both true, and `applyRefractionMaster()` derives `refractionEnabled` and `terrestrialRefraction` from them. `TERRESTRIAL_REFRACTION_DEFAULTS.enabled` is deliberately left `false`; it is never the operative path, because `Sit.terrestrialRefraction` is always written by the master. WHO IS AFFECTED, and this is a behaviour change for MOST EXISTING SAVES rather than only for new sitches: `ensureRefractionSettings` preserves only a setting that was actually RECORDED in the file. A sitch saved by 2.113.0 or later serializes the master triple `refraction`/`refractionSky`/`refractionTerrain` (`CustomManagerSerialize.js` `SitNeeded`) and comes back exactly as saved. Older saves SPLIT, because the pre-master default-write in `CNodeDisplayNightSky`'s constructor was guarded — `if (Sit.refractionEnabled === undefined) Sit.refractionEnabled = REFRACTION_DEFAULTS.enabled;` — so the key only entered `Sit`, and hence the save (the serializer skips `undefined`), when that node happened to be constructed before the save was written. Measured across the 38 saved regression sitches: 14 carry `"refractionEnabled": false` alongside pressure 1010 / temp 10 — Qianfan Over UK and Europe, Rocket Launch Example, the satellite-mode and wind tests among them — and those come back OFF, since `Sit.refraction` is undefined and the `??` yields the recorded `false`. The other 24 contain no occurrence of the string `refract` anywhere in the file (e.g. *Moon terminator test*, 63,455 bytes, zero matches), so both `Sit.refraction` and `Sit.refractionEnabled` are undefined, the `??` falls through to the new default, and they come back ON. Corroborated independently by the fast visual regression suite, where 21 of 38 sitches changed their rendering on the flip and required baseline regeneration (38/38 pass afterwards) — a result only possible if saved sitches take the new default; the 21 sit inside the 24 keyless ones, the remaining 3 having nothing refraction-sensitive in frame. No file under `data/` sets a refraction flag, so every built-in and Featured sitch also takes the new default. `tests/refractionSettings.test.js` inverts its fresh-sitch assertion accordingly.
- **The terrestrial refraction sweep reaches models, tracks and LOS lines, and the material patcher is hardened** (`f10d8d27`, `ce88ace6`, merged as `a6c69bae`; `src/atmosphere/terrestrialRefraction.js` `sweepTerrestrialRefraction` / `excludeFromTerrestrialRefraction` / `NO_TERRESTRIAL_REFRACTION`, `src/atmosphere/refractionSettings.js`, `src/Globe.js`, `src/LongExposure.js`, `src/ModelLoader.js`, `src/nodes/CNode3DObject.js`, `CNodeSynthClouds.js`, `CNodeDisplayWindField.js`, `CNodeGroundOverlay.js`, `CNodeSpriteGroup.js`, `CNode3DLight.js`, `CNodeView3D.js`). 2.113.0 shipped with glTF models, Line2 tracks and LOS lines left geometric under lofted terrain; a pruned DFS in the scene hook now patches them. Pruned rather than `Object3D.traverse()`, which recurses unconditionally after its callback and so cannot skip a subtree — terrain and 3D tiles hold thousands of meshes already patched at creation. Measured in the Copenhagen sitch: 283 objects in 0.023 ms against 9,413 in 0.193 ms unpruned. Throttled to 2 Hz (`SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS` = 500) and skipped entirely when refraction is off, with `resetTerrestrialRefractionSweep()` forcing an immediate sweep when the terrain half is switched back on. 200 of 200 materials in scope are patched — 36 `LineMaterial`, 78 `MeshStandardMaterial`, plus sprites, points, phong, lambert and ten hand-written `ShaderMaterial`s (globe, ground overlay, flow orbs, synth clouds, wind field, model lights, gradient, PLY point cloud, Gaussian splats, aerial depth prepass), which share one GLSL entry point `applyTerrestrialRefraction_clip(mvPosition)` and one JS installer rather than ten bespoke edits. Four subtrees are excluded by flag, each for its own reason: satellites and their tracks (the dots are already CPU-refracted into `ecefApparent`, so warping again would add ~19' at 500 km on top of ~30' already applied); the CAPITALISED celestial arrow groups (pointing at directions Saemundsson has already bent — note lowercase `sunArrowGroup` is satellite-flare diagnostic geometry, excluded separately as an analytical construction); the Brocken glory (50–5000 m out, 0.17' at k = 0.13, below the width of the effect); and terrain/3D tiles, pruned for cost not correctness. The fallback globe is deliberately NOT lofted and `f10d8d27`'s warp of it is reverted: at 80×80 segments (~500 km per edge) a per-vertex warp is linearly interpolated across the edge, and the midpoint error is inherently about HALF the bend at that scale (~7'), barely responding to tessellation because finer edges shrink the bend they approximate too — 0.25' would need ~2860 segments and 16 million triangles. Four defects in the shipped patcher were fixed first, all of which bite only once the patch is applied broadly: the wrapper dropped `this` (Three invokes `onBeforeCompile` with the material as `this`, which `StableShadowReceiver`'s callback reads); it collapsed Three's program cache keys, because the default `customProgramCacheKey` returns `this.onBeforeCompile.toString()` and wrapping made every patched material report the same key, so a material carrying `patchMaterialForLinearOutput` could silently share a program with one that does not; clones inherited the install marker without the patch, since `Material.copy()` JSON-copies `userData` but not an instance's `onBeforeCompile` (state moved to a module-private `WeakSet`); and an unmatched shader was reported as success, leaving a custom projection silently geometric (the patcher now returns `{vertexShader, matched}` and warns once per material, naming it). The per-render uniform update moved to a chained `GlobalScene.onBeforeRender`, because `GlobalScene` is also rendered by the aerial-perspective depth prepass, the long-exposure occlusion mask, video export, scripted video, XR, and six times with six cameras by `CubeCamera.update()` — that last already captured env maps with whichever camera last wrote the uniforms. Sprites and fat lines get their own patterns since neither goes through `<project_vertex>`, and both keep a PHYSICAL copy of the view position restored before `<clipping_planes_vertex>` and `<fog_vertex>` so clipping and fog stay geometric. One trap recorded for the next person: the injection guard tested for the function NAME, so a shader that CALLS `applyTerrestrialRefraction_chunk` looked like it already had the definition — injection skipped, shader dead with "no matching overloaded function found", which took the synthetic clouds out of the Beaver sitch at 12.6% of the frame. Guarded on a definition-only marker comment now. That failure mode is invisible with refraction disabled, because it breaks at COMPILE time rather than at `uTerrK == 0`: the bit-identical-when-off guarantee protects the arithmetic, not the plumbing. Still deliberately absent: restricting the depth prepass and occlusion mask to a real occluder set — built and backed out, because layer masks are ASSIGNED wholesale in twenty-odd places so a dedicated layer bit is silently dropped (patching the two central propagators still left 138 of 2257 opaque meshes untagged, with a near-empty depth buffer as the failure mode).
- **SitrecBridge leases ports instead of owning them, and keeps the service worker alive** (`8f933f03`; `tools/SitrecBridge/lifecycle.js`, `mcp-server.js`, `diagnostics.js`, `extension/background.js`, `extension/content-script.js`, manifest 1.0.58 → 1.0.59). Developer tooling — the MCP bridge offered under **Help → Download MCP Bridge**, not part of the Sitrec app itself. Three defects made it need constant reconnecting. Ports leaked: every process that started an AI coding session bound a port at startup and held it until its parent died — measured 9 of 20 ports held, every one by a bridge that had never served a tool call, parents being pre-warm spares, remote-control instances and app-server daemons up to three days old (one held three, because Codex starts a bridge per conversation thread and never unsubscribes them). Reclaiming was fatal: with the pool full the only recovery was to kill a victim bridge, permanently destroying that session's MCP server, and a bridge that found no free port called `process.exit(1)`. And the MV3 service worker died every ~30 s, because the keepalive used WebSocket protocol ping frames, which Chrome answers in the network stack without waking the extension's JavaScript — a permanent sawtooth of worker death, socket closure and alarm-driven rebuild. A port is now a lease, released when unused (3 min if never used, 30 min after going quiet) and re-acquired transparently; releasing is not fatal, so peers ask for `/release` rather than shutdown and an unbound bridge stays alive retrying. Four things pin a lease — in-flight work, a paired sandbox origin, a connected Local Compute client, and being the extension's active fallback — honoured on both the voluntary and involuntary paths, and the oldest bound bridge anchors the range so it never goes empty (the Sitrec page discovers Local Compute by scanning ports directly, with no MCP call involved). Keepalive is application-level in both directions: a JSON server-ping every 10 s and a content-script port heartbeat every 20 s. Discovery drops from ≤30 s to ~4 s. Adds `sitrec_diagnostics`, answered locally so it works when the extension does not, reporting a port census naming which parent process holds each port and whether it has ever relayed a call, a JSONL trail merged across all bridge processes, and the extension's own log kept in `chrome.storage.local` so it survives the worker restarts that used to erase the console. Verified live: ports went 9/20 held (all unused) to 3/20 (all in use). The keepalive fix needs an extension reload to take effect.

### Bug Fixes
- **Fixed terrestrial refraction lofting the Earth from an elevated viewpoint** (`src/atmosphere/terrestrialRefraction.js` `atmosphericDensityFactor` / `pathDensityFactor` / `saturateLift` / `ellipsoidAltitude`, `TERRESTRIAL_REFRACTION_DEFAULTS.scaleHeightM` = 8500 and `maxLiftM` = 3 × 8500, uniforms `uTerrObsAlt` / `uTerrInvH` / `uTerrMaxLift`, GLSL `sitrecPathDensity`; `tests/terrestrialRefraction.test.js`). Exposed by turning refraction on by default. The shader applied `lift = d * bend`, and while `bend` saturated at `maxBendRad` (34') the LIFT did not — `d * maxBend` grows linearly with range forever, about 9.9 km per 1000 km — and nothing in the model knew the observer's or the target's height, so the full surface `k` was charged over a sight line that is mostly vacuum. Measured in the default sitch, main camera at 237.3 km: the visible limb of the Earth lofted 15,578 m and the far limb 62,684 m. Two layers fix it. First, `k` is scaled by the MEAN relative air density along the path, `mean = H*(e^(-h1/H) - e^(-h2/H))/(h2-h1)` with `H` = 8500 m, the pressure scale height — `k` carries pressure linearly, so the ray's curvature dies away on the same scale the air does. A ray only curves where there is air. The limits are the point of it: ground-to-ground returns EXACTLY 1 (asserted with `toBe`, not `toBeCloseTo`), observer high and target low returns `H/h_obs`, and both endpoints above the air returns ~0. Measured attenuation: 0 km → 1.0000, 1 km → 0.9434, 4 km → 0.7977, 9.96 km → 0.5890, 237 km → 0.0358. This is first-order — it takes P's exponential fall-off and holds `k`'s temperature and gradient terms fixed, capturing where the air IS but not how the lapse rate varies with height, which is the dominant term by a wide margin and was missing entirely. Second, the lift itself saturates at `maxLiftM` using the same algebraic sigmoid `u/sqrt(1+u^2)` as the bend angle, so the two saturators behave alike and neither creases the terrain; three scale heights (25.5 km) is far outside the surveying law's regime — a ground observer at their 300 km horizon lifts ~1.2 km — so it never bites on real geometry, and even at the far end of what a ground observer can see it shaves ~0.1% (1.3 m in 1200), orders of magnitude under the spread in `k` itself. In the shader the target's height is recovered as `uTerrObsAlt + upComponent + 0.5*d*d*uTerrInvR`: `upComponent` is the rise above the observer's tangent PLANE, and the ground falls away from that plane by `d^2/(2R)`, so adding the curvature drop back puts an equal-altitude target at the observer's own altitude, as it must. `uTerrObsAlt` is published per camera from `ellipsoidAltitude(cameraWorldPosition)` — `updateTerrestrialRefractionUniforms` is called from the scene's `onBeforeRender`, which fires once per view per frame, so the space view and the cockpit view of the same scene each get their own observer altitude; `uTerrInvH` and `uTerrMaxLift` are set alongside it but are constants. `ellipsoidAltitude` is the RADIAL height along the position's own direction rather than a geodetic solution, needing no latitude iteration, and agrees with a Bowring closed-form inverse to 0 m at 10 km and 1 m at 237 km — ample for a quantity only ever fed to `exp(-h/H)`. It is NOT interchangeable with `|pos| - equatorRadius`, which is wrong by the ellipsoid's latitude variation, 6 km at mid-latitudes, enough to put a 10 km camera at "4 km". Net measured effect: visible-limb lift 15,578 m → 1,404 m, an 11.1x reduction, and the main view is visually indistinguishable with refraction on versus off from orbit. USER-VISIBLE CAVEAT: an ELEVATED observer now gets LESS bend than 2.113.0 gave, because the air above is thinner — the default sitch's look camera at 9.96 km drops to 0.589x its previous bend. Ground-level observers are exactly unchanged. This is a correction, not a regression, but a re-run of an elevated-camera analysis will produce a different number. 22 new tests; `sitrecPathDensity` in the GLSL is the twin of `pathDensityFactor` and the two must stay in step, or the scene renders differently from every number the CPU side reports about it.
- **Fixed a mask saved with a sitch not being in effect when the sitch is reopened** (`36370c8f`; `src/nodes/CNodeMaskOverlay.js` `scheduleMaskRestore` / `removeMaskRestoreListener` / `loadMask` / `encodeMaskForSave`, `SAVED_MASK_MAX_WIDTH` = 1024). Two separate faults, one of them latent since the mask was first serialized. `modDeserialize` runs BEFORE the video has loaded, so there were no dimensions to size a canvas to and the restored pixels sat in `maskData` doing nothing — `maskImageData` null, `isPointMasked` false for every point — until some user action happened to call `ensureMaskInitialized` and let `initMask` redraw them. The node now waits on the `"videoAvailabilityChanged"` event and removes its own listener once the canvas exists, so a later video swap cannot resurrect an old mask behind the clear-on-import path added in 2.113.0. Separately, `loadMask` drew the saved image 1:1, which was silently correct only while the saved copy matched the canvas; it now scales to the canvas as `initMask` already did. Both were exposed by capping the SAVED copy at 1024 px wide: the mask was serialized at the video's own resolution — 760 KB of base64 for a 5472-wide frame, rewritten on EVERY brush stroke — against 67 KB at 1024, an 11x saving. Not a compromise: a mask is a coarse region map, `initMask` already rescales a restored one, and every consumer thresholds at alpha > 128. The ratio beats the pixel count because PNG compresses flat runs almost for free and nearly all the bytes go on the boundary, which is exactly the detail the alpha threshold discards.
- **Fixed a sitch saved with the look camera synced to the star field coming back unsynced** (`36370c8f`; `src/starTrack/StarTrackerUI.js` `CNodeControllerStarTrack.bakeFrom` / `posesAt` / `modSerialize` / `modDeserialize`, `makeStarTrackCameraController`, `attachStarTrackCamera`; `src/CustomManagerSetup.js`). The camera track is now BAKED to plain numbers at Sync Camera time — four numbers per analysed frame, the sky position of the frame's centre and of a point above it, giving boresight and roll together — because the live path read `result.identify.solved.refToSky`, a CLOSURE over the plate solution rather than data, which no amount of serialization could carry. Baking also frees a saved track from the solver that made it, so it survives changes to the solver, the lens model or the identify stage, at the price of being frozen, which is the right trade for a recorded result. Rounded to 5 decimal places of a degree (~36 mas, far finer than the solve) because full float precision would triple the saved size for digits that are noise. `starTrackCameraController` is now created up front in `CustomManagerSetup` alongside `videoMask`, since a mod is only ever applied to a node that already EXISTS — created empty and inert, with `apply()` returning immediately and no dropdown entry until it has a track. `attachStarTrackCamera` is shared by Sync Camera and by the controller's own `modDeserialize`, so a reloaded sitch takes exactly the path a freshly synced one does; its `select` argument is false on restore, leaving `CNodeSwitch`'s `pendingChoice` to reinstate the saved choice, so a sitch saved on *Manual* comes back on *Manual* even though a track is present. Attachment is tested on `lookCamera.inputs[controller.id]` because controllers are attached as INPUTS, and attaching twice would run the pose twice per frame; *Tracking Wobble* is kept last, since an absolute pose applied before it would be wobbled and applied after it would wipe the wobble.
- **Fixed documentation that was factually wrong** (`0b005576`; `docs/GIS.md`, `docs/Tracks.md`, `docs/UserInterface.md`, `docs/Football.md`, `docs/CustomModels.md`, `docs/Wind.md`, `docs/satcam.md`). Four persona reviews all made the same criticism of the docs plan — it asked "what is thin?" and never "what is wrong?". Each fix verified against the implementing source. `GIS.md` said KML absolute altitudes are "treated as HAE"; they are treated as MSL and the geoid IS added (`CTrackFileKML` → `TrackManager` → `CTrackFile.isAltitudeHAE = false`), so acting on the doc applied a compensating offset that DOUBLED the error, ~60 m in CONUS. Also in `GIS.md`: the HAE→MSL sign (`H = h - N`), pressure-altitude magnitudes understated ~3x, a wrong worked example, the geoid range, the stale egm96-universal claim, and 3DEP's datum (NAVD88). `Tracks.md` said the altitude lock is MSL; `AltitudeLock.js` says HAE. `UserInterface.md` said hold Shift to move a view — the key is Q, and `CNodeView.js` explicitly collapsed the old Shift gesture onto it, so the documented gesture did nothing; the stale terrain section was rewritten and "Export Custom/Mod" removed, commented out since Save/Save As replaced it. `Football.md` gave 96°/42° where `Football.js` says 121.4/38, and now carries the code's own disclosure that key values are estimates chosen to reproduce the described flight, plus the evidentiary dispute it had omitted. Smaller: the splat PLY header in `CustomModels.md` (`scale_0`/`rot_0`, not Sitrec's internal names), generic-CSV aliases in `Tracks.md`, wind altitude is HAE, satcam's "up" is the ellipsoid normal, and the AI was being told `.gltf` imports when it does not. REPORTED BUT NOT FIXED, being behaviour changes rather than doc errors: `elevationScale` multiplies the geoid undulation along with the terrain (`QuadTreeMapElevation.js`; correct form is `N + zScale*H`, ~35 m error per unit in CONUS, and `CustomTerrainSources.md` tells users to set it to 10); and camera FOV is excluded from the traverse-analysis cache fingerprint (`AnalyzeTraverse.js`), which is sound for boresight LOS but wrong for pixel-derived LOS, where changing FOV can serve a stale gallery.
- **Fixed every anchored link in the generated documentation pages landing nowhere** (`0b005576`; `webpack.common.js` `rewriteMdLinks` / `addHeadingIds`). The `.md` → `.html` rewrite required a literal `".md)"`, so a link written as `Foo.md#some-heading` was left pointing at the raw markdown file, which the browser renders as plain text instead of opening the page. The pattern now carries a trailing anchor through. That exposed the other half: `markdown-it` emits bare `<h1>`–`<h6>` with no `id`, so even a correctly rewritten fragment had nothing to jump to. GitHub-style slug ids are now added after rendering, decoding the entities markdown-it emits so "What's New" slugs to `whats-new` rather than `what39s-new`, and disambiguating repeats with `-1`, `-2` as GitHub does.
